questions.stem: A pathologist reviewing a tumor specimen explains to a student that all of the cancer cells in the mass descend from a single 'mother' cell and are essentially copies of that original cell. This description best captures which fundamental property that defines neoplasia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Physiologic increase in cell number in response to demand

choices.label: B
choices.text: Polyclonal proliferation of several cell lineages

choices.label: C
choices.text: Programmed cell death of damaged cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reversible adaptive replacement of one cell type by another

explanation.summary: Neoplasia is the unregulated, monoclonal proliferation of cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neoplasia literally means 'new growth' and refers to the unregulated monoclonal proliferation of cells. Monoclonal means the descendant cells all derive from a single original 'mother' cell and are copies of it, which is exactly the scenario described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This describes hyperplasia, a controlled physiologic response, not the unregulated growth of a neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neoplasms are monoclonal, not polyclonal; they arise from one transformed cell, not multiple separate lineages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This describes apoptosis, which is unrelated to the definition of a tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This describes metaplasia, an adaptive change, not neoplasia.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has a lung mass biopsied. The pathology report notes cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, pleomorphism, and frequent mitotic figures, and states that the tumor has invaded adjacent tissue and seeded a distant lymph node. Which single feature most specifically establishes that this tumor is malignant rather than benign?

choices.label: D
choices.text: A rapid overall rate of growth

explanation.summary: The potential for metastasis is the characteristic feature that defines a malignant tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the potential for metastasis is the characteristic feature of a malignant tumor. Benign tumors, by definition, cannot metastasize. Spread to a distant lymph node therefore establishes malignancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Poor prognosis frequently accompanies malignancy but is a consequence, not the defining feature.
whyWrongByChoice.B: High mitotic activity is common in malignancy but is a supportive finding, not the defining characteristic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pleomorphism is a cytologic feature of malignant cells but does not by itself define malignancy the way metastatic potential does.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Malignant tumors often grow quickly, but growth rate alone is not the defining feature; some benign tumors also grow.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman develops progressive headaches, seizures, and a visual field deficit. Imaging shows a well-circumscribed extra-axial mass arising from the meninges, and resection confirms a meningioma with no evidence of invasion or metastasis. Which principle best explains how this histologically benign tumor produced life-threatening symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A benign tumor can compress vital structures

choices.label: B
choices.text: Benign tumors always contain large areas of necrosis that damage the brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Benign tumors frequently transform into carcinoma within the skull

choices.label: D
choices.text: Benign tumors typically lack a capsule and therefore invade brain tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor must have metastasized to the brain to cause seizures

explanation.summary: Benign tumors can still be dangerous by compressing adjacent structures, especially in confined spaces like the skull.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that benign tumors are not necessarily harmless: a meningioma is a benign tumor of the meninges that can compress brain tissue and cause neurologic problems such as seizures, paralysis, and vision changes. The limited space of the skull makes benign brain tumors particularly dangerous.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Benign tumors typically do not contain areas of necrosis; that is a feature of malignant tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Benign tumors do not routinely transform into carcinoma; the harm here is from mass effect, not malignant transformation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Benign tumors are usually well demarcated and often encapsulated; they generally do not invade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no metastasis; the symptoms result from local compression of brain tissue.

questions.stem: A biopsy of a uterine mass is reported as a leiomyosarcoma. Applying the standard rules of tumor nomenclature, which of the following is true of this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a benign tumor of glandular cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a benign tumor of smooth muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a malignant tumor of epithelial origin

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a malignant tumor of skeletal muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a malignant tumor of smooth muscle

explanation.summary: 'Leiomyo-' denotes smooth muscle and the '-sarcoma' suffix denotes a malignant mesenchymal tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: In tumor nomenclature the prefix indicates the cell of origin (leiomyo- = smooth muscle) and the suffix indicates the nature. Sarcoma is added for malignant tumors of mesenchymal tissue, so leiomyosarcoma is a malignant smooth muscle tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A benign glandular tumor is an adenoma; leiomyo- refers to smooth muscle, not glands.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A benign smooth muscle tumor would be a leiomyoma (-oma), not a sarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malignant epithelial tumors carry the suffix carcinoma, not sarcoma; smooth muscle is mesenchymal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Skeletal muscle uses the prefix rhabdomyo-; leiomyo- specifically denotes smooth muscle.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a 10-year history of chronic acid reflux undergoes endoscopy. Biopsy of the distal esophagus shows that the normal stratified squamous epithelium has been replaced by simple columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. This change is best classified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Barrett esophagus is metaplasia: squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium in response to chronic acid injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metaplasia is the replacement of one cell type by another as an adaptive response to chronic stress. In Barrett esophagus, chronic gastric acid exposure leads the squamous esophageal epithelium to be replaced by protective mucus-secreting columnar epithelium with goblet cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anaplasia refers to undifferentiated tumor cells that do not resemble any tissue of origin, not an orderly epithelial switch.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carcinoma in situ requires cancerous cells confined by the basement membrane; the described cells are non-neoplastic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dysplasia is disordered growth of atypical cells; here one mature cell type is orderly replaced by another, which is metaplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Invasive adenocarcinoma is a later complication that can arise in a minority of untreated cases, but the biopsy shows metaplasia, not invasion.

questions.stem: A cervical biopsy shows epithelial cells with marked pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, loss of polarity, and disorderly architecture, but the changes do not extend through the full thickness and no invasion is present. The likelihood of this lesion progressing to cancer is most directly related to which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The presence or absence of a fibrous capsule

choices.label: C
choices.text: The size of the biopsy specimen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether the tissue is epithelial or mesenchymal

explanation.summary: The degree of dysplasia is directly correlated with the likelihood of developing cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes a spectrum of dysplasia (mild, moderate, severe; CIN I to CIN III) and states that the degree of dysplasia is directly correlated with the likelihood of developing cancer. Mild dysplasia may revert to normal, whereas severe dysplasia carries a very high chance that cancer will follow.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A capsule is a feature of benign tumors, not a determinant of dysplastic progression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The size of the biopsy is a sampling parameter and has no bearing on cancer risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Differentiation describes how tumor cells resemble their origin; the dysplasia grade, not differentiation, predicts progression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue class matters for naming a resulting cancer, but it is the severity of dysplasia that predicts progression here.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman has an abnormal Pap smear followed by a cervical biopsy read as carcinoma in situ. Which feature most accurately characterizes this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cancer cells have not breached the basement membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cancer cells have penetrated the basement membrane into underlying tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lesion has already metastasized to regional lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lesion is a benign tumor that cannot become invasive

choices.label: E
choices.text: The lesion represents an adaptive, fully reversible change

explanation.summary: Carcinoma in situ is cancer that remains confined by the basement membrane and is therefore pre-invasive (stage 0).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines carcinoma in situ as cells that are cancerous but pre-invasive: they have not broken through the basement membrane into underlying tissue. It is the earliest stage of cancer (stage 0), and removal at this point is curative because the tumor has not metastasized.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Once cells breach the basement membrane the lesion becomes invasive carcinoma, not carcinoma in situ.
whyWrongByChoice.C: By definition CIS has not metastasized; that is why excision is curative.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CIS is a true early cancer, not a benign tumor, and can progress to invasive cancer if untreated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CIS cells are already cancerous, unlike a reversible adaptive change such as metaplasia.

questions.stem: Two patients have malignant tumors of the same organ. Tumor A is composed of cells that closely resemble the normal cells of that organ, whereas Tumor B is composed of cells so primitive that the tissue of origin cannot be identified. Based on differentiation, which statement is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both tumors must be benign because they arose from normal tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Differentiation has no relationship to prognosis in malignant tumors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tumor A is anaplastic and Tumor B is well-differentiated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tumor A is well-differentiated and tends to carry a better prognosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor B is well-differentiated and carries a better prognosis

explanation.summary: Well-differentiated malignant tumors resemble their origin and generally have a better prognosis than poorly differentiated or anaplastic tumors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Differentiation is the degree to which tumor cells resemble their normal counterparts. Tumor A's cells look like the normal organ, so it is well-differentiated; Tumor B's cells show no resemblance and are anaplastic/undifferentiated. Well-differentiated malignant tumors tend to have a better prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both are explicitly malignant; resemblance to normal tissue reflects differentiation, not benignity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Differentiation is prognostically important: better differentiation is associated with better outcomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the terms: cells resembling the origin are well-differentiated, while unrecognizable cells are anaplastic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor B is anaplastic, not well-differentiated, and carries a worse prognosis.

questions.stem: A tumor arising from the glandular epithelium of the colon is found to invade through the bowel wall. Using the standard rules of tumor nomenclature, this malignant tumor is best termed which of the following?

explanation.summary: A malignant tumor of glandular (epithelial) cells is an adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glandular cells are epithelial. Malignant tumors of epithelial tissue take the suffix carcinoma, and the prefix adeno- denotes glandular origin, giving adenocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Adenoma (-oma) is the benign glandular tumor; this lesion is malignant and invasive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sarcoma applies to malignant mesenchymal tumors, not epithelial glands.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A hamartoma is a non-neoplastic disorganized mass, not a malignant glandular tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant smooth muscle tumor, unrelated to glandular epithelium.

questions.stem: A routine chest radiograph in a 50-year-old man reveals a solitary pulmonary nodule. Resection shows a well-circumscribed mass composed of disorganized but mature cartilage, fat, and respiratory epithelium that are all cell types normally found in the lung. This lesion is best classified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: A hamartoma is a non-neoplastic, disorganized mass of tissue elements indigenous to the site.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hamartomas are non-neoplastic regions of disorganized tissue that are indigenous to the organ in which they are found. A pulmonary hamartoma is a localized area of disorganized but native tissue (such as cartilage) within the lung. Despite the -oma suffix, it is not a true neoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenocarcinoma is a malignant glandular tumor with invasion, not a well-circumscribed mass of mature native tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carcinoma in situ is early confined cancer, whereas this lesion is non-neoplastic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A choristoma is normal tissue in an abnormal location; here the tissue is native to the lung, making it a hamartoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A papilloma is a benign epithelial neoplasm with finger-like projections, not disorganized cartilage and fat.

questions.stem: During surgery, a small nodule of microscopically normal thyroid tissue is discovered within the thymus of a patient with no thyroid disease. Which term best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: A choristoma is growth of microscopically normal cells in an abnormal location.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines a choristoma as the growth of microscopically normal cells in an abnormal location. A nodule of normal-appearing thyroid tissue located within the thymus is the classic example given.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An adenoma is a benign glandular neoplasm, whereas this tissue is normal and non-neoplastic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A hamartoma is disorganized tissue that is native (indigenous) to the site; thyroid tissue is not native to the thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metaplasia is replacement of one cell type by another at a single site, not normal tissue appearing at an ectopic site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A teratoma contains tissues from multiple germ layers; this is a single focus of normal thyroid tissue.

questions.stem: A dermatologist removes a pigmented skin lesion and, when discussing tumor terminology, notes that a benign tumor of these cells is conventionally given a name that would normally suggest malignancy for other tissues. Which pair correctly reflects this naming exception for melanocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both the benign and malignant tumors are called melanomas

choices.label: B
choices.text: The benign tumor is a melanocarcinoma and the malignant tumor is a nevus

choices.label: C
choices.text: The benign tumor is a melanoma and the malignant tumor is a nevus

choices.label: D
choices.text: The benign tumor is a nevus and the malignant tumor is a melanoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: The benign tumor is a papilloma and the malignant tumor is a melanoma

explanation.summary: The benign melanocytic tumor is a nevus, while melanoma denotes the malignant form.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that a nevus (mole) is a benign tumor of melanocytes. By the usual rules a benign melanocyte tumor would be called a 'melanoma,' but for historical reasons the term melanoma is reserved for the malignant version, so the benign tumor is called a nevus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only the malignant tumor is called melanoma; the benign tumor is a nevus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 'Melanocarcinoma' is not the standard term; the benign melanocytic tumor is a nevus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the terms; melanoma is the malignant form and nevus is benign.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A papilloma is a benign epithelial tumor, not a melanocytic lesion.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Bimanual examination reveals a 6-cm uterine mass, and transvaginal ultrasound shows a hyperechoic mass. Endometrial biopsy shows uterine smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts with a large amount of extracellular matrix and no evidence of cancer. Which of the following is the most accurate term for this lesion?

explanation.summary: A uterine fibroid is a benign, localized growth of uterine smooth muscle, properly termed a leiomyoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: A uterine fibroid is the growth of uterine smooth muscle that is not cancer. By the rules of benign tumor nomenclature, leiomyo- (smooth muscle) plus the suffix -oma gives leiomyoma. Benign means the growth is localized and will not spread or metastasize, which matches the biopsy showing smooth muscle cells with no evidence of cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumor of glandular epithelium, not a benign smooth muscle growth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A sarcoma is malignant by definition; this lesion is benign, and its dominant cell type is smooth muscle rather than fibrous tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leiomyosarcoma is the malignant smooth muscle tumor; the biopsy shows no evidence of cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rhabdomyo- refers to skeletal muscle, whereas the uterus contains smooth muscle.

questions.stem: A medical student notices that an older textbook uses the word 'tumor' to describe an inflamed, swollen joint, whereas a modern pathology text uses the same word only for neoplasms. Which statement best explains this discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 'Tumor' once meant any mass or swelling, and its definition has since narrowed

choices.label: B
choices.text: The modern text is incorrect because 'tumor' still formally includes all swellings

choices.label: C
choices.text: The older text confuses 'tumor' with 'metaplasia,' which describes swelling

choices.label: D
choices.text: The older text is using a term that only ever referred to malignant lesions

choices.label: E
choices.text: The word 'tumor' has always been restricted to monoclonal proliferations of cells

explanation.summary: 'Tumor' originally described any mass or swelling, but today it is used only for neoplastic masses of tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although neoplasm is the most accurate medical term, tumor is often used instead. Originally the word tumor described a mass or swelling of any kind, but over time the definition narrowed, and today it describes only neoplastic masses of tissue. The terms tumor and neoplasm are now used interchangeably.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The modern usage is the accepted one; tumor now refers to neoplastic masses, not all swellings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metaplasia is the replacement of one cell type by another and has nothing to do with swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The historical meaning of tumor was any swelling, not a term restricted to malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Monoclonal proliferation defines neoplasia; the word tumor only later narrowed to that meaning.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman undergoes resection of a thyroid nodule. Histology shows a well-differentiated glandular tumor completely surrounded by a fibrous rim, with a small amount of normal thyroid tissue at the periphery of the specimen. The surgeon reports that the lesion 'shelled out' easily and that the prognosis is excellent. Which feature of this tumor best accounts for its ease of removal?

explanation.summary: Benign tumors such as a thyroid adenoma are usually surrounded by a capsule, which makes them more surgically removable and improves prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Benign tumors are usually surrounded by a capsule, making them more surgically removable and leading to a better prognosis. The brick's thyroid adenoma is shown surrounded by a capsule with normal thyroid tissue adjacent, exactly as this specimen is described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Benign tumors do not contain areas of necrosis; necrosis is a feature of malignant tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Benign tumors have little mitotic activity; high mitotic activity is a malignant feature and would not aid removal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Invasion is a malignant behavior and would work against clean surgical removal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Benign tumors are well demarcated; poorly demarcated borders characterize malignant tumors and make removal harder.

questions.stem: A pathology report on a lung biopsy notes that the tumor nuclei show marked 'pleomorphism.' Which of the following does this term describe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of keratin within the tumor cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: An increased ratio of nuclear to cytoplasmic volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Presence of numerous cells arrested in mitosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replacement of one cell type by another

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variation in the size and shape of the nuclei

explanation.summary: Pleomorphism is variation in nuclear size and shape, one of the cytologic features of malignant tumor cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's figure of malignant tumor cells labels nuclear pleomorphism as variation in size and shape. It is listed alongside increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, large cells with open chromatin, and increased mitotic activity as the cytologic features of malignancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Keratin accumulations are keratin pearls, associated with squamous cell carcinoma, not a nuclear feature.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This describes the increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, a distinct feature from pleomorphism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cells arrested in mitosis are mitotic figures, a separate feature indicating increased mitotic activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Replacement of one cell type by another is metaplasia, not a cytologic feature of a tumor cell.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has a colonic tumor that has grown directly through the bowel wall into the surrounding mesenteric fat. Extensive imaging shows no tumor in lymph nodes, liver, or lungs. Which term most precisely describes the behavior demonstrated by this tumor?

explanation.summary: Invasion is local growth of a tumor into surrounding tissue, whereas metastasis is spread to distant sites.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's terminology table defines invasion as local growth of a tumor into surrounding tissue and metastasis as spread of a tumor to distant sites in the body. Growth through the bowel wall into adjacent fat without disease at distant sites is invasion, not metastasis. Malignant tumors are those that can invade tissues or spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anaplasia describes the differentiation of tumor cells, not their pattern of local growth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carcinoma in situ has not broken through the basement membrane; this tumor has grown through the entire wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metaplasia is an adaptive replacement of one cell type by another, not tumor growth into adjacent tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metastasis requires spread to distant sites, and imaging shows none.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has a soft-tissue mass excised from his thigh. Two years later the mass regrows at the same site, and it fails to shrink with chemotherapy. Based on the standard definitions of tumor behavior, which of the following is most likely true of this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a choristoma, because ectopic normal tissue is resistant to chemotherapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a hamartoma, because disorganized native tissue regrows after removal

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is benign, because benign tumors characteristically recur after excision

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is malignant, because such tumors may resist treatment and recur after removal

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is metaplastic, because adaptive changes return when the stressor persists

explanation.summary: Malignant tumors may be resistant to treatment and recur after removal, in addition to their potential to metastasize.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's terminology table defines a malignant tumor as one that may metastasize, may be resistant to treatment, and may recur after removal. A mass that regrows after excision and does not respond to chemotherapy displays these malignant behaviors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A choristoma is microscopically normal tissue in an abnormal location and is not described as recurring or resisting therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A hamartoma is a non-neoplastic, usually harmless region of disorganized native tissue; recurrence with treatment resistance is not how the brick characterizes it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Benign tumors are localized lesions that are usually encapsulated and surgically removable with a better prognosis; recurrence and treatment resistance are malignant features.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metaplasia is a reversible replacement of one cell type by another, not a mass that recurs after excision.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a long smoking history has a biopsy of an oral mass. The tumor cells are polygonal with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, and there are rounded accumulations of keratin within the nests of tumor cells. A strip of normal stratified squamous epithelium is present at the edge of the specimen for comparison. Which of the following best describes this tumor?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Benign squamous papilloma with papillary fronds

explanation.summary: Polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and keratin pearls indicate a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's example of a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma describes tumor cells that are polygonal with a lot of eosinophilic cytoplasm, like normal squamous cells. Keratin pearls are accumulations of keratin associated with tumors like squamous cell carcinoma. Because the cells closely resemble their squamous cell of origin, the tumor is well-differentiated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An anaplastic tumor does not resemble its tissue of origin at all; these cells clearly resemble squamous epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A papilloma is a benign epithelial tumor with a finger-like papillary growth pattern, not a carcinoma with keratin pearls.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chondrosarcoma is a cartilage-derived tumor and would resemble cartilage, not keratinizing squamous cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adenocarcinoma arises from glandular cells; keratin pearls and eosinophilic polygonal cells point to squamous origin.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a large tumor resected from the femur. On one side of the specimen, the tumor cells sit in lacunae within a bluish matrix and clearly resemble hyaline cartilage. On the other side, sheets of cells show no features that would allow a pathologist to identify their cell type without seeing the rest of the specimen. Which term best describes this tumor?

explanation.summary: A cartilage-derived malignant tumor containing both a cartilage-like component and an anaplastic component is a de-differentiated chondrosarcoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick illustrates de-differentiated chondrosarcoma, a tumor derived from cartilage cells that contains both a well-differentiated component that still resembles cartilage and a de-differentiated/anaplastic component whose cells do not resemble cartilage at all. Without the rest of the picture it would be hard to say what those anaplastic cells are, which is the true definition of de-differentiation/anaplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A hamartoma is non-neoplastic disorganized native tissue and would not contain undifferentiated cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dysplasia refers to disordered growth in epithelial cells that precedes cancer, not an anaplastic component within a mesenchymal tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metaplasia is the replacement of one cell type by another in non-neoplastic tissue, not a tumor with an anaplastic component.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An osteoma is a benign tumor of bone; this tumor is derived from cartilage and contains an anaplastic component, indicating malignancy.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is told his prostate biopsy shows adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score, and that further imaging is needed to determine the extent of disease. His son asks what the score means. Which of the following most accurately distinguishes what the tumor's grade conveys from what its stage conveys?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grade and stage both reflect degree of differentiation but use different scales

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grade reflects response to treatment; stage reflects the mitotic rate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grade reflects the cell of origin; stage reflects whether the tumor is encapsulated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grade reflects the microscopic appearance; stage reflects size and spread

choices.label: E
choices.text: Grade reflects tumor size and spread; stage reflects the microscopic appearance

explanation.summary: Grade describes how a tumor looks under the microscope (including differentiation); stage describes its size and how far it has spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor grading is a histological tool that incorporates the degree of differentiation of a cancer, among other things, with specific systems such as Gleason grading for prostate cancer. Grading is not the same as staging: the grade refers to the way a tumor looks under the microscope, while the stage refers to its size and the degree to which it has spread (metastasized).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only grade incorporates differentiation; stage is about size and spread.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Treatment response and mitotic rate are not the definitions of grade and stage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither grade nor stage is defined by the cell of origin or by encapsulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the two concepts; size and spread define stage, not grade.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule resected. Microscopically, the tumor cells form follicles that look nearly identical to normal thyroid tissue, with minimal pleomorphism and rare mitoses. Despite this appearance, the pathologist reports the lesion as malignant. Which finding most likely allowed this determination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio in most cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: A thick fibrous capsule surrounding the nodule

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complete absence of any recognizable follicles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Large areas of necrosis within the nodule

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor cells invading adjacent tissue and blood vessels

explanation.summary: The malignant nature of a well-differentiated tumor is usually revealed by invasion of adjacent tissues and the ability to metastasize.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick asks how we can tell that a well-differentiated tumor is malignant and answers that the malignant nature of those tumors is usually revealed by their invasion of adjacent tissues and their ability to metastasize. Malignant tumors can be anywhere on the differentiation spectrum, so resemblance to normal tissue does not exclude malignancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stem specifies minimal cytologic atypia; a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio is a cytologic feature, not what reveals malignancy in a well-differentiated tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A capsule is characteristic of benign tumors and would not establish malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Absence of recognizable structure would indicate anaplasia, contradicting the well-differentiated appearance described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Necrosis is a feature that malignant tumors often show, but the stem describes a well-differentiated tumor, and it is invasion that establishes malignancy in that setting.

questions.stem: A researcher studying bronchial biopsies from smokers observes that regions of ciliated columnar epithelium have been replaced by squamous epithelium. A colleague proposes that the mature columnar cells themselves transform directly into squamous cells. Which statement best describes how this change actually occurs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Columnar cells accumulate keratin and flatten into squamous cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Columnar cells undergo malignant transformation into carcinoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mature columnar cells directly convert into squamous cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Squamous cells migrate in from the adjacent skin surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stem cells start producing a different cell type

explanation.summary: In metaplasia the cells do not change from one type to another; the change occurs at the stem cell level.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that in metaplasia the cells don't actually change from one type to another. Instead, the change occurs at the stem cell level: instead of producing the normal cell type, the stem cells start producing cells of a different type. Airway epithelial metaplasia in response to irritants is one of the two classic examples.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Keratin accumulation is not the mechanism; the new cell type is generated by stem cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metaplasia is an adaptive, typically reversible change, not malignant transformation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is the misconception the brick explicitly corrects; mature cells do not convert directly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metaplasia arises from local stem cells reprogramming their output, not from migration of cells from another site.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history has a bronchial biopsy showing squamous metaplasia of the airway epithelium. He quits smoking completely. Which of the following is the most likely fate of the metaplastic epithelium over the following years?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion into a hamartoma of disorganized native tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Permanent persistence because metaplasia is inherently irreversible

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progression to anaplastic carcinoma regardless of cessation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reversion to the original epithelial type once the stressor is removed

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transformation into columnar epithelium with goblet cells

explanation.summary: Metaplasia is typically reversible: if the stressor is removed, the cells can revert to their original type.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metaplasia often occurs as an adaptive change in response to repeated or chronic cell stress. Typically it is reversible, meaning that if the stressor is removed, the cells can revert back to their original type. Removing the irritant (cigarette smoke) is therefore expected to allow the airway epithelium to revert.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A hamartoma is a non-neoplastic developmental mass of native tissue, unrelated to metaplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metaplasia is described as typically reversible, not inherently irreversible.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Progression is not inevitable; the brick's figure shows the change becomes irreversible only if the chronic irritant persists.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Columnar epithelium with goblet cells describes Barrett esophagus, not the outcome of airway metaplasia after stressor removal.

questions.stem: A biopsy of the trachea from a long-term smoker shows that the normal lining epithelium has been replaced by a different epithelial type as an adaptation to chronic irritation. Which of the following correctly identifies the normal epithelium and the epithelium that replaces it in this form of metaplasia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pseudostratified columnar replaced by squamous epithelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Simple columnar replaced by pseudostratified columnar epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Simple cuboidal replaced by transitional epithelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Squamous epithelium replaced by ciliated columnar epithelium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stratified squamous replaced by simple columnar with goblet cells

explanation.summary: In airway epithelial metaplasia, the pseudostratified columnar epithelium of the airways undergoes squamous metaplasia in response to irritants.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick names airway epithelial metaplasia as one of two classic examples of metaplasia: the pseudostratified columnar epithelium of the airways undergoes squamous metaplasia in response to irritants.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pseudostratified columnar is the normal airway epithelium that is lost, not the replacement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither cuboidal nor transitional epithelium is involved in airway metaplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the direction of the change; the airway starts as columnar and becomes squamous.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is the change in Barrett esophagus, the other classic example, in which esophageal squamous epithelium becomes columnar.

questions.stem: A pathology instructor shows two slides of the same organ. Slide 1 shows an orderly epithelium in which the expected cell type has been replaced by a different, but normal-appearing, mature cell type. Slide 2 shows the expected cell type, but the cells are abnormal-looking and piled on top of each other. Which of the following correctly pairs each slide with the type of change it represents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Slide 1 shows a change in cell number; Slide 2 shows a change in cell size

choices.label: B
choices.text: Slide 1 shows a change in cell structure; Slide 2 shows a change in cell type

choices.label: C
choices.text: Slide 1 shows a change in cell type; Slide 2 shows a change in cell structure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slide 1 shows atrophy; Slide 2 shows hypertrophy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Slide 1 shows neoplasia; Slide 2 shows hyperplasia

explanation.summary: Metaplasia is a change in cell type, whereas dysplasia is a change in cell structure (disordered growth).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's figure of cellular adaptations shows that metaplasia is a change in cell type, whereas dysplasia is a change in cell structure; both are reversible responses of normal cells. Slide 1, with one mature cell type replacing another, is metaplasia; Slide 2, with abnormal-appearing cells showing disorderly architecture, is dysplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A change in cell number is hyperplasia and a change in cell size is hypertrophy or atrophy; neither slide shows these.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the pairing; metaplasia is the change in cell type and dysplasia is the change in cell structure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Atrophy and hypertrophy are changes in cell size, not the changes in cell type and structure shown.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neoplasia is an irreversible change in cell type and structure with unregulated proliferation, and hyperplasia is a change in cell number; neither matches the slides.

questions.stem: A cervical biopsy report describes dysplastic epithelial cells with 'loss of polarity.' Which of the following best defines this morphologic change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A nucleus that occupies most of the cell volume

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cells that vary widely in size and shape from one another

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lack of distinction between the top and bottom of the cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nuclei that stain darker than normal because of excess chromatin

explanation.summary: Loss of polarity means there is no longer a distinction between the top and bottom of the cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists the morphologic changes of dysplastic cells and defines loss of polarity as lack of distinction between the top and bottom of the cell. It accompanies other dysplastic features such as pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, irregularly shaped nuclei, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and disorderly architecture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This describes a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Variation in size and shape is pleomorphism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dark-staining nuclei are hyperchromatic nuclei, a separate listed feature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This describes irregularly shaped nuclei.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman's cervical biopsy is reported as CIN II. Using the spectrum of dysplasia described for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, this finding corresponds to which of the following?

explanation.summary: CIN I is mild dysplasia, CIN II is moderate dysplasia, and CIN III is severe dysplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes a spectrum of dysplasia on cervical biopsy from normal to CIN I (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, mild dysplasia), CIN II (moderate dysplasia), and CIN III (severe dysplasia). CIN II therefore corresponds to moderate dysplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carcinoma in situ is the stage after severe dysplasia, beyond the CIN II grade.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Invasive carcinoma requires breach of the basement membrane and is not a grade of intraepithelial dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mild dysplasia is CIN I.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Severe dysplasia is CIN III.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has a cervical biopsy showing CIN I. She is anxious and asks whether this means she will develop cancer. Based on the natural history of dysplasia, which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cancer will almost certainly follow because any dysplasia is irreversible

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mildly dysplastic cells often revert to normal and may never progress to cancer

choices.label: C
choices.text: The finding represents metaplasia and carries no cancer risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lesion is a benign tumor and cannot become cancerous

choices.label: E
choices.text: The lesion is already carcinoma in situ and requires immediate removal

explanation.summary: Mild dysplasia frequently disappears with the cells reverting to normal, whereas severe dysplasia carries a very high chance of progressing to cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that sometimes dysplasia disappears and the cell reverts to normal, never progressing to become cancerous, and that this is especially true for cells that are mildly dysplastic. In contrast, once dysplastic changes become severe, chances are very high that cancer will follow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dysplasia, particularly mild dysplasia, can revert to normal; it is not irreversible.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metaplasia is replacement of one cell type by another; CIN I is dysplasia and does carry some risk of progression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dysplasia is disordered growth in non-neoplastic epithelial cells, not a benign tumor, and it can precede cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CIN I is mild dysplasia; carcinoma in situ is the stage after severe dysplasia.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old asymptomatic woman undergoes routine cervical screening in which cells are collected with a swab and examined microscopically. Which principle provides the rationale for this screening test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Benign cervical tumors are usually encapsulated and easily detected

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carcinoma of the cervix metastasizes only after it becomes anaplastic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dysplasia precedes cancer and can be removed before cancer develops

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metaplasia of the cervix is irreversible once established

choices.label: E
choices.text: Well-differentiated cervical tumors cannot be identified on biopsy

explanation.summary: The Pap smear is based on the fact that dysplasia precedes cancer; detecting severe dysplasia allows its removal before cancer develops.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Papanicolaou (Pap) smear is based on the fact that dysplasia precedes cancer. Cells from the cervix are removed with a swab and examined under the microscope for dysplastic changes. If severe dysplasia is present, the patient can undergo a separate procedure to remove the dysplastic epithelium, preventing cancer from developing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The test screens for dysplastic cells, not encapsulated benign tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metastasis is not tied to anaplasia in this way, and this is not the basis of screening.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metaplasia is typically reversible, and the Pap smear looks for dysplasia, not metaplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Well-differentiated tumors are identifiable; this is unrelated to the screening rationale.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a cervical biopsy that shows malignant squamous cells extending beyond the basement membrane into the underlying stroma. Six months earlier a biopsy had shown cancerous cells confined above the basement membrane. Which term best describes the current lesion?

explanation.summary: Once cancer cells break through the basement membrane into underlying tissue, the lesion is invasive carcinoma rather than carcinoma in situ.
explanation.whyCorrect: In carcinoma in situ the cells are cancerous but pre-invasive: they have not broken through their basement membrane and penetrated the underlying tissue. The brick notes that once there is invasion beyond the basement membrane, the lesion is referred to as invasive carcinoma. The earlier biopsy was CIS; the current one shows invasion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carcinoma in situ requires that the basement membrane has not been breached; here it has.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Severe dysplasia is a pre-cancerous change confined to the epithelium, not cancer cells invading stroma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metaplasia is an adaptive replacement of one cell type by another, not malignant invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A papilloma is a benign epithelial tumor with finger-like projections and does not invade.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child has a soft, compressible mass in the neck. Excision shows a benign proliferation of dilated lymphatic channels. Applying the standard rules for naming benign tumors, this lesion is best termed which of the following?

explanation.summary: Lymphangio- refers to lymphatic vessels, and the suffix -oma denotes a benign tumor, giving lymphangioma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Benign tumor names have two parts: a prefix for the cell or tissue of origin and the suffix -oma. The brick lists lymphangio- as the prefix for lymphatic vessels, so a benign tumor of lymphatic vessels is a lymphangioma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vessel tumor; this lesion is benign and should carry the -oma suffix.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemangio- refers to blood vessels, whereas this tumor is composed of lymphatic channels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipo- refers to fat cells; a lipoma is a benign fat tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lymphoma is a malignant tumor of lymphocytes, one of the names that sounds benign but is malignant.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has a large retroperitoneal mass resected. Histology shows a malignant tumor whose cells are derived from fat cells. Which of the following is the correct name for this tumor?

explanation.summary: Fat is mesenchymal tissue, so a malignant tumor of fat cells takes the prefix lipo- and the suffix sarcoma: liposarcoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lipo- refers to fat cells. Fat is one of the mesenchymal ('soft') tissues, and when a malignant tumor is derived from mesenchymal tissue, 'sarcoma' is added. The malignant tumor of fat cells is therefore a liposarcoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumor of glandular epithelium, not fat.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrosarcoma would be a malignant tumor of fibrous connective tissue, not fat cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carcinoma is reserved for malignant tumors of epithelial tissue; fat is mesenchymal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipoma is the benign fat tumor (-oma); this tumor is malignant.

questions.stem: A pathologist explains that a patient's osteosarcoma and a different patient's squamous cell carcinoma belong to two fundamentally different classes of malignant tumor based on their tissue of origin. The osteosarcoma arises from tissue derived from which of the following embryonic sources?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mesoderm, via the gelatinous embryonic mesenchyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neural crest cells migrating from the neural tube

choices.label: E
choices.text: Surface epithelium resting on a basement membrane

explanation.summary: Sarcomas arise from mesenchymal tissues, which derive from mesenchyme, a gelatinous embryonic substance that arises from mesoderm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mesenchymal tissues are the 'soft' tissues or connective tissues that make up the bulk of the body (muscle, bone, cartilage, fat, and connective tissue). These tissues are derived from mesenchyme, a gelatinous substance present during early embryogenesis, and mesenchyme arises from mesoderm, the germ cell layer sandwiched between the ectoderm and the endoderm. Bone is mesenchymal, so an osteosarcoma is a sarcoma of mesodermal origin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ectoderm is the outer germ layer; the brick places mesenchyme's origin in the mesoderm between ectoderm and endoderm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endoderm is the inner germ layer, not the source of mesenchyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes mesenchymal tissues to mesoderm-derived mesenchyme, not neural crest.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Epithelium consists of densely packed cells atop a basement membrane and gives rise to carcinomas, not sarcomas.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has a painless testicular mass. The pathology report reads 'seminoma.' His partner, noting that the name ends in -oma, asks whether the tumor is therefore benign. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, seminoma is a choristoma of normal germ cells in an abnormal location

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, seminoma is a hamartoma of disorganized testicular tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: No, seminoma is a malignant tumor of male germ cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, because germ cell tumors of the testis cannot metastasize

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yes, because the -oma suffix always indicates a benign tumor

explanation.summary: Seminoma is one of several malignant tumors whose names sound benign because they end in -oma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some malignant tumor names don't follow the rules; they sound like benign tumors but are definitely malignant. The brick lists seminoma (malignant tumor of male germ cells) among these, alongside lymphoma (lymphocytes), leukemia (white blood cells), mesothelioma (mesothelial cells), and melanoma (melanocytes).

whyWrongByChoice.A: A choristoma is microscopically normal tissue in an abnormal site; seminoma is a malignant tumor arising in the testis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A hamartoma is a non-neoplastic mass of disorganized native tissue; seminoma is a true malignant neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Seminoma is malignant, and malignant tumors by definition have the potential to metastasize.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The -oma suffix usually indicates a benign tumor, but seminoma, lymphoma, mesothelioma, and melanoma are exceptions.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with seizures and developmental delay has several firm facial skin lesions and, on brain imaging, multiple nodular lesions of the central nervous system. Biopsy of a lesion shows a disorganized but non-neoplastic collection of tissue elements native to the site. His father has similar skin findings. This presentation is most characteristic of which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carcinoma in situ of the skin with CNS spread

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metastatic melanoma to the skin and brain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tuberous sclerosis with hamartomas of skin and CNS

explanation.summary: Hamartomas of the skin and central nervous system are characteristic of the autosomal dominant disease tuberous sclerosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hamartomas are non-neoplastic regions of disorganized tissue that are indigenous to the organ in which they are found. The brick's clinical correlation notes that a characteristic of the autosomal dominant disease tuberous sclerosis is hamartomas of the skin and central nervous system. Non-neoplastic disorganized native tissue in both sites, with an affected parent, fits this diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tuberous sclerosis is autosomal dominant, and the lesions are hamartomas (native tissue), not choristomas (ectopic tissue).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carcinoma in situ is pre-invasive cancer confined by the basement membrane; it cannot spread, and these lesions are not neoplastic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Melanoma is a malignant melanocytic tumor; the lesions here are non-neoplastic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A meningioma is a benign neoplasm of the meninges, not a non-neoplastic hamartoma, and would not explain the skin lesions.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with a mass in the upper outer quadrant of her breast. Mammography shows a nodule in that region, and core needle biopsy demonstrates invasive ductal carcinoma. At surgery a sentinel lymph node biopsy is planned. Based on the location of this tumor, which group of lymph nodes is most likely to be involved first?

explanation.summary: Lymph node involvement follows the path of lymphatic drainage from the primary tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Breast cancers arising in the upper outer quadrant drain first to the nearby axillary lymph nodes because of the anatomy of lymphatic drainage. These are therefore the sentinel and most likely first-involved nodes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Infraclavicular nodes are more distal and would typically be involved only later in the sequence of spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mediastinal (internal mammary) nodes are associated with drainage from the inner quadrants of the breast, not the upper outer quadrant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Submandibular nodes drain the head and neck and are rarely involved in breast cancer spread.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Supraclavicular nodes are distal nodes that become involved later in metastatic progression.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman noticed a mole enlarging over the past several years. A dermatologist performs a biopsy that shows melanoma, and a sentinel lymph node biopsy reveals metastatic disease. Inactivation of which normal cell structure most directly permits tumor cells to detach from one another and begin invasion?

explanation.summary: Loss of E-cadherin frees tumor cells from one another, an early step in invasion.
explanation.whyCorrect: E-cadherin connects epithelial cells to one another; its inactivation leads to loss of intercellular adhesion, one of the first steps of invasion. Loss of E-cadherin classically produces the single-file infiltration pattern of invasive lobular carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Actin filaments drive migration of the tumor cell through the extracellular matrix rather than mediating cell-cell adhesion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmoplakin is part of the normal cell structure but does not itself trigger the invasion of tumor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gap junctions mediate cell-to-cell communication; their inactivation would not lead to invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Keratin is an important structural component, but loss of keratin does not result in invasion.

questions.stem: A researcher is describing the metastatic cascade to a class of students. She defines one step as the tumor cell breaching the basement membrane, migrating through the extracellular matrix, and entering a vessel. Which step of metastasis is she describing?

explanation.summary: Intravasation is tumor cell invasion through the ECM and entry into a vessel.
explanation.whyCorrect: The steps of metastasis are invasion, intravasation, extravasation, and growth at secondary sites. Intravasation corresponds to tumor cell invasion through the extracellular matrix and entry into the bloodstream or lymphatics to travel toward a secondary site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angiogenesis is new vessel formation and is not the step of entering a vessel described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Colonization is the later outgrowth at a distant organ, which depends on a favorable stromal environment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extravasation is the opposite directional step: tumor cells exit the bloodstream or lymphatics and infiltrate outside the capillaries.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor dormancy refers to failure to grow at a distant site, not entry into a vessel.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with colon adenocarcinoma undergoes staging imaging that reveals multiple hepatic lesions consistent with metastases. Which feature best explains why the liver is the most common initial site of metastasis for colon cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colon cancer cells preferentially spread through the lymphatics to the liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: Portal venous blood from the colon drains into the liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Seeding across the peritoneal cavity deposits cells directly onto the liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: The liver has an unusually high oxygen content that favors tumor growth

choices.label: E
choices.text: The liver secretes chemokines that specifically attract colonic tumor cells

explanation.summary: Hematogenous spread often follows normal venous drainage to the first capillary bed.
explanation.whyCorrect: In hematogenous spread, tumor cells follow the normal venous drainage pattern and embed in the first capillary bed they reach. All portal blood from the colon, stomach, and pancreas drains into the liver, which is why the liver is a common first site of metastasis for these cancers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The described colon-to-liver pattern is hematogenous through the portal vein, not lymphatic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seeding requires an open cavity and does not describe the venous drainage responsible for hepatic metastasis here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arteries carry higher oxygen content, but this makes arterial spread less common; it does not explain hepatic metastasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: While tropism and chemokine receptors influence some metastases, the brick attributes colon-to-liver spread to anatomic vascular drainage, not liver-secreted chemokines.

questions.stem: A pathologist notes that although most carcinomas spread through the lymphatics, a small group of carcinomas is classically known for spreading hematogenously. Which of the following carcinomas belongs to that group?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colonic adenocarcinoma spreading to regional nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast

choices.label: E
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

explanation.summary: Four carcinomas are classically known for hematogenous spread: follicular thyroid, choriocarcinoma, renal cell, and hepatocellular.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although most carcinomas spread lymphatically, four are known for hematogenous spread: follicular thyroid carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Renal cell carcinoma is a member of this group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Regional nodal spread of colon cancer is lymphatic; it is not part of the classic hematogenous carcinoma group.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric adenocarcinoma is not among the four carcinomas singled out for hematogenous spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Breast carcinoma is the brick's classic example of lymphatic (axillary node) spread, not the hematogenous exception group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Squamous cell carcinoma is a carcinoma that follows the usual lymphatic route and is not in the four-carcinoma hematogenous group.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is diagnosed with osteosarcoma of the distal femur. When counseling about the most likely route by which this tumor will disseminate, which pattern of spread should be emphasized?

explanation.summary: Sarcomas, being of mesenchymal origin, are associated with hematogenous spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sarcomas are of mesenchymal origin and are associated with hematogenous spread through the bloodstream, in contrast to carcinomas, which are associated with lymphatic spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Perineural spread is not the route emphasized for sarcomas in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphatic spread is the pattern classically associated with carcinomas (epithelial-derived tumors), not sarcomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peritoneal seeding requires shedding into an open cavity, as with ovarian carcinoma, and is not the typical route for a bone sarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subarachnoid seeding is characteristic of CNS tumors such as glioblastoma, not osteosarcoma.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with high-grade ovarian carcinoma is found at laparotomy to have numerous tumor nodules studding the omentum and peritoneal surfaces, without an intervening path through lymphatics or blood vessels. Which mechanism of tumor spread best accounts for this distribution?

explanation.summary: Seeding disseminates tumor across an open body cavity such as the peritoneum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Seeding requires an open space such as the peritoneal, pleural, subarachnoid, or joint cavities. Ovarian carcinoma is a classic example of a tumor that seeds the peritoneal cavity, producing widespread surface implants such as omental involvement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hematogenous spread deposits cells in capillary beds of organs, not as surface seeding across a cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphatic spread travels through lymphatic channels to nodes and would not produce diffuse peritoneal surface implants.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Perineural invasion is spread along nerves and does not explain diffuse peritoneal implants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor dormancy describes failure to grow at a distant site, not the mechanism producing peritoneal implants.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with glioblastoma develops new neurologic deficits, and imaging reveals tumor deposits within the spinal subarachnoid space. Which route of spread best explains dissemination of this tumor from the brain to the spinal cord?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematogenous spread through the vertebral veins

explanation.summary: Glioblastomas use the open subarachnoid space to seed the brain and spinal cord.
explanation.whyCorrect: Seeding occurs within open spaces, and glioblastomas use the subarachnoid space to seed within the brain and spinal cord. The cerebrospinal fluid within this open space carries cells to distant CNS surfaces.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Direct extension through bone does not explain deposits floating within the subarachnoid space.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes CNS glioblastoma dissemination to seeding through the subarachnoid space rather than hematogenous venous spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The CNS lacks conventional lymphatics used for this spread, and the brick describes seeding, not lymphatic dissemination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Retrograde perineural spread is not the mechanism the brick describes for glioblastoma.

questions.stem: In an experiment, tumor cells are engineered to overexpress a receptor that binds a major component of the basement membrane, which markedly increases their adhesion to basement membranes and their ability to invade surrounding tissues and blood vessels. Overexpression of a receptor for which molecule best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: Laminin receptor overexpression promotes tumor adhesion to and invasion through basement membranes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cells can overexpress laminin receptors. These receptors bind laminin, a major component of the basement membrane, facilitating tumor cell adhesion to basement membranes, migration, and invasion into surrounding tissues and blood vessels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin is a plasma transport protein and is not a basement membrane component mediating invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmoplakin is part of desmosomes and does not serve as the basement membrane ligand described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin is an intracellular oxygen carrier in red blood cells and is unrelated to basement membrane adhesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Keratin is an intracellular structural protein of epithelial cells, not a basement membrane ligand for an invasion-promoting receptor.

questions.stem: During intravasation, most single circulating tumor cells die, yet some survive to establish distant metastases. According to the theory described, which behavior most improves a circulating tumor cell's chance of survival in the bloodstream?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Downregulating all surface adhesion molecules to travel as single cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Shrinking below the diameter of a red blood cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traveling as multicellular aggregates bound to platelets

explanation.summary: Tumor cells that clump and bind platelets survive circulation better than lone cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: A theory of which tumor cells ultimately metastasize holds that circulating cells are much more likely to migrate as multicellular aggregates than as single cells. Tumor cells bind to one another or to platelets to survive in the bloodstream and may activate coagulation factors, forming emboli.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of adhesion promotes apoptosis, and single cells are far more likely to die than aggregates, so this reduces survival.
whyWrongByChoice.B: High shear stress from flow kills circulating tumor cells rather than protecting them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tumor cells are significantly larger than most blood cells; they do not shrink below a red blood cell, and their size helps them lodge in capillary beds.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tumor cells tend to activate coagulation factors to form protective emboli, so suppressing coagulation would not aid survival.

questions.stem: A student asks why tumor cells more readily enter lymphatic vessels than blood vessels during metastasis. Which property of the lymphatic system best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It actively secretes proteases that pull tumor cells inward

choices.label: B
choices.text: It carries a higher oxygen content that attracts tumor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It directs all cells immediately to the liver and lungs

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has thicker, muscular walls that trap tumor cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It lacks the tight junctions and basement membrane of blood vessels

explanation.summary: Lymphatics are a low-shear, loosely walled system that tumor cells enter easily.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reason a tumor cell intravasates lymphatically is largely mechanical. The lymphatic pathway is a low-shear system that lacks the tight junctions and basement membrane associated with blood vessels, making it easier for a tumor cell to enter a lymphatic vessel than a blood vessel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphatics do not actively secrete proteases to pull in tumor cells; proteases come from tumor cells and nearby stromal cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Higher oxygen content describes arterial blood; it is not a feature that draws tumor cells into lymphatics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Drainage to the liver and lungs reflects venous/portal hematogenous patterns, not lymphatic entry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymphatic vessels are thin-walled and low-shear, not thick and muscular; that is a feature of arteries.

questions.stem: To avoid the morbidity of a full axillary dissection, a breast surgeon injects tracer around a tumor and removes the first node that takes up the tracer to assess for metastasis. Which statement best describes the node being sampled?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a node selected at random from the axilla for biopsy

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a node that filters hematogenously spread tumor emboli

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the contralateral supraclavicular node

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the first node in a regional lymphatic basin

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the most distal node in the lymphatic chain draining the tumor

explanation.summary: The sentinel node is the first node in a regional basin receiving lymph from the tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: In breast cancer, axillary lymph node assessment guides prognosis and therapy. To avoid the morbidity of a full dissection, the surgeon biopsies the sentinel lymph node, defined as the first node in a regional lymphatic basin that receives lymph flow from the primary tumor and is thus the likely first site of spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: It is not selected at random; it is specifically identified as the first draining node via tracer uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The sentinel node concept is based on lymphatic drainage, not on filtering hematogenous tumor emboli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A contralateral supraclavicular node is not the first regional draining node and is not the sentinel node of an axillary basin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The sentinel node is the first, most proximal node receiving drainage, not the most distal node in the chain.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman undergoes biopsy of a breast mass. Microscopy shows carcinoma cells that have breached the basement membrane and entered the underlying stroma. Enzymatic cleavage of which of the following basement membrane components most directly permitted this breach?

explanation.summary: Tumor cells breach the basement membrane by protease cleavage of type IV collagen.
explanation.whyCorrect: After losing intercellular adhesion, mobile tumor cells must invade the basement membrane, which is accomplished by cleaving it with proteases. The brick's figure of this step specifically depicts type IV collagen cleavage as the event that opens the basement membrane to invading cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Desmoplakin is a desmosomal protein within the cell, not an extracellular basement membrane target.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Elastin is not depicted as the basement membrane substrate of protease cleavage in this process.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Keratin is an intracellular structural protein of epithelial cells, not a basement membrane component.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type I collagen is not the basement membrane component the brick identifies as cleaved during invasion.

questions.stem: Investigators studying an invasive carcinoma find that much of the protease activity degrading the stroma around the tumor is produced not by the tumor cells themselves but by non-neoplastic cells in the surrounding tissue that the tumor has induced. Which of the following cells are the most likely source?

explanation.summary: Invasion-promoting proteases come from the tumor cells or from macrophages and fibroblasts induced in the surrounding tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: The proteases used to cleave the basement membrane and stroma are secreted from the tumor cells themselves or are induced by macrophages or fibroblasts within the surrounding tissues. Signaling between tumor and stromal cells is a recurring theme of invasion in the brick.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adipocytes and chondrocytes are not the stromal cells the brick names as protease producers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphatic endothelium is described as a low-shear, loosely walled pathway, not as a protease-secreting stromal population.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neural elements are not identified as protease sources in the brick's account of invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets figure in the survival of circulating tumor cells, not as the stromal source of proteases; erythrocytes have no such role.

questions.stem: A study blocks protease release by an invasive tumor and observes not only reduced invasion but also a marked slowing of tumor cell proliferation. Which of the following best explains the effect on proliferation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Protease release increases shear stress within lymphatic vessels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Protease release liberates growth-promoting agents from the stroma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protease release prevents platelet binding to tumor emboli

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protease release restores E-cadherin-mediated adhesion between cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protease release triggers apoptosis of circulating tumor cells

explanation.summary: Proteases do double duty: they degrade the stroma and release growth-promoting agents that drive tumor growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: The release of proteases not only degrades the stroma but also promotes tumor cell growth by releasing growth-promoting agents. Blocking proteases therefore removes both the path through the matrix and a source of growth stimulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Shear stress is a property of blood or lymphatic flow, not something tumor proteases alter, and it kills rather than feeds tumor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Platelet binding protects circulating tumor cells; proteases are not described as preventing it, and this would not explain reduced proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Invasion begins with loss of E-cadherin adhesion; proteases do not restore adhesion, and restored adhesion would not explain slowed growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Apoptosis of circulating cells results from loss of adhesion during intravasation, not from protease release.

questions.stem: Time-lapse microscopy of invasive tumor cells shows them moving through the extracellular matrix in an amoeboid-type pattern, ratcheting forward in response to signals exchanged with nearby stromal cells. Which of the following intracellular structures primarily drives this movement?

explanation.summary: Tumor cells migrate through the matrix in an amoeboid pattern powered by the actin skeleton.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor cells migrate in an amoeboid-type pattern, using the actin skeleton and signaling between the tumor and stromal cells to ratchet through the extracellular matrix. Actin filaments are the structure involved in migration of the tumor cell through the ECM.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Desmosomes (containing desmoplakin) are adhesive structures; they do not drive amoeboid movement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gap junctions mediate cell-to-cell communication and play no role in locomotion through the matrix.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Keratin is an important structural component, but the brick assigns migration to actin, not keratin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The nuclear envelope does not generate the force for cell migration.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has a poorly defined breast mass. Histology shows loss of normal architecture, with tumor cells infiltrating the stroma in a single-file pattern. Immunohistochemistry shows a complete absence of E-cadherin staining in the tumor cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Single-file infiltration with absent E-cadherin staining is the signature of invasive lobular carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's figure of invasive lobular carcinoma shows cancer cells demonstrating loss of architecture and single-file infiltration due to loss of E-cadherin, seen as lack of brown immunohistochemical staining. Loss of the E-cadherin connections between cells frees the cells to infiltrate individually in a line.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endometrial stromal sarcoma is shown in the brick as a sarcoma with vascular invasion, not as an E-cadherin-negative breast tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Follicular thyroid carcinoma is cited for hematogenous spread and does not arise in the breast.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Invasive ductal carcinoma is the breast tumor the brick uses to illustrate axillary nodal spread, not the single-file, E-cadherin-negative pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Melanoma appears in the brick as a skin tumor with sentinel node metastasis, not as a single-file breast infiltrate.

questions.stem: Circulating tumor cells are isolated from the blood of a patient with metastatic carcinoma. When followed in the circulation, the large majority of single cells die within hours. Which of the following pairs of insults best explains their death?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypoxia and glucose deprivation in the plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osmotic swelling and rupture of the cell membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Platelet aggregation and coagulation factor activation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shear stress from flow and apoptosis from lost adhesion

explanation.summary: Most circulating tumor cells die from shear stress or from apoptosis triggered by loss of adhesion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intravasation involves entry into the bloodstream or lymphatics, and many circulating tumor cells will die from shear stress from blood or lymphatic flow or from apoptosis due to loss of adhesion. This is why cells traveling as aggregates bound to one another or to platelets fare better.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes circulating tumor cell death to mechanical shear and adhesion-loss apoptosis, not to immune lysis or phagocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nutrient or oxygen deprivation is not the cause of death the brick describes for circulating cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osmotic rupture is not a described mechanism of circulating tumor cell death.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet binding and coagulation activation protect tumor cells and form emboli; they aid survival rather than cause death.

questions.stem: A tumor embolus enters the venous circulation from a primary tumor and travels toward the heart. Rather than circulating widely, it becomes lodged in the first capillary bed it encounters. Which of the following properties of tumor cells best explains this behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are attracted by the higher oxygen content of capillaries

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are pulled inward by proteases secreted by pericytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are significantly larger than most blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are slowed by the low-shear flow of capillaries

choices.label: E
choices.text: They express receptors specific for capillary endothelium

explanation.summary: Tumor cells are much larger than blood cells, so they get stuck at the first capillary bed they cross.
explanation.whyCorrect: A tumor cell is significantly larger than most blood cells and for this reason will likely get stuck at the first capillary bed it crosses, getting closer to its final destination. This size-based trapping underlies why venous drainage predicts the first site of hematogenous metastasis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Higher oxygen content is a feature of arteries that makes arterial spread less common; it does not explain capillary trapping.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Proteases are secreted by tumor cells or induced macrophages and fibroblasts to degrade stroma; they do not pull cells into capillaries.
