whyWrongByChoice.D: Low-shear flow describes the lymphatic system and explains ease of lymphatic entry, not why emboli lodge in capillaries.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trapping in the first capillary bed is a mechanical consequence of size, not receptor-specific recognition of capillary endothelium.

questions.stem: A tumor cell that has survived transit in the bloodstream lodges in a capillary, passes out through the vessel wall, and infiltrates the surrounding tissue of a distant organ. Which of the following terms describes this step of metastasis?

explanation.summary: Extravasation is the exit of tumor cells from the bloodstream or lymphatics into tissue outside the capillaries.
explanation.whyCorrect: Extravasation is the exit from the bloodstream and into the tissue. In extravasation, tumor cells exit the bloodstream or lymphatics and infiltrate outside of the capillaries, after which growth at the secondary site depends on the local environment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Intravasation is the opposite movement: entry into the bloodstream or lymphatics from the primary site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Invasion is the earlier step at the primary tumor in which cells lose adhesion and breach the basement membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Seeding is spread across an open space such as the peritoneal cavity, not exit from a capillary.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor dormancy is the failure of cells to grow at a distant site after they have arrived.

questions.stem: A carcinoma repeatedly metastasizes to an organ that is not the first capillary bed downstream of its venous drainage. Analysis shows the tumor cells express chemokine receptors and adhesion molecules whose ligands are found preferentially in that organ. Which of the following factors best accounts for this metastatic pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Escape from tumor dormancy at the secondary site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Location and vascular drainage of the primary tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of E-cadherin at the primary tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low-shear entry into the lymphatic system

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tropism of the tumor cells for a specific tissue

explanation.summary: Tropism explains metastasis to organs whose ligands and "soil" match the tumor cell's adhesion molecules and chemokine receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Where circulating tumor cells end up depends on three key factors: location and vascular drainage of the primary, tropism of particular tumor cells for specific tissues, and escape from dormancy. Tropism arises because tumor cells may express adhesion molecules whose ligands are found preferentially in certain organs, some express chemokine receptors, and some tissues provide a favorable environment, or "soil", for growth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escape from dormancy concerns whether lodged cells eventually grow, not which organ they are attracted to.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vascular drainage predicts the first downstream organ, which the stem states is not where this tumor lands.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E-cadherin loss initiates invasion at the primary site and does not direct cells to a particular organ.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Low-shear lymphatic entry explains why cells enter lymphatics, not organ-specific homing.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman was treated for a carcinoma 9 years ago and has had no recurrence. She dies of an unrelated cause, and at autopsy small clusters of viable tumor cells are found lodged in a distant organ; they never proliferated into a detectable mass. Which of the following terms best describes the state of these cells?

explanation.summary: Tumor cells that reach a distant site but fail to grow there are in a state of tumor dormancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor cells may fail to grow in distant sites, a state the brick calls tumor dormancy. Growth of a tumor at a distant site relies on the environment of that tissue; without the proper stromal environment, such as cytokines and growth factors, survival and outgrowth of the tumor cannot occur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intravasation is entry into a vessel at the primary site; these cells have already completed that step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Invasion is the initial breach of the basement membrane at the primary tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seeding describes spread across an open cavity, not the growth status of lodged cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tropism describes preferential homing to particular tissues, not failure to proliferate after arrival.

questions.stem: Tumor cells that lodged in a distant organ years earlier and remained dormant begin to proliferate into a clinically evident metastasis. Which of the following changes most directly enabled this escape from dormancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of coagulation factors that generate tumor emboli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of E-cadherin connections between adjacent tumor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Overexpression of laminin receptors that bind basement membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protease cleavage of type IV collagen in the basement membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretion of cytokines and growth factors that act on resident stromal cells

explanation.summary: Tumor cells escape dormancy by secreting factors that remodel the resident stroma into a habitable environment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because tumor cells may fail to grow in distant sites, tumor cells secrete cytokines, growth factors, and extracellular matrix molecules that act on resident stromal cells and make the environment more habitable for the tumor cell. This is the brick's mechanism of escape from tumor dormancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coagulation factor activation helps circulating cells form protective emboli during intravasation, before they lodge.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E-cadherin loss is the initial step of invasion at the primary tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Laminin receptor overexpression facilitates adhesion to basement membranes and invasion at the primary site, not outgrowth of dormant cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type IV collagen cleavage is how cells breach the basement membrane during invasion, not how dormant cells begin to grow.

questions.stem: A pathologist notes that hematogenous metastasis through arteries occurs far less often than through veins. Which of the following properties of arteries best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent tight junctions and basement membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct drainage into the hepatic portal system

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thicker walls and higher oxygen content

explanation.summary: Arteries are thicker, harder to penetrate, and carry higher oxygen content, making arterial spread the less common hematogenous route.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hematogenous spread can occur through arteries or veins. Arteries are thicker and harder to penetrate and have a higher oxygen content, so this is a less common route. With venous spread, tumor cells follow the normal venous drainage pattern and become embedded in the first capillary bed they reach.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lack of tight junctions and basement membrane describes lymphatic vessels, which are easy to enter, not arteries.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Portal drainage into the liver is a venous pattern from the colon, stomach, and pancreas, not an arterial feature.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Low-shear flow is a property of the lymphatic pathway, not of arteries.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Arteries are not described as having valves that trap aggregates; this is not the brick's explanation.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is diagnosed with a soft-tissue sarcoma of the thigh, a tumor that spreads hematogenously. Staging imaging is ordered to look for distant disease. Metastases are most likely to be found in which of the following pairs of organs?

explanation.summary: The liver and lung are the most common sites of hematogenous metastasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because tumor cells follow the normal venous drainage pattern and embed in the first capillary bed they reach, the liver (receiving portal blood) and the lung (receiving caval blood) are the most common sites of hematogenous metastasis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adrenal and pancreas are not the first capillary beds reached by venous drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Brain and bone are not the organs the brick identifies as the most common first capillary beds for venous emboli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kidney and spleen do not receive the systemic or portal venous return that funnels tumor emboli.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skin and thyroid are not common capillary-bed targets of hematogenous spread in the brick.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with carcinoma of the urinary bladder develops multiple pulmonary nodules that prove to be metastatic bladder carcinoma. Tumor emboli most likely reached the lungs by traveling through which of the following vessels?

explanation.summary: Systemic venous blood reaches the lungs through the venae cavae, so caval drainage delivers tumor emboli to the pulmonary capillary bed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Venous blood from the superior and inferior vena cava flows to the lungs, and metastases to the lung are commonly from cancers of the bladder, colon, breast, and prostate. Venous blood from the bladder returns through the inferior vena cava, so bladder carcinoma emboli are carried to the first capillary bed they reach: the lungs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The hepatic artery supplies the liver and is an arterial route, which is the less common pathway and does not lead to the lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphatic spread to mediastinal nodes would produce nodal disease, not parenchymal lung nodules via the venous circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The portal vein carries blood from the colon, stomach, and pancreas to the liver, not from the bladder to the lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thoracic duct is a lymphatic channel; the pulmonary nodules here reflect hematogenous venous spread.

questions.stem: A woman with breast cancer is found to have stage IV disease with involvement of her axillary lymph nodes and lungs. Which of the following best describes the routes by which her tumor reached these two sites?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hematogenous spread through the portal vein to both the nodes and lungs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematogenous spread to the nodes and lymphatic spread to the lungs via the thoracic duct

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphatic spread to the nodes and hematogenous spread to the lungs via the superior vena cava

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lymphatic spread to the nodes and seeding of the lungs via the subarachnoid space

choices.label: E
choices.text: Seeding of the pleural cavity accounts for both the nodal and lung lesions

explanation.summary: Breast cancer reaches the axillary nodes lymphatically and the lungs hematogenously via the superior vena cava.
explanation.whyCorrect: Breast cancer can spread to the axillary lymph nodes directly through lymphatic drainage and to the lungs via the superior vena cava through the process of intravasation and extravasation. Venous blood from the superior vena cava flows to the lungs, and the lung is a common site of metastasis for breast cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The portal vein drains the colon, stomach, and pancreas to the liver; it does not carry breast cancer cells to nodes or lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The routes are reversed: nodal disease is lymphatic and pulmonary disease is hematogenous.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The subarachnoid space is the seeding route of glioblastoma within the CNS and has no connection to the lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Seeding requires an open cavity and cannot explain metastases within lymph nodes; the brick describes venous, not pleural, spread to the lungs here.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman undergoes thyroidectomy for a nodule that proves to be follicular thyroid carcinoma. Staging studies reveal distant metastases in the lung, yet no cervical lymph node involvement is found. Which of the following best explains this pattern of spread?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cervical lymphatic channels have tight junctions that exclude all tumor cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Follicular thyroid carcinoma is a carcinoma known for hematogenous spread

choices.label: C
choices.text: Follicular thyroid carcinoma seeds the pleural cavity as surface implants

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thyroid carcinomas are tumors of mesenchymal rather than epithelial origin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thyroid venous blood drains directly into the hepatic portal system

explanation.summary: Follicular thyroid carcinoma is one of four carcinomas that classically spread hematogenously rather than lymphatically.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although most carcinomas spread lymphatically, four types are known for spreading hematogenously: follicular thyroid carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Hematogenous spread through the venous system carries emboli to the lungs, bypassing regional nodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphatics lack the tight junctions and basement membrane of blood vessels; they do not exclude tumor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seeding requires an open cavity and produces surface implants, not parenchymal lung metastases via the bloodstream.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carcinomas are epithelial-derived; mesenchymal origin defines sarcomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Portal drainage applies to the colon, stomach, and pancreas, not the thyroid.

questions.stem: A student is reviewing tumors whose route of metastasis departs from the usual pattern for their tissue of origin. Which of the following carcinomas typically spreads through the lymphatics rather than hematogenously?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Choriocarcinoma of the placenta or gonads

choices.label: B
choices.text: Follicular carcinoma of the thyroid gland

choices.label: D
choices.text: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal cell carcinoma, clear cell type

explanation.summary: Breast carcinoma follows the usual carcinoma pattern of lymphatic spread; the four exceptions spread hematogenously.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carcinomas, epithelial-derived tumors, are associated with lymphatic spread, and breast cancer is the brick's example, traveling to axillary lymph nodes along the path of lymphatic drainage. The four carcinomas known for hematogenous spread are follicular thyroid carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Choriocarcinoma is one of the four carcinomas known for hematogenous spread.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Follicular thyroid carcinoma is one of the four carcinomas known for hematogenous spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatocellular carcinoma is one of the four carcinomas known for hematogenous spread.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal cell carcinoma is one of the four carcinomas known for hematogenous spread.

questions.stem: A histologic section of an axillary lymph node removed from a woman with breast carcinoma shows aggregates of tumor cells within the substance of the node and a dilated lymphatic channel containing tumor cells. Which of the following pathways of metastasis do these findings demonstrate?

explanation.summary: Tumor aggregates within a lymph node and a dilated tumor-filled lymphatic channel are the histologic picture of lymphatic spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's figure of an axillary lymph node with metastatic breast carcinoma highlights aggregates of tumor cells within the substance of the node and the dilated lymphatic channel that delivered them. Breast cancer is the brick's example of a tumor that shows lymphatic spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escape from dormancy describes outgrowth of previously quiescent cells, not the route of arrival shown here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Arterial spread is the least common hematogenous route and is not demonstrated by tumor within lymphatics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Venous spread deposits emboli in capillary beds of organs such as liver and lung, not within lymphatic channels of a node.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Seeding produces implants across an open cavity, not aggregates inside a lymph node.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with invasive breast carcinoma is scheduled for surgery. The surgeon plans a sentinel lymph node biopsy rather than a complete axillary lymph node dissection. Which of the following is the primary rationale for choosing the sentinel node procedure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It assesses for metastasis while avoiding the morbidity of a full dissection

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detects circulating hematogenous tumor emboli filtered by the axillary nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It eliminates the need to determine prognosis from axillary nodal status

choices.label: D
choices.text: It removes every axillary node that could conceivably harbor metastasis

choices.label: E
choices.text: It samples the most distal node of the axillary lymphatic drainage chain

explanation.summary: Sentinel node biopsy assesses nodal metastasis while sparing the patient the morbidity of a full axillary dissection.
explanation.whyCorrect: In breast cancer, axillary lymph node assessment is used to determine prognosis and therapeutic options. To avoid the morbidity of a full axillary lymph node dissection, the surgeon often biopsies the sentinel lymph node, the first node in the regional basin receiving lymph from the tumor, to assess for the presence or absence of metastasis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The sentinel node concept is based on lymphatic drainage, not on filtering of hematogenous emboli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nodal status still determines prognosis and therapy; the sentinel biopsy is the less morbid way to obtain it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A sentinel biopsy removes only the first draining node, deliberately avoiding removal of the entire nodal basin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The sentinel node is the first, not the most distal, node receiving lymph flow from the primary tumor.

questions.stem: A biopsy of a malignant tumor demonstrates that it is derived from epithelium. Based on its tissue of origin alone, which of the following routes of metastasis is most typically associated with this tumor?

explanation.summary: Carcinomas, being epithelial-derived, are associated with lymphatic spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carcinomas, epithelial-derived tumors, are associated with lymphatic spread, whereas sarcomas of mesenchymal origin are associated with hematogenous spread. In many cases the route of metastasis is determined by the type of cancer, although this is not a set rule.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Arterial spread is the less common hematogenous route and is not the pattern tied to epithelial origin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Venous hematogenous spread is the route associated with sarcomas of mesenchymal origin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peritoneal seeding is characteristic of particular tumors such as ovarian carcinoma, not a consequence of epithelial origin per se.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subarachnoid seeding is the route used by glioblastomas within the CNS.

questions.stem: A tumor is determined to have disseminated by seeding, with tumor cells sown across a surface much as a gardener sows seeds in an open space. Which of the following locations is consistent with this mechanism of spread?

explanation.summary: Seeding occurs within open spaces: the peritoneal, pleural, and subarachnoid spaces and joint cavities.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer seeding requires an open space, such as within the peritoneal cavity, pleural cavity, subarachnoid space, or joint cavities. A joint cavity is one of the open spaces the brick lists as a site of seeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A lymph node is reached by lymphatic spread through lymphatic channels, not by seeding across an open space.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The portal vein is a route of hematogenous spread to the liver, not an open cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pulmonary capillary bed traps hematogenous emboli; it is not an open space that is seeded.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thoracic duct is a lymphatic channel and is not a cavity that can be seeded.

questions.stem: At thoracoscopy, a patient with a malignant tumor bordering the pleura is found to have numerous small tumor implants studding the pleural surfaces. Which of the following features of the pleural cavity permits this pattern of spread?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contains stromal cells that secrete chemokines

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has low-shear lymphatic flow lacking tight junctions

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an open space into which shed tumor cells can implant

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is drained directly by the superior vena cava

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the first capillary bed downstream of the tumor

explanation.summary: Seeding requires an open space, and the pleural cavity is one of the open spaces tumors can seed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Seeding is another mechanism of cancer spread, imagined as a gardener sowing seeds in an open space. It requires an open space such as the peritoneal cavity, pleural cavity, subarachnoid space, or joint cavities, where shed tumor cells implant on the surfaces.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chemokine ligands in target organs explain tropism of circulating cells, not implantation across an open space.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Low-shear flow without tight junctions describes lymphatic vessels and explains lymphatic entry, not seeding of a cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Venous drainage to the lungs is a hematogenous pathway and is unrelated to surface seeding of the pleura.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Capillary-bed trapping explains hematogenous metastasis to organs such as liver and lung, not surface implants in a cavity.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is found to have an invasive breast carcinoma located in the inner quadrant of the breast, near the sternum. Based on the location of this tumor, which of the following groups of lymph nodes is most likely to be involved first?

explanation.summary: Inner-quadrant breast carcinomas drain to and involve the mediastinal nodes, whereas outer-quadrant tumors go to the axilla.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lymph node involvement is based on the path of lymphatic drainage. Whereas breast cancers of the upper outer quadrant first travel to the nearby axillary nodes, mediastinal nodes are the nodes involved in the metastasis of breast carcinoma found in the inner quadrant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Axillary nodes are the first site of spread for tumors of the upper outer quadrant because that drainage is nearby, not for inner-quadrant tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Infraclavicular nodes are distal nodes that could be involved later in metastasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Submandibular nodes drain the head and neck and are rarely involved in breast cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Supraclavicular nodes are distal nodes that could be involved later in metastasis.

questions.stem: A sarcoma is resected along with a regional lymph node that is found to contain metastatic sarcoma. A student states that this is impossible because sarcomas spread only hematogenously. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lymphatic spread by a sarcoma requires overexpression of laminin receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mesenchymal tumors cannot enter the low-shear lymphatic system

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sarcomas reach lymph nodes only by first seeding an adjacent joint cavity

choices.label: D
choices.text: The association is a tendency, not a set rule; the reverse pattern can occur

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor must be a carcinoma that was misclassified as a sarcoma

explanation.summary: Carcinoma-to-lymphatic and sarcoma-to-hematogenous are associations, not absolute rules; the reverse can occur.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carcinomas are associated with lymphatic spread and sarcomas with hematogenous spread. However, the brick explicitly states this is not a set rule because the reverse can also occur, just as four carcinomas are known for hematogenous spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Laminin receptor overexpression facilitates adhesion to basement membranes and invasion; it is not a stated requirement for lymphatic spread.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lymphatic system is easy to enter precisely because it is low-shear and lacks tight junctions; nothing excludes mesenchymal tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seeding requires an open cavity and produces surface implants; it is not a prerequisite for nodal metastasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nodal spread by a sarcoma does not require reclassification; the brick acknowledges the reverse pattern occurs.

questions.stem: Which of the following proto-oncogenes encodes a membrane-bound protein that binds guanosine triphosphate (GTP) in its active, on-state?

explanation.summary: Ras-family proteins are membrane-bound G proteins that are active when GTP-bound.
explanation.whyCorrect: HRAS is a member of the Ras family of membrane-bound G proteins that toggle between an active GTP-bound state and an inactive GDP-bound state. In the GTP-bound state, Ras drives pro-growth signaling through the MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathways.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ABL encodes a nonreceptor tyrosine kinase, not a GTP-binding G protein.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BRAF encodes a serine/threonine kinase that phosphorylates MEK; it does not bind GTP as its switch mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EGFR encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase activated by ligand binding, not a GTP-binding G protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PIK3CA encodes a catalytic subunit of PI3K, a lipid kinase, not a GTP-binding G protein.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with insidious fatigue and is found to have 110,000 white blood cells/microL. A bone marrow biopsy is hypercellular with a predominance of granulocytes and increased small, hypolobated megakaryocytes. A therapy targeting which of the following oncogenic protein products would be most helpful?

explanation.summary: Chronic myeloid leukemia is driven by the BCR::ABL fusion, the target of imatinib.
explanation.whyCorrect: The presentation of marked leukocytosis with a hypercellular, granulocyte-rich marrow and small hyposegmented megakaryocytes is classic for chronic myeloid leukemia, which is driven by the constitutively active BCR::ABL tyrosine kinase fusion. Imatinib (Gleevec) targets this fusion protein and is effective in many cases.

whyWrongByChoice.B: BRAF is targeted in cutaneous melanoma, not the myeloid disorder described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EGFR alterations are seen in lung adenocarcinoma, not chronic myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MEK inhibitors such as trametinib are used in melanoma, not for this leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PIK3CA is targeted in advanced breast carcinoma, not in this marrow disorder.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A pediatric patient presents with an abdominal mass that undergoes biopsy. Microscopic examination shows small round blue cells arranged around a textured, acellular center, and molecular testing reveals MYCN amplification. What is the most likely identity of this neoplasm?

explanation.summary: Neuroblastoma is a neural crest tumor with Homer Wright rosettes and MYCN amplification.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neuroblastoma is a malignant neural crest tumor, the most common neoplasm of the first year of life, that often arises in the adrenal gland or abdominal sites. It is composed of small round blue cells that may form Homer Wright rosettes (cells radially arranged around a fibrillar acellular center), and MYCN amplification is its major oncogenic driver and a poor prognostic factor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Burkitt lymphoma shows a starry-sky pattern of B-cells with tingible-body macrophages and an IG::MYC rearrangement, not MYCN amplification.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia is a marrow-based myeloid malignancy driven by BCR::ABL, not a pediatric abdominal small round blue cell tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cutaneous melanoma arises from melanocytes and shows brown melanin pigment, not small round blue cells with rosettes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma forms duct-like glandular spaces and is driven by KRAS, not MYCN.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A never-smoker presents with cough and hemoptysis, and imaging reveals a lung mass. Biopsy confirms lung adenocarcinoma whose cells overexpress EGFR. Which of the following agents directly blocks the extracellular domain of this receptor to prevent ligand binding?

explanation.summary: Necitumumab is a monoclonal antibody that blocks the extracellular domain of EGFR.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lung adenocarcinomas that overexpress EGFR can be treated with necitumumab, a monoclonal antibody that binds the extracellular domain of EGFR and prevents ligand binding and subsequent receptor activation. Unlike squamous cell and small cell lung carcinoma, many lung adenocarcinomas occur in never-smokers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpelisib is a PI3K inhibitor used for PIK3CA-mutated breast cancer, not an EGFR antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dabrafenib is a small-molecule BRAF inhibitor used in melanoma, not an EGFR-blocking antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor of the BCR::ABL fusion in CML, not an EGFR antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trametinib is a MEK inhibitor and acts downstream in the MAPK pathway, not at the EGFR receptor.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A brown, irregular skin lesion is excised from an adult with a history of ultraviolet light exposure, and histology shows melanin pigment within transformed melanocytes. The tumor harbors an activating BRAF mutation. In the MAPK cascade, BRAF directly phosphorylates and activates which of the following?

explanation.summary: In the MAPK pathway, BRAF phosphorylates MEK, which then activates ERK.
explanation.whyCorrect: BRAF is a RAF-family kinase in the MAPK pathway. RAF kinases phosphorylate and activate MEK, which in turn phosphorylates and activates ERK; ERK then drives proliferation and survival through cyclin D1 and MYC. Cutaneous melanoma commonly carries activating BRAF mutations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AKT is activated within the PI3K/AKT pathway downstream of PIP3, not directly by BRAF.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ERK is activated by MEK, one step downstream of BRAF, not directly by BRAF.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PI3K is activated by GTP-bound Ras, not by BRAF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ras lies upstream of BRAF and activates it, so BRAF does not phosphorylate Ras.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old smoker reports decreased appetite, weight loss, altered bowel movements, and fatigue. A pancreatic biopsy shows neoplastic cells forming duct-like glandular spaces. Which of the following gene mutations is most commonly responsible for this malignancy?

explanation.summary: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is most commonly driven by KRAS mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical picture of weight loss, decreased appetite, and altered bowel habits in a smoker with pancreatic duct-like glandular spaces on biopsy indicates pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, in which KRAS mutations are extremely common. Cigarette smoking is the leading risk factor due to inhaled carcinogens that damage DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BCR::ABL drives chronic myeloid leukemia, not pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BRAF mutations characterize cutaneous melanoma and other tumors, not pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MYCN amplification drives neuroblastoma, a pediatric tumor, not pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PIK3CA gain-of-function mutations are associated with breast carcinoma, not pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes PTEN and its role in cellular signaling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A G protein that toggles between GTP- and GDP-bound states

choices.label: B
choices.text: A receptor tyrosine kinase activated by ligand binding

choices.label: C
choices.text: A transcription factor that drives cell-cycle gene expression

choices.label: D
choices.text: A tumor suppressor that converts PIP3 back to PIP2, shutting down signaling

choices.label: E
choices.text: An oncogene amplified in breast cancer that increases pro-growth signaling

explanation.summary: PTEN is a tumor suppressor that dephosphorylates PIP3 to PIP2 to shut off PI3K/AKT signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: PTEN is a negative regulator of the PI3K/AKT pathway. It converts PIP3 back to PIP2, shutting down the signaling cascade and preventing AKT activation; loss of PTEN therefore removes a brake on pro-growth signaling, consistent with its function as a tumor suppressor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A GTP/GDP-toggling G protein describes Ras, not PTEN.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A receptor tyrosine kinase description fits EGFR, not PTEN.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A transcription factor that drives cell-cycle genes describes MYC, not PTEN.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PTEN opposes growth signaling rather than promoting it; PIK3CA and AKT are the pro-growth players amplified in breast cancer.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A biopsy of an enlarged lymph node shows a diffuse growth of medium-sized lymphocytes with a starry-sky appearance created by interspersed tingible-body macrophages. The characteristic t(8;14) translocation places which of the following genes under the control of the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, causing its overexpression?

explanation.summary: Burkitt lymphoma results from t(8;14), an IG::MYC rearrangement that overexpresses MYC.
explanation.whyCorrect: The starry-sky pattern with tingible-body macrophages describes Burkitt lymphoma, a B-cell malignancy driven by the t(8;14) IG::MYC rearrangement. The immunoglobulin heavy chain locus normally produces high levels of IG in B-cells, so juxtaposition places MYC under its control and drives MYC overexpression as an oncogene.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ABL is involved in the BCR::ABL fusion of chronic myeloid leukemia, not Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BRAF is an oncogene in melanoma and other tumors, not the gene rearranged in Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EGFR is altered in lung adenocarcinoma and is not involved in the t(8;14) rearrangement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MYCN amplification drives neuroblastoma; Burkitt lymphoma involves MYC, not MYCN.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A woman with advanced breast carcinoma is found to have a gain-of-function mutation in PIK3CA, the gene encoding a catalytic subunit of PI3K. Which of the following targeted therapies is most appropriate for this molecular alteration?

explanation.summary: PIK3CA-mutated breast cancer can be treated with the PI3K inhibitor alpelisib.
explanation.whyCorrect: PIK3CA gain-of-function mutations cause overactivation of PI3K and downstream pro-growth signaling in breast carcinoma. Certain patients with advanced breast cancer demonstrating PIK3CA mutations can be treated with PI3K inhibitors such as alpelisib.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cetuximab is a monoclonal antibody against EGFR approved for colorectal adenocarcinoma, not a PI3K inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dabrafenib is a BRAF inhibitor used in melanoma, not for PIK3CA-mutated breast cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Imatinib targets the BCR::ABL fusion in chronic myeloid leukemia, not PI3K.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trametinib is a MEK inhibitor acting in the MAPK pathway, not on PI3K.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: Ras signaling is limited by GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) that bind Ras and accelerate hydrolysis of GTP to GDP, returning Ras to its inactive state. A gene that encodes such a GAP would most appropriately be classified as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A guanine nucleotide exchange factor gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: A housekeeping gene unrelated to growth control

choices.label: C
choices.text: A proto-oncogene requiring gain-of-function to transform

explanation.summary: A GAP turns Ras off, so its gene acts as a tumor suppressor.
explanation.whyCorrect: GTPase-activating proteins accelerate the intrinsic GTPase activity of Ras, converting active GTP-bound Ras to inactive GDP-bound Ras and safeguarding against unchecked pro-growth signaling. Because this action restrains growth, loss of such a gene would promote tumorigenesis, which is the defining behavior of a tumor suppressor gene.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) removes GDP to activate Ras, the opposite function of a GAP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A GAP is directly involved in growth control by limiting Ras signaling, so it is not merely a housekeeping gene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proto-oncogenes become harmful through activating (gain-of-function) mutations, whereas a GAP restrains signaling and is inactivated by loss-of-function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An oncogene promotes excessive growth; a GAP does the opposite by shutting Ras off.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A patient in their late 40s has fatigue, easy bleeding, weight loss, and splenomegaly. Peripheral blood shows leukocytosis, and a bone marrow biopsy shows hypercellularity with increased granulocytes, eosinophilia, and increased megakaryocytes of reduced size with nuclear hyposegmentation. Which cytogenetic abnormality is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Chronic myeloid leukemia is caused by the t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome producing BCR::ABL.
explanation.whyCorrect: This presentation is chronic myeloid leukemia, which is driven by translocation of the ABL oncogene from chromosome 9 next to the BCR locus on chromosome 22, t(9;22). This Philadelphia chromosome creates the BCR::ABL fusion that constitutively activates tyrosine kinase signaling and drives the uncontrolled granulocytic proliferation seen here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BRAF V600E is characteristic of cutaneous melanoma, not this leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: KRAS point mutation is common in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, not chronic myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MYCN amplification drives neuroblastoma, a pediatric solid tumor, not chronic myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: t(8;14) causes Burkitt lymphoma, a B-cell malignancy, not this myeloid marrow picture.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: In the MAPK pathway, activation of ERK drives proliferation in part by promoting progression of the cell cycle from the G1 to the S phase. Which of the following proteins most directly mediates this G1-to-S transition?

explanation.summary: ERK drives proliferation through cyclin D1, which moves the cell cycle from G1 to S phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the MAPK cascade, RAF phosphorylates MEK, which activates ERK; ERK then drives proliferation and survival through cyclin D1, a protein that helps push the cell cycle from the G1 to the S phase, and through the transcription factor MYC.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A guanine nucleotide exchange factor activates Ras by removing GDP; it acts upstream and does not directly control cell-cycle phase transitions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: mTOR contributes to cellular metabolism, growth, and survival in the PI3K/AKT pathway rather than directly driving G1-to-S progression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PIP3 is a lipid second messenger in the PI3K/AKT pathway that activates AKT, not a cell-cycle protein driving G1 to S.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PTEN is a tumor suppressor that shuts down PI3K/AKT signaling and does not promote the G1-to-S transition.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher characterizes a normal cellular gene whose product promotes cell proliferation and growth in response to external signals. When this gene acquires an activating mutation, its product drives excessive growth independently of external signaling. Which of the following terms best describes the normal, unmutated gene?

explanation.summary: Proto-oncogenes are normal growth-promoting genes; activating mutations convert them into oncogenes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that promote cell proliferation and growth. Activating mutations of these genes result in oncogenes, which are mutated genes that cause excessive growth independently of external signaling. The unmutated gene in the vignette is therefore a proto-oncogene.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A GTPase-activating protein shuts off Ras signaling and behaves as a tumor suppressor, not a growth-promoting gene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The immunoglobulin heavy chain gene encodes an antibody subunit in B-cells and is not itself a growth-promoting gene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An oncogene is the mutated, activated version of the gene, not the normal gene described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A tumor suppressor gene restrains growth; loss of its function promotes cancer, which is the opposite of the growth-promoting gene described.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman who has never used tobacco presents with cough, shortness of breath, and hemoptysis. Imaging reveals a lung mass, and biopsy shows lung adenocarcinoma. Which of the following features most clearly distinguishes this tumor from squamous cell carcinoma and small cell carcinoma of the lung?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Detection as a mass on imaging

explanation.summary: Unlike squamous and small cell lung carcinoma, lung adenocarcinoma frequently occurs in never-smokers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung and small cell lung carcinoma are both associated with tobacco smoke, whereas many patients with lung adenocarcinoma are never-smokers. This epidemiologic difference is a key distinguishing feature of lung adenocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A mass on imaging is common to lung carcinomas and is not a distinguishing feature.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transformed melanocytes give rise to melanoma, not lung adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cough, shortness of breath, and hemoptysis are presenting symptoms of lung masses generally and do not distinguish adenocarcinoma from other lung carcinomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A strong tobacco association characterizes squamous cell and small cell carcinoma, not lung adenocarcinoma.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A biopsy of a peripheral lung mass shows neoplastic epithelial cells that in some areas form solid, invasive nests and in adjacent areas line the pre-existing alveolar septa. Which of the following histologic growth patterns is characteristic of the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neoplastic cells forming duct-like glandular spaces

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neoplastic cells growing along alveolar walls

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pigmented cells containing brown melanin granules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small round blue cells surrounding fibrillar centers

explanation.summary: Lung adenocarcinoma can form solid invasive nests or grow along the alveolar walls.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lung adenocarcinoma shows many different histologic appearances. It can form solid, invasive nests or grow along the alveolar walls, and both patterns may coexist in a single tumor, as in this biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diffuse medium-sized lymphocytes with tingible-body macrophages describe the starry sky pattern of Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Duct-like glandular spaces describe pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, not a lung tumor lining alveoli.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Brown melanin pigment in neoplastic cells is a clue to cutaneous melanoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Small round blue cells around fibrillar acellular centers are Homer Wright rosettes of neuroblastoma.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with colorectal adenocarcinoma is found to have tumor cells that overexpress EGFR. Which of the following agents prevents ligand binding to EGFR and is approved for this tumor type?

explanation.summary: Cetuximab blocks ligand binding to EGFR and is approved for colorectal adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Non-lung tumors with EGFR overexpression can be treated with strategies similar to those used in lung adenocarcinoma. Cetuximab prevents ligand binding to EGFR and is approved for colorectal adenocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpelisib is a PI3K inhibitor used in PIK3CA-mutated breast cancer and does not act on EGFR.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dabrafenib is a BRAF inhibitor used in melanoma, not an EGFR-directed agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor of the BCR::ABL fusion in chronic myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trametinib is a MEK inhibitor acting in the MAPK pathway, not at the EGFR receptor.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 54-year-old never-smoker with lung adenocarcinoma has no EGFR alteration on molecular testing, but an ALK fusion is identified, prompting selection of a different targeted therapy. The ALK protein belongs to which of the following classes?

explanation.summary: Lung adenocarcinomas may carry ALK receptor tyrosine kinase fusions requiring different targeted therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: A particular type of cancer can have different molecular drivers. Lung adenocarcinomas may demonstrate KRAS (G protein) mutations or ALK (receptor tyrosine kinase) fusions in addition to EGFR alterations, and each would require a different targeted therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A lipid kinase describes PI3K, which phosphorylates PIP2, not ALK.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A membrane-bound G protein describes KRAS, another alternative driver in lung adenocarcinoma, not ALK.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A serine/threonine kinase describes BRAF or AKT, not ALK.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A transcription factor describes MYC, not ALK.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A growth factor binds its receptor tyrosine kinase, and a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) is recruited to Ras at the plasma membrane. Which of the following best describes the action of the GEF on Ras?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accelerates intrinsic GTPase activity of Ras

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrolyzes GTP to GDP, inactivating Ras

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phosphorylates Ras on serine and threonine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Removes GDP so that GTP can bind, activating Ras

choices.label: E
choices.text: Removes Ras from the plasma membrane

explanation.summary: GEFs remove GDP from Ras so GTP can bind, producing the active Ras form.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ras proteins toggle between an active GTP-bound state and an inactive GDP-bound form. Guanine nucleotide exchange factors aid in removing GDP so that GTP can bind the G protein, leading to the active Ras form and pro-growth signaling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Accelerating GTPase activity is the role of GTPase-activating proteins, which oppose, rather than promote, Ras activation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydrolysis of GTP to GDP is GTPase activity, which inactivates Ras; it is an intrinsic ability of Ras, not the action of a GEF.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ras is regulated by nucleotide binding, not by serine/threonine phosphorylation from a GEF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ras is a membrane-bound G protein; the GEF exchanges nucleotides rather than displacing Ras from the membrane.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A colorectal cancer carries a KRAS point mutation that abolishes the intrinsic GTPase activity of the Ras protein and prevents GTPase-activating proteins from accelerating GTP hydrolysis. Which of the following is the most likely consequence for the mutant Ras protein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dependence on GEF activity for signaling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhanced conversion of PIP3 to PIP2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Persistence in the GDP-bound inactive state

choices.label: E
choices.text: Persistence in the GTP-bound active state

explanation.summary: Loss of GTPase activity locks Ras in its GTP-bound active state, causing constitutive pro-growth signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ras signaling is limited by GTPase activity, the removal of a phosphate from GTP to form GDP, which is an intrinsic ability of Ras and is also aided by GTPase-activating proteins. Point mutations in RAS identified in many cancers result in constitutive activation of pro-growth signals because the protein cannot return to the inactive GDP-bound form.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A Ras protein that cannot hydrolyze GTP no longer needs GEF-mediated exchange to stay active; it signals constitutively.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Conversion of PIP3 to PIP2 is the action of PTEN and is unrelated to Ras GTPase activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mutation affects hydrolysis of bound GTP, not the ability to bind guanine nucleotides.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Without GTP hydrolysis, Ras cannot return to the GDP-bound inactive form; it remains active.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: Molecular profiling is performed on a cutaneous melanoma that lacks a BRAF mutation, and an activating mutation in a RAS family gene is identified. Which RAS family member is most frequently mutated in melanoma, a subset of thyroid cancers, and certain lymphomas?

explanation.summary: NRAS mutations are frequently encountered in melanoma, a subset of thyroid cancers, and certain lymphomas.
explanation.whyCorrect: The major RAS genes altered in human cancers are HRAS, KRAS, and NRAS, and the types of mutations differ by tumor type. NRAS mutations are frequently encountered in melanomas, a subset of thyroid cancers, and certain lymphomas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HRAS is a RAS family member but is not the one the brick associates with melanoma, thyroid cancer, and lymphomas.
whyWrongByChoice.B: KRAS mutations are common in lung adenocarcinoma, pancreatic cancer, and colorectal cancer rather than melanoma and lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MYCN is not a RAS family gene; its amplification drives neuroblastoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PIK3CA is not a RAS family gene; it encodes a PI3K subunit mutated in breast carcinoma.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history is diagnosed with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Which of the following best explains the relationship between his smoking history and this malignancy?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nicotine binds the EGFR extracellular domain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tobacco smoke amplifies MYCN gene copies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tobacco smoke converts PIP3 to PIP2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tobacco smoke induces a t(9;22) translocation

explanation.summary: Cigarette smoking is the leading risk factor for pancreatic cancer because inhaled carcinogens damage DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cigarette smoking is the leading risk factor for pancreatic cancer due to the inhalation of carcinogens that damage DNA. This DNA damage underlies the acquisition of oncogenic mutations such as those in KRAS that are extremely common in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: EGFR activation is by ligand binding to the extracellular domain; nicotine binding is not the mechanism of smoking-related pancreatic cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MYCN amplification drives neuroblastoma and is not a consequence of tobacco smoke.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Conversion of PIP3 to PIP2 is the tumor-suppressive action of PTEN, not an effect of tobacco smoke.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The t(9;22) translocation is the Philadelphia chromosome of chronic myeloid leukemia, not a smoking-related event in the pancreas.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman is diagnosed with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma harboring a KRAS mutation. Her family asks about the expected outcome and available targeted treatment. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Almost always fatal, with Ras-pathway therapies still experimental

choices.label: B
choices.text: Highly curable, because Ras-pathway therapies are now standard of care

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rarely fatal once treated with the PI3K inhibitor alpelisib

choices.label: D
choices.text: Usually cured by dabrafenib directed at the MAPK signaling pathway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Usually cured by imatinib directed at the mutant kinase product

explanation.summary: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is almost always fatal; Ras-pathway-targeting therapies remain experimental.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is almost always fatal. Experimental investigations are exploring therapies targeting the Ras pathway, but these are not established curative treatments.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ras-pathway therapies are experimental, not standard, and the tumor is not highly curable.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpelisib is a PI3K inhibitor for PIK3CA-mutated breast cancer and does not change the poor prognosis of pancreatic cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dabrafenib is a BRAF inhibitor used in certain melanomas, not a cure for KRAS-driven pancreatic cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Imatinib targets the BCR::ABL fusion of chronic myeloid leukemia, not mutant KRAS in pancreatic cancer.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: BRAF is a common oncogene in many cancers, including cutaneous melanoma and papillary thyroid cancer. Which of the following additional malignancies is also commonly associated with BRAF alterations?

explanation.summary: BRAF is a common oncogene in cutaneous melanoma, papillary thyroid cancer, and hairy cell leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: BRAF, a member of the RAF family of protein kinases in the MAPK pathway, is a common oncogene in many cancers, including cutaneous melanoma, papillary thyroid cancer, and hairy cell leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Burkitt lymphoma is driven by the IG::MYC rearrangement from t(8;14), not BRAF.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia is driven by the BCR::ABL fusion from t(9;22), not BRAF.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neuroblastoma is driven by MYCN, not BRAF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is characteristically driven by KRAS mutation, not BRAF.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with metastatic cutaneous melanoma harboring a BRAF V600E mutation is started on dabrafenib. His oncologist adds trametinib to target a second point in the same signaling cascade. Trametinib inhibits which of the following proteins?

explanation.summary: Trametinib is a MEK inhibitor that can be paired with the BRAF inhibitor dabrafenib in melanoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: BRAF inhibitors such as dabrafenib can be paired with therapeutics that target other aspects of the MAPK pathway, such as trametinib, a MEK inhibitor. MEK is the kinase directly phosphorylated and activated by RAF kinases, so the combination blocks two consecutive steps of the same pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AKT is in the PI3K/AKT pathway; AKT inhibitors are under investigation but trametinib is not one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BRAF is the target of dabrafenib, the drug the patient is already receiving.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PI3K is part of the separate PI3K/AKT pathway and is targeted by alpelisib, not trametinib.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ras lies upstream of BRAF and is not the target of trametinib.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: GTP-bound Ras activates phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) at the plasma membrane. Which of the following reactions is directly catalyzed by PI3K?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrolysis of GTP to GDP on Ras

explanation.summary: PI3K phosphorylates PIP2 to form PIP3, which leads to activation of AKT.
explanation.whyCorrect: GTP-bound Ras activates PI3K, which in turn phosphorylates phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3). PIP3 action then leads to activation of AKT, a key signaling protein for growth, survival, and proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dephosphorylation of PIP3 back to PIP2 is the action of PTEN, which shuts down the pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GTP hydrolysis on Ras is intrinsic GTPase activity aided by GTPase-activating proteins, not PI3K.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ERK is phosphorylated by MEK in the MAPK pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MEK is phosphorylated by RAF kinases in the MAPK pathway.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: Following activation of PI3K, the accumulation of PIP3 leads to activation of AKT. Which of the following best characterizes the AKT protein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lipid kinase acting on a membrane phospholipid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Membrane-bound G protein cycling GTP and GDP

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phosphatase converting PIP3 back to PIP2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receptor tyrosine kinase activated by ligand

explanation.summary: AKT is a serine and threonine kinase with more than 150 protein targets that drives growth, survival, and proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: PIP3 action leads to activation of AKT, a serine and threonine kinase that has over 150 protein targets and is a key signaling protein for growth, survival, and proliferation. Activation of mTOR is also achieved downstream.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A lipid kinase acting on a membrane phospholipid describes PI3K, which phosphorylates PIP2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A membrane-bound G protein cycling GTP and GDP describes Ras.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A phosphatase converting PIP3 back to PIP2 describes PTEN.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A ligand-activated receptor tyrosine kinase describes EGFR.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: Activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway also leads to activation of mTOR. Which of the following cellular processes is mTOR described as contributing to?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of PIP3 back to PIP2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrolysis of GTP bound to Ras

explanation.summary: mTOR, activated downstream of PI3K/AKT, contributes to cellular metabolism, growth, and survival.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the PI3K/AKT pathway, activation of mTOR is also achieved. mTOR is a protein that contributes to cellular metabolism, growth, and survival, complementing AKT's roles in growth, survival, and proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Converting PIP3 back to PIP2 is the function of PTEN, which shuts the pathway down.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GTP hydrolysis on Ras is intrinsic GTPase activity aided by GTPase-activating proteins, not a function of mTOR.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphorylation of MEK is performed by RAF kinases in the MAPK pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immunoglobulin heavy chain production is a normal B-cell function related to the IG locus, not mTOR.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A tumor is found to have inactivating mutations in both copies of PTEN. Compared with a normal cell receiving the same growth factor stimulus, which of the following changes in the PI3K/AKT pathway would most directly result from this loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased GTP-bound Ras with reduced MEK activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased mTOR activity with reduced cell growth

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased GTPase activity with Ras inactivation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased PIP2 with decreased AKT activation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased PIP3 with increased AKT activation

explanation.summary: Loss of PTEN prevents conversion of PIP3 to PIP2, so PIP3 accumulates and AKT signaling persists.
explanation.whyCorrect: PTEN is a negative regulator of the PI3K/AKT pathway and acts to convert PIP3 back to PIP2, shutting down the signaling cascade. When PTEN function is lost, PIP3 generated by PI3K is not removed, so PIP3 accumulates and continues to drive activation of AKT and downstream mTOR, promoting growth, survival, and proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PTEN acts on PIP3, not on Ras; Ras GTP loading and MEK activation are not directly changed by PTEN loss.
whyWrongByChoice.B: mTOR lies downstream of AKT; with more AKT activation, mTOR activity would increase, not decrease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GTPase activity on Ras is controlled by intrinsic Ras activity and GTPase-activating proteins, not by PTEN.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PTEN loss reduces, not increases, the conversion of PIP3 to PIP2, so PIP2 does not accumulate and AKT is not suppressed.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with ovarian carcinoma has tumor sequencing showing marked amplification and overexpression of AKT with increased pro-growth signaling. Which of the following best describes the current status of therapy directed at this specific alteration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AKT inhibitors are under investigation in clinical trials

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpelisib is the approved standard for AKT amplification

choices.label: C
choices.text: Imatinib is the approved standard for AKT amplification

choices.label: D
choices.text: Necitumumab is the approved standard for AKT amplification

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trametinib is the approved standard for AKT amplification

explanation.summary: AKT amplification occurs in breast, ovarian, and colorectal carcinomas; AKT inhibitors are still under investigation.
explanation.whyCorrect: AKT overexpression and amplification, leading to increased pro-growth signaling, has been reported in breast, ovarian, and colorectal carcinomas, among others. AKT inhibitors are under investigation in clinical trials, representing another potential application of treatment to the PI3K/AKT pathway rather than an established standard.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpelisib is a PI3K inhibitor used for PIK3CA-mutated breast cancer; it is not an approved AKT inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imatinib targets the BCR::ABL fusion in chronic myeloid leukemia and does not target AKT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Necitumumab is an EGFR-blocking antibody used in lung adenocarcinoma and does not target AKT.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trametinib is a MEK inhibitor in the MAPK pathway, not an AKT-directed agent.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A pathologist reviewing a pediatric abdominal tumor identifies ring-like arrangements of small round blue cells around pink, textured, acellular centers. Which of the following statements about this histologic finding is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Composed of tingible-body macrophages around lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Indicates MYCN amplification and a poor prognosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Indicates neoplastic B-cell origin of the tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Not specific for neuroblastoma and seen in other embryonal tumors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Specific for neuroblastoma and excludes other embryonal tumors

explanation.summary: Homer Wright rosettes are helpful in neuroblastoma but are not specific and occur in other embryonal tumors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The finding described is a Homer Wright rosette, a ring-like arrangement of tumor cells around a pink, textured, acellular center. It is a helpful pathologic feature in neuroblastoma, but Homer Wright rosettes are not specific for neuroblastoma and can be seen in other embryonal tumors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tingible-body macrophages among lymphocytes produce the starry sky pattern of Burkitt lymphoma, not rosettes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rosette formation is a histologic feature; MYCN amplification is a separate molecular finding present in only a subset of neuroblastomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neoplastic B-cells characterize Burkitt lymphoma, not the small round blue cells of neural crest origin forming rosettes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Homer Wright rosettes do not exclude other embryonal tumors, in which they can also be seen.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: The ABL kinase, whose constitutive activity drives chronic myeloid leukemia after fusion with BCR, is best classified as which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lipid kinase of the PI3K family

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serine/threonine kinase of the RAF family

explanation.summary: ABL is a nonreceptor tyrosine kinase; its BCR::ABL fusion is constitutively active in CML.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many non-receptor tyrosine kinases involved in stimulating cell proliferation and survival may be altered in cancers. An illustrative example is the constitutively active ABL tyrosine kinase in chronic myeloid leukemia, where BCR::ABL is a nonreceptor tyrosine kinase fusion created by chromosomal translocation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A ligand-activated receptor tyrosine kinase describes EGFR or ALK, which span the membrane, unlike ABL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A lipid kinase of the PI3K family describes the product of PIK3CA, not ABL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A membrane-bound G protein describes the Ras family, not ABL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A serine/threonine kinase of the RAF family describes BRAF, not ABL.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: Both Burkitt lymphoma and chronic myeloid leukemia are driven by chromosomal translocations that activate an oncogene. Which of the following best distinguishes the molecular consequence of t(8;14) from that of t(9;22)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: t(8;14) amplifies MYC gene copies, whereas t(9;22) amplifies ABL gene copies

choices.label: B
choices.text: t(8;14) creates an IG::MYC fusion kinase, whereas t(9;22) overexpresses intact ABL via the BCR locus

choices.label: C
choices.text: t(8;14) deletes a tumor suppressor gene, whereas t(9;22) deletes the BCR locus

choices.label: D
choices.text: t(8;14) introduces an activating MYC point mutation, whereas t(9;22) introduces an ABL point mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: t(8;14) overexpresses intact MYC via the IG locus, whereas t(9;22) creates a BCR::ABL fusion kinase

explanation.summary: t(8;14) places MYC under IG heavy chain control causing overexpression; t(9;22) creates a constitutively active BCR::ABL fusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Burkitt lymphoma, the t(8;14) IG::MYC rearrangement places MYC next to the IG heavy chain locus, which is normally highly expressed in B-cells, so MYC becomes overexpressed as an oncogene rather than being tightly controlled. In chronic myeloid leukemia, translocation of the ABL oncogene from chromosome 9 next to the BCR locus on chromosome 22 forms a BCR::ABL fusion whose constitutively active tyrosine kinase drives uncontrolled proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neither translocation works by gene amplification; amplification with extra gene copies is the MYCN mechanism in neuroblastoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the two mechanisms: the fusion kinase belongs to CML (BCR::ABL), and the overexpressed intact gene belongs to Burkitt lymphoma (MYC).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither translocation is described as deleting a tumor suppressor or the BCR locus; both activate oncogenes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither translocation acts through a point mutation; point mutations are the mechanism for RAS activation.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: MYC is an important transcription factor whose proto-oncogene activates many genes that contribute to cancer formation. Which of the following groups of processes is driven by MYC target genes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cell cycle progression, ribosome assembly, and pluripotency

choices.label: B
choices.text: GTP hydrolysis, GDP release, and Ras inactivation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunoglobulin assembly, antibody secretion, and B-cell homing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Melanin synthesis, UV damage repair, and melanocyte maturation

choices.label: E
choices.text: PIP3 dephosphorylation, AKT inhibition, and mTOR suppression

explanation.summary: MYC activates genes involved in the cell cycle, ribosome assembly, and pluripotency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transcription factors are proteins involved in transcribing RNA from DNA, and MYC is an important example. The MYC proto-oncogene activates many genes that contribute to cancer formation, such as those involved in the cell cycle, ribosome assembly, and pluripotency, among others.

whyWrongByChoice.B: GTP hydrolysis and Ras inactivation are functions of intrinsic GTPase activity and GTPase-activating proteins, not MYC targets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunoglobulin production is a normal B-cell function of the IG locus; it is the IG locus, not MYC, that drives it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Melanin synthesis relates to melanocytes and melanoma histology, not to MYC target genes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PIP3 dephosphorylation and shutdown of AKT signaling describe the tumor-suppressive action of PTEN, not growth-promoting MYC targets.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma with an activating KRAS mutation shows markedly increased MYC protein, yet no MYC translocation or amplification is detected. Which of the following best explains the elevated MYC activity in this tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A BCR::ABL fusion protein phosphorylating MYC

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amplification of MYCN substituting for MYC in tumor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: An undetected IG::MYC rearrangement in the tumor cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of PTEN increasing MYC transcription in tumor cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of MYC downstream of oncogenic Ras and MAPK signaling

explanation.summary: MYC upregulation is a downstream consequence of oncogenic Ras and MAPK activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The mechanisms of increased MYC activity differ by tumor type. Beyond translocation (Burkitt lymphoma) and amplification (MYCN in neuroblastoma), upregulation of MYC is also a downstream consequence of other signaling alterations, such as oncogenic activation of Ras and MAPK signaling, in which ERK drives proliferation through cyclin D1 and MYC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BCR::ABL is the driver of chronic myeloid leukemia and is not present in KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MYCN amplification is the mechanism in neuroblastoma; it is a distinct gene and does not explain MYC protein elevation here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The IG::MYC rearrangement is the mechanism in Burkitt lymphoma, a B-cell malignancy, and the stem states no translocation was found.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PTEN acts on the PI3K/AKT pathway by converting PIP3 to PIP2; the brick links MYC upregulation to Ras/MAPK signaling, not PTEN loss.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is brought in for abdominal distension and constipation. Imaging shows a mass arising from the adrenal gland. Which of the following statements about the most likely tumor is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Characterized by a starry sky histologic pattern

choices.label: C
choices.text: Derived from neoplastic B-cells of germinal centers

choices.label: E
choices.text: The most common neoplasm arising in the first year of life

explanation.summary: Neuroblastoma is the most common neoplasm of the first year of life and often arises in the adrenal gland.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neuroblastoma is a malignant neoplasm of neural crest origin that is the third most common pediatric tumor and the most common neoplasm arising in the first year of life. Because neuroblastomas often arise in the adrenal gland or abdominal sites, the first signs and symptoms may be abdominal distension or constipation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The starry sky pattern belongs to Burkitt lymphoma; neuroblastoma shows small round blue cells and Homer Wright rosettes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transformed melanocytes give rise to melanoma, not an adrenal tumor of infancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neoplastic B-cells characterize Burkitt lymphoma, not this neural crest tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Activating BRAF mutations characterize cutaneous melanoma and related tumors, not neuroblastoma, which is driven by MYCN.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy shows a diffuse proliferation of medium-sized B-cells with scattered pale macrophages containing ingested debris, producing a starry sky appearance. In non-neoplastic tissue, the macrophages responsible for this pattern are normally found in which of the following locations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alveolar walls of the lung parenchyma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vascular sinusoids of the bone marrow

explanation.summary: Tingible-body macrophages, which create the starry sky of Burkitt lymphoma, normally reside in lymph node germinal centers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Burkitt lymphoma is often described as having a starry sky appearance composed of a diffuse growth of medium-sized lymphocytes with interspersed tingible-body macrophages. A tingible-body macrophage is a type of macrophage that is usually found in the germinal centers of lymph nodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alveolar walls are where lung adenocarcinoma cells may grow, not where tingible-body macrophages are normally found.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The adrenal gland is a common site of origin for neuroblastoma, not the normal location of tingible-body macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pancreatic ducts are the site of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, unrelated to tingible-body macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bone marrow is where the granulocyte and megakaryocyte changes of chronic myeloid leukemia are seen, not the usual home of tingible-body macrophages.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A healthy newborn is found to carry a germline mutation that inactivates one copy of a tumor suppressor gene. His cells currently divide and function normally, and he has no tumors. Which of the following best explains why his cells remain phenotypically normal at this time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both alleles must be mutated in the germline for any cancer to develop

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epigenetic silencing has repaired the mutant allele

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gene has been converted into an activated oncogene

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mutation acts in a dominant-negative fashion

choices.label: E
choices.text: The remaining wild-type allele preserves near-normal protein function

explanation.summary: By the two-hit (Knudson) hypothesis, one intact tumor suppressor allele is usually enough to maintain normal function.
explanation.whyCorrect: In most cases the functionally intact tumor suppressor allele compensates for the mutant allele, resulting in relatively normal cellular function. The cell is now vulnerable to a 'second hit' that knocks out the remaining allele, at which point uncontrolled proliferation can occur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only one allele is mutated in the germline; the second hit occurs later as a somatic mutation, so germline biallelic mutation is not required.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epigenetic changes silence gene expression; they do not repair a mutated allele.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of function of a tumor suppressor is not the same as activation of a proto-oncogene into an oncogene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tumor suppressors are typically lost through the two-hit loss-of-function model; a single mutant allele does not poison the wild-type product here.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 14-month-old girl is diagnosed with retinoblastoma in both eyes. Her father was treated for retinoblastoma as a child. Compared with sporadic, unilateral disease, which of the following best explains this bilateral, familial presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gain-of-function mutation in pRB promotes proliferation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A germline RB1 mutation is present in all retinal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Amplification of the RB1 gene drives tumor growth

choices.label: D
choices.text: Environmental carcinogen exposure caused simultaneous tumors in both eyes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two independent somatic mutations occurred in a single retinal cell of each eye
