explanation.summary: Inherited retinoblastoma carries a germline RB1 mutation in every retinal cell, so a single somatic 'second hit' can produce tumors, including bilateral disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the inherited form, a faulty RB1 allele is present in all somatic (including all retinal) cells. Because only one additional somatic mutation is needed to knock out the remaining allele, tumors readily arise in both eyes, making bilateral disease much more likely than in the sporadic setting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Retinoblastoma results from loss of pRB function, not a gain-of-function mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RB1 is a tumor suppressor that is inactivated (lost), not amplified.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The familial, bilateral pattern reflects an inherited germline mutation, not environmental exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Requiring two separate somatic hits in the same cell describes the sporadic pathway, which typically produces unilateral, single tumors rather than bilateral disease.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought in after his parents noticed his pupil appears white in photographs. On fundoscopic exam the normal red reflex is absent and is replaced by a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria). Which of the following neoplasms is the most likely underlying cause?

explanation.summary: Leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex replacing the red reflex) is an important clinical sign of retinoblastoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leukocoria refers to a white pupillary reflex on direct fundoscopic exam, in contrast to the normal red reflex, and is a key sign suggesting retinoblastoma, an intraocular tumor of childhood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A colonic adenoma is a polypoid gastrointestinal lesion unrelated to the eye.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cutaneous melanoma is a skin malignancy and does not produce a white pupillary reflex.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neurofibromas are peripheral nerve tumors of neurofibromatosis 1 that present as cutaneous nodules, not an intraocular white reflex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osteosarcoma is a malignant bone tumor (associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome); it does not arise in the eye or cause leukocoria.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: Investigators study a retinal cell line in which functional pRB (the retinoblastoma protein) has been completely lost. Compared with normal cells, which of the following changes is most likely?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cells become unable to replicate their DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cells fail to progress from G1 into S phase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cells pass unchecked from G1 into S phase

explanation.summary: pRB restrains the cell cycle at the G1/S checkpoint, so loss of pRB permits uncontrolled entry into S phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: pRB plays an important role in halting the cell cycle, and loss of this protein is permissive to uncontrolled growth and proliferation. Without pRB, cells advance from G1 into S phase without restraint.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of the pRB brake causes proliferation, not permanent arrest in G0.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA replication proceeds (in fact excessively); it is not blocked.
whyWrongByChoice.C: pRB loss removes the restraint on the G1/S transition, so cells advance rather than fail to.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of pRB favors proliferation; it does not primarily increase apoptosis.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: In an unstressed, healthy cell, p53 protein is kept at very low levels. Which of the following mechanisms is most directly responsible for maintaining these low baseline levels?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATM phosphorylates p53 to stabilize it

choices.label: B
choices.text: BAX degrades p53 within the mitochondria

choices.label: E
choices.text: p53 forms tetramers that activate transcription

explanation.summary: In healthy cells MDM2 tags p53 for ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation, keeping p53 levels low.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally p53, a transcription factor, is controlled by MDM2, a protein that tags p53 for proteasomal degradation via ubiquitination. This keeps p53 at low levels until cellular stress downregulates MDM2 and frees p53.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATM phosphorylation occurs in response to DNA damage and raises p53 levels, the opposite of baseline suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BAX is a downstream pro-apoptotic effector transcribed by p53; it does not degrade p53.
whyWrongByChoice.D: p14/ARF stabilizes p53 during oncogenic stress; it is not the baseline mechanism keeping p53 low.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tetramer formation is the active state that follows stabilization, not the mechanism that keeps p53 low.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast carcinoma. Her family history is notable for a brother who had osteosarcoma as a teenager and a mother with early-onset breast cancer. A germline mutation in which of the following genes is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Li-Fraumeni syndrome results from a germline TP53 mutation and predisposes to many cancers, including early breast carcinoma and osteosarcoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is due to a germline mutation of TP53, leaving only one functioning tumor suppressor allele. These patients are at increased risk for developing many cancers, including breast carcinoma and osteosarcoma, matching this family's pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A germline APC mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis with hundreds of colonic polyps, not this breast/osteosarcoma cancer spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: KRAS is a proto-oncogene activated somatically in tumors; it is not the germline gene of this predisposition syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NF1 mutations cause neurofibromatosis 1 with cafe-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, not this cancer pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A germline RB1 mutation classically presents with childhood retinoblastoma (leukocoria), which is absent from this family history.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A cell sustains irreversible DNA damage, and stabilized p53 directs it toward programmed cell death. Which of the following best describes how p53 accomplishes this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds Fas ligand to activate death receptors of the extrinsic pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: It directly cleaves executioner caspases in the cytoplasm

choices.label: C
choices.text: It methylates the promoters of anti-apoptotic genes

choices.label: D
choices.text: It phosphorylates MDM2 to prevent its own degradation

choices.label: E
choices.text: It transcribes pro-apoptotic genes such as BAX

explanation.summary: For irreversible damage, p53 induces apoptosis by transcribing pro-apoptotic genes such as BAX, activating the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: For irreversible damage, p53 guides the cell to apoptosis by directing transcription of pro-apoptotic genes such as BAX, causing cell death through the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway and serving as an immediate safeguard against propagation of a damaged genome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: As taught here, p53 drives the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway through BAX rather than acting primarily through death-receptor/extrinsic signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.B: p53 acts by transcription of target genes, not by directly cleaving caspases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p53 induces apoptosis by transcribing BAX, not by DNA methylation of anti-apoptotic gene promoters.
whyWrongByChoice.D: p53 is a transcription factor; it does not phosphorylate MDM2. It is ATM/Chk2 that phosphorylates p53.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A colonic epithelial cell loses function of the APC protein. Which of the following is the most likely direct consequence?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-catenin is degraded by the proteasome

choices.label: C
choices.text: p53 is stabilized and halts the cell cycle

choices.label: E
choices.text: WNT ligand can no longer bind its surface receptor

explanation.summary: APC normally directs degradation of beta-catenin; loss of APC lets beta-catenin accumulate and drive proliferation with TCF/LEF.
explanation.whyCorrect: APC and the destruction complex normally direct proteasomal degradation of beta-catenin. When APC is lost, the destruction complex cannot form, so beta-catenin is released to interact with the TCF/LEF transcription factor and promote expression of pro-proliferation genes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: With APC lost, the destruction complex cannot form, so beta-catenin is NOT degraded; it accumulates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: APC loss promotes proliferation; it does not stabilize p53 or arrest the cell cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The APC/WNT pathway is separate from Ras; loss of APC does not inhibit Ras signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: APC acts intracellularly; its loss does not affect WNT ligand binding to the surface receptor.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy undergoes colonoscopy because his father developed colon cancer at age 40. Hundreds of adenomatous polyps are found throughout the colon, and he is told he has an essentially 100% lifetime risk of colorectal adenocarcinoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate standard of care?

explanation.summary: Familial adenomatous polyposis carries an essentially 100% risk of colorectal cancer, so prophylactic colectomy is the standard of care.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has familial adenomatous polyposis, with hundreds of adenomatous polyps and an essentially 100% risk of colorectal adenocarcinoma by age 45. For this reason, prophylactic colectomy (removal of the colon) before cancer develops is the standard of care.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Given the essentially 100% cancer risk, surveillance alone is insufficient; definitive colectomy is indicated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no standard chemoprevention that eliminates the near-certain cancer risk; definitive management is surgical.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenectomy is unrelated to colonic polyposis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Corticosteroids do not address the neoplastic adenomatous polyps.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child has multiple cafe-au-lait macules and several soft cutaneous nodules that are tumors of peripheral nerve cells. Genetic testing reveals a loss-of-function mutation on chromosome 17. The affected protein normally functions in which of the following ways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It degrades beta-catenin in the WNT pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinase

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a GTPase-activating protein that inactivates Ras

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a transcription factor that promotes apoptosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: It phosphorylates pRB to advance the cell cycle

explanation.summary: Neurofibromin 1 (NF1, chromosome 17) is a GTPase-activating protein that inactivates Ras; its loss leads to unchecked Ras signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neurofibromin 1 is a GTPase-activating protein that accelerates inactivation of Ras and is encoded by the NF1 gene on chromosome 17. Without its GTPase-activating action, Ras signaling is unchecked, producing the cafe-au-lait macules and neurofibromas of neurofibromatosis 1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Degrading beta-catenin in the WNT pathway describes APC, not neurofibromin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neurofibromin is an intracellular GTPase-activating protein, not a surface receptor tyrosine kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A transcription factor promoting apoptosis describes p53, not neurofibromin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neurofibromin does not phosphorylate pRB; it regulates Ras.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: In the classic colonic adenoma-carcinoma sequence, which accounts for up to 80% of sporadic colorectal adenocarcinomas, which of the following is the initiating (first driver) mutation?

explanation.summary: The classic colonic adenoma-carcinoma sequence begins with a 'first hit' that knocks out APC.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sequence begins with a hit that knocks out the APC gene, either sporadically or inherited, predisposing the cell to a second hit that leads to unchecked beta-catenin-induced signaling and adenoma formation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EGFR is a proto-oncogene altered in various sporadic cancers but is not the initiating mutation of this sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oncogenic KRAS mutation classically follows APC loss to enlarge the adenoma; it is not the initiating event.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RB1 loss is characteristic of retinoblastoma, not the colonic adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of TP53 occurs later in the sequence, driving progression toward carcinoma.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A colorectal cancer shows transcriptional silencing of a tumor suppressor gene despite an intact, non-mutated DNA coding sequence. Which of the following epigenetic mechanisms most likely explains the loss of expression?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chromosomal translocation creating a chimeric fusion protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: A point mutation within the gene's coding region

choices.label: C
choices.text: Amplification of the gene to many copies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypermethylation of CpG islands in the gene's promoter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypomethylation across the body of the gene

explanation.summary: Promoter CpG-island hypermethylation silences transcription without altering the DNA sequence and can inactivate a tumor suppressor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methyl groups at CpG islands normally silence gene promoter regions. DNA hypermethylation (abnormally increased methylation) of a promoter can silence a tumor suppressor gene without changing the coding sequence, matching this scenario.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A translocation is a structural genetic change, and the stem specifies the sequence is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The stem states the coding sequence is intact and non-mutated, excluding a point mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gene amplification increases expression and is a genetic, not epigenetic, change.
whyWrongByChoice.E: DNA hypomethylation de-represses promoters and can allow aberrant oncogene expression, rather than silencing a gene.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is diagnosed with a single retinoblastoma in the left eye. There is no family history of retinoblastoma or other childhood cancers. Sequencing of the tumor shows inactivation of both RB1 alleles. Genetic testing of DNA from his peripheral blood leukocytes is most likely to show which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A germline mutation in one APC allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: A germline mutation in one RB1 allele

choices.label: C
choices.text: A germline mutation in one TP53 allele

choices.label: D
choices.text: Germline loss of both RB1 alleles

explanation.summary: In sporadic retinoblastoma the patient inherits two functioning RB1 alleles; both hits are somatic mutations confined to the tumor cell line.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the sporadic pathway, the patient inherits two functioning RB1 alleles. One sporadic mutation in a somatic (retinal) cell knocks out one allele, and a second somatic mutation in the same cell line knocks out the remaining allele. Because neither hit is in the germline, non-tumor cells such as blood leukocytes carry two wild-type RB1 alleles, which fits this unilateral, single tumor with no family history.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A germline APC mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis, not retinoblastoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A germline RB1 mutation would be present in all somatic cells and typically produces familial, often bilateral disease; this sporadic, unilateral, single tumor with no family history does not fit that pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A germline TP53 mutation is the basis of Li-Fraumeni syndrome, not retinoblastoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Germline loss of both alleles would leave no functional pRB in any cell; the two-hit model involves one inherited allele at most, with the second hit occurring somatically.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl who was treated for bilateral retinoblastoma as an infant now presents with a painful, enlarging mass of the distal femur. Biopsy shows a sarcoma. Which of the following best explains her development of this second, extraocular malignancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquisition of a new germline mutation in TP53

choices.label: B
choices.text: Constitutive Ras activation from loss of neurofibromin 1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hematogenous spread of the original ocular tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of APC function within bone-forming cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The faulty RB1 allele is present in all of her somatic cells

explanation.summary: In inherited retinoblastoma the germline RB1 mutation is in every somatic cell, so patients are prone to extraocular malignancies such as sarcomas and intracranial tumors (Retinoblastoma syndrome).
explanation.whyCorrect: With an inherited RB1 mutation, the faulty allele is not limited to retinal cells but is present in all somatic cells of the patient. Such patients are prone to developing extraocular malignancies, including intracranial malignancies and sarcomas, because any cell needs only one additional somatic hit to lose pRB. This heritable cancer predisposition is referred to as Retinoblastoma syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Germline mutations are inherited through gametes, not newly acquired later in life; her predisposition comes from the RB1 mutation she already carries.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of neurofibromin 1 causes neurofibromatosis 1 with cafe-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, which is not this patient's history.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A new primary sarcoma arising years later in bone reflects the inherited predisposition, not metastasis of the treated ocular tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: APC loss underlies colorectal adenomas and FAP, not sarcomas in a retinoblastoma survivor.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: An enucleated eye from a child with leukocoria is examined histologically. The tumor cells are arranged in rosettes that surround true central lumens. Which of the following best describes this finding?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polypoid growth with too many glands

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spindled cells of peripheral nerve origin

explanation.summary: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes have true lumens in the center, whereas Homer Wright rosettes surround an acellular center; both can be seen in retinoblastoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Retinoblastoma can show two rosette types. Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes have true lumens in the center, matching this description. Homer Wright rosettes, by contrast, are composed of a radial arrangement of cells around an acellular center rather than a true lumen.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Homer Wright rosettes are a radial arrangement of cells around an acellular center, not around a true lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neoplastic bone formation is the helpful clue to osteosarcoma, not a retinoblastoma finding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polypoid growths with too many glands describe colorectal adenomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spindled cells characterize neurofibromas, the peripheral nerve tumors of neurofibromatosis 1.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A pathologist reviewing molecular data from a large series of human tumors of many different organs notes that one tumor suppressor gene is mutated in over half of all the tumors. Which of the following is this gene?

explanation.summary: TP53 mutations are found in over half of all human tumors, highlighting its critical importance as a tumor suppressor.
explanation.whyCorrect: TP53, nicknamed the guardian of the genome, has multifaceted roles in cell cycle progression, DNA repair, cellular senescence, and apoptosis. Its mutations are frequently encountered in human cancers, in over half of all human tumors, which highlights the gene's critical importance as a tumor suppressor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APC loss is seen in the majority of colorectal carcinomas and adenomas specifically, not in over half of all human tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NF1 is mutated in neurofibromatosis 1 and some sporadic neoplasms but not in the majority of all human tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PTEN is a tumor suppressor of the PI3K/AKT pathway but is not described as mutated in over half of all tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RB1 loss classically underlies retinoblastoma; it is not the gene mutated in over half of all human tumors.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A cell is exposed to a stress that downregulates and suppresses MDM2, freeing p53 from degradation. In order to act as a transcription factor and promote expression of cell cycle and apoptosis genes, p53 must first assume which of the following forms?

explanation.summary: Once freed from MDM2, p53 forms tetramers that act as the transcription factor driving cell cycle arrest and apoptosis genes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under stress, MDM2 is downregulated and suppressed, freeing p53 to form tetramers and act as a transcription factor to promote the expression of genes involved in the cell cycle and apoptosis. p53 activation is achieved through tetramer formation, after which the cell is prevented from entering S phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-catenin functions in the WNT pathway with APC; it does not partner with p53.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TCF/LEF is the transcription factor partner of beta-catenin in the WNT pathway, not of p53.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding to MDM2 leads to ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of p53, the opposite of activation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polyubiquitination marks p53 for proteasomal degradation and keeps its levels low in unstressed cells.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A cell sustains DNA double-strand breaks after irradiation. Within minutes, p53 accumulates because a kinase has phosphorylated it at its MDM2 binding site, preventing MDM2 from ubiquitinating it. Which of the following proteins most directly phosphorylates p53 in this response?

explanation.summary: ATM senses double-strand breaks and activates Chk2, and it is Chk2 that phosphorylates p53 at the MDM2 binding site.
explanation.whyCorrect: ATM (ataxia-telangiectasia mutated) responds to DNA damage such as double-strand breaks and activates Chk2, which in turn phosphorylates p53 at the MDM2 binding site. This prevents MDM2 from ubiquitinating p53, so p53 can form a tetramer and exert effects that prevent cell growth and proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATM is the upstream sensor of double-strand breaks; it activates Chk2 rather than directly phosphorylating p53 at the MDM2 binding site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BAX is a pro-apoptotic gene product transcribed downstream of p53, not a kinase acting on p53.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MDM2 ubiquitinates p53 to target it for degradation; the phosphorylation described blocks MDM2 rather than being performed by it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: p14/ARF stabilizes p53 during oncogenic stress by binding MDM2, not by phosphorylating p53 after DNA damage.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A cell acquires a mutation that produces constitutively activated PI3K/AKT signaling. Despite the absence of any DNA damage, p53 levels rise and its tetramers exert anti-tumor transcriptional activity. Which of the following best explains the rise in p53?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of beta-catenin from the destruction complex

explanation.summary: Oncogenic stress raises p53 through increased p14/ARF (encoded by CDKN2A), which binds MDM2 and prevents ubiquitination of p53.
explanation.whyCorrect: Levels of p53 also rise in response to oncogenic stress, meaning increased oncoprotein action such as uninhibited Ras in the MAPK pathway or constitutively activated PI3K/AKT signaling. Though the exact mechanism is not fully known, this is typically carried out through increased p14/ARF expression, encoded by CDKN2A, which binds MDM2 to prevent ubiquitination of p53. As a result, p53 levels rise and the p53 tetramer exerts its anti-tumor transcriptional action.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATM responds to DNA damage such as double-strand breaks; the stem describes oncogenic stress without DNA damage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: In the DNA damage response, Chk2 phosphorylates p53 (not MDM2), and this stem specifies there is no DNA damage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: BAX transcription is a downstream consequence of p53 activation that drives apoptosis; it does not raise p53 levels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-catenin release occurs with WNT stimulation or APC loss and promotes proliferation; it does not stabilize p53.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A cultured cell with intact p53 experiences a spike in p53 levels after modest DNA damage, and the cell cycle is suspended. Over the next several hours the damage is fully repaired. Which of the following is the most likely subsequent fate of this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: p53 levels fall and the cell returns to a normal state

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cell divides while carrying the unrepaired lesion

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cell enters permanent cell cycle arrest

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cell loses its remaining TP53 allele

explanation.summary: When p53-mediated arrest allows DNA repair to succeed, p53 levels fall and the cell resumes normal function.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spikes in p53 levels, usually due to DNA damage, suspend the cell cycle and give the cell a chance to repair the DNA. If the damage is remedied, p53 levels will fall, and the cell can return to a normal state. Senescence and apoptosis are reserved for damage that is not remedied or is irreversible.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The stem states the damage was fully repaired, so no unrepaired lesion is propagated; that outcome describes cells lacking p53.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Senescence (permanent cell cycle arrest) is an alternative p53 outcome for cells that should not divide, not the fate of a cell whose damage has been fully repaired.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Successful repair does not cause loss of a TP53 allele; the cell's p53 remains intact.
whyWrongByChoice.E: p53 guides the cell to apoptosis via BAX for irreversible damage; here the damage has been remedied.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: In response to sustained cellular stress, p53 drives a damaged cell into a state of permanent cell cycle arrest so that it cannot divide and pass potentially neoplasia-evoking genes to daughter cells. Which of the following terms describes this state?

explanation.summary: Senescence is p53-induced permanent cell cycle arrest that prevents a damaged cell from dividing.
explanation.whyCorrect: p53 actions may cause the cell to enter a state of senescence, that is, permanent cell cycle arrest, to prevent it from dividing and passing potentially neoplasia-evoking genes to daughter cells. Cellular senescence is one of the multifaceted roles that earned TP53 the nickname guardian of the genome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angiogenesis is the formation of new blood vessels, a hallmark that cancers acquire, unrelated to cell cycle arrest.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, which p53 induces for irreversible damage via BAX; the cell described remains alive but permanently arrested.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metastasis is a cancer hallmark involving spread to distant sites, not a protective arrest state.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Necrosis is a form of cell death resulting from severe damage, not a p53-directed arrest of the cell cycle.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy from a family with a known germline TP53 mutation develops a painful mass in the metaphysis of the distal femur. A biopsy is obtained. Which of the following histologic findings would be the most helpful clue to the diagnosis of osteosarcoma?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spindled cells of nerve sheath origin

explanation.summary: Osteosarcoma, a Li-Fraumeni-associated cancer, is recognized histologically by neoplastic bone formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Li-Fraumeni syndrome, caused by a germline TP53 mutation, increases the risk of many cancers including breast carcinoma and osteosarcoma. On histology, neoplastic bone formation by the tumor is a helpful clue to diagnosing osteosarcoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Collections of heavily pigmented melanocytes make up the cafe-au-lait macules of neurofibromatosis 1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes with true lumens are a feature of retinoblastoma, not osteosarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Invasion of neoplastic glands into the lamina propria defines colorectal adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spindled cells characterize neurofibromas, the peripheral nerve tumors of neurofibromatosis 1.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: In a normal, non-neoplastic epithelial cell with fully functional APC, the WNT signal glycoprotein binds its surface receptor. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of this binding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: APC is degraded by the proteasome

choices.label: D
choices.text: p53 tetramers halt the cell cycle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ras is inactivated by a GTPase-activating protein

explanation.summary: WNT binding prevents the APC destruction complex from forming, releasing beta-catenin to partner with TCF/LEF and drive pro-proliferation genes.
explanation.whyCorrect: WNT is a signal glycoprotein that stimulates cell growth and differentiation. In the resting state the WNT receptor is unbound and beta-catenin is bound by APC and the destruction complex, which directs its proteasomal degradation. When WNT binds the surface receptor, the destruction complex with APC is prevented from forming, and beta-catenin is released to interact with the TCF/LEF (T-cell factor/lymphoid enhancer-binding factor) transcription factor, promoting expression of pro-proliferation genes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APC itself is not degraded on WNT binding; rather, the destruction complex it forms is prevented from assembling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-catenin degradation is the resting-state event when the WNT receptor is unbound; WNT binding stops this degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: p53 tetramer formation is part of the stress/DNA damage response, not the WNT pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GTPase-activating protein inactivation of Ras is the function of neurofibromin 1 in Ras signaling, unrelated to WNT binding.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man undergoes colonoscopy, and a polyp is removed. The pathologist must decide whether the lesion is a colorectal adenoma or a colorectal adenocarcinoma. Which of the following features would establish the diagnosis of adenocarcinoma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An excessive number of crowded glands within the mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Biallelic loss of APC function in the lesion's epithelial cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clonal proliferation of the epithelium with nuclear hyperchromasia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Invasion of neoplastic epithelium into the lamina propria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pedunculated polypoid growth of the lesion into the bowel lumen

explanation.summary: Colorectal adenocarcinoma is defined by invasion of neoplastic epithelium into the lamina propria or beyond; adenomas are non-invasive polypoid growths with too many glands.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under the microscope, colorectal adenomas consist of polypoid growths with too many glands, whereas colorectal adenocarcinomas demonstrate invasion of the neoplastic epithelium into the lamina propria (loose connective tissue) or beyond. Invasion is the defining feature that separates the malignant lesion from the benign, non-invasive adenoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Too many glands is the microscopic description of an adenoma and is not evidence of malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of APC function is the initiating event shared by both colorectal adenomas and adenocarcinomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The adenoma that emerges after APC loss is already a clonal neoplasm; clonality does not indicate invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adenomas are themselves polypoid growths, so polypoid architecture does not distinguish adenocarcinoma.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man who underwent prophylactic colectomy for familial adenomatous polyposis in his early twenties is now planning a family. He asks how the condition is passed on. Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern of familial adenomatous polyposis?

explanation.summary: Familial adenomatous polyposis is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by inheritance of a non-functioning APC allele.
explanation.whyCorrect: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by the inheritance of a non-functioning APC allele. Affected patients have only one working copy of the tumor suppressor, and a second-hit mutation that removes the remaining copy starts the road to neoplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FAP requires inheritance of only one non-functioning APC allele to confer the syndrome, which is dominant rather than recessive inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FAP is caused by a nuclear tumor suppressor gene, APC, not by mitochondrial DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although APC loss also occurs sporadically in colorectal tumors, FAP by definition is the inherited form.
whyWrongByChoice.E: APC is not an X-linked gene, and FAP is not transmitted in an X-linked fashion.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with neurofibromatosis 1 has several flat, brown, well-demarcated patches on her trunk. Which of the following best describes the cellular basis of these skin lesions?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Invasion of neoplastic epithelium into the dermis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neoplastic proliferation of peripheral nerve cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Radial arrangement of cells around an acellular center

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spindled cells forming a subcutaneous nodule

explanation.summary: Cafe-au-lait macules of neurofibromatosis 1 are brown patches due to collections of heavily pigmented melanocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Manifestations of NF1 include cafe-au-lait macules, which are brown patches due to collections of heavily pigmented melanocytes, and multiple neurofibromas. The flat brown patches described are cafe-au-lait macules.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Invasion of neoplastic epithelium describes colorectal adenocarcinoma, not a skin macule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A tumor of peripheral nerve cells is a neurofibroma, which presents as a cutaneous nodule rather than a flat brown macule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radial arrangement of cells around an acellular center describes Homer Wright rosettes of retinoblastoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spindled cells forming a nodule describe the histology of a neurofibroma, not a pigmented macule.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with neurofibromatosis 1 has numerous soft, dome-shaped cutaneous nodules over her back. One is excised and examined microscopically. Which of the following histologic appearances is most likely?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polypoid growth with too many glands

explanation.summary: Neurofibromas, tumors of peripheral nerve cells seen in NF1, appear as spindled cells on histology.
explanation.whyCorrect: Multiple neurofibromas are a manifestation of neurofibromatosis 1. A neurofibroma is a tumor of peripheral nerve cells that appears as spindled cells on histology, matching these cutaneous nodules.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Collections of heavily pigmented melanocytes form the flat cafe-au-lait macules, not the nodular neurofibromas.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neoplastic bone formation is the diagnostic clue for osteosarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Polypoid growth with too many glands describes a colorectal adenoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rosettes with true lumens (Flexner-Wintersteiner) are a feature of retinoblastoma.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: Researchers study the cell signaling pathways that also feature important tumor suppressor genes. One tumor suppressor is described as a component of the PI3K/AKT pathway. Which of the following is this gene?

explanation.summary: PTEN is the tumor suppressor that functions as a component of the PI3K/AKT pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cell signaling pathways covered with oncogenes also feature important tumor suppressor genes: NF1, which affects Ras activity, and PTEN, a component of the PI3K/AKT pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APC is a component of the WNT signaling pathway that regulates beta-catenin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NF1 encodes neurofibromin 1, a GTPase-activating protein that restrains Ras signaling, not the PI3K/AKT pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RB1 encodes pRB, which halts the cell cycle at the G1/S transition rather than acting in PI3K/AKT signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TP53 encodes the p53 transcription factor that responds to DNA damage and oncogenic stress; it is not a PI3K/AKT pathway component.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A patient is evaluated for a tumor predisposition syndrome after multiple hamartomas are identified. Which of the following syndromes is most consistent with this finding?

explanation.summary: Multiple hamartomas are encountered in Cowden syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the tumor predisposition syndromes, multiple hamartomas are the characteristic finding encountered in Cowden syndrome, distinguishing it from the other syndromes whose hallmark lesions are different.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Familial adenomatous polyposis features innumerable colonic adenomatous polyps, not hamartomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (germline TP53 mutation) predisposes to many cancers such as breast carcinoma and osteosarcoma, not multiple hamartomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neurofibromatosis 1 presents with cafe-au-lait macules and neurofibromas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retinoblastoma syndrome presents with retinoblastoma (leukocoria) and extraocular malignancies such as sarcomas.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: Cells cultured from an aggressive colorectal adenocarcinoma continue to divide indefinitely, far beyond the number of divisions that normal colonic epithelial cells can undergo. Which of the following hallmarks of cancer does this observation best illustrate, and through what mechanism is it acquired in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evasion of apoptosis via oncogenic KRAS

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evasion of the host immune response via inflammation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Invasion via breach of the lamina propria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sustained angiogenesis via new vessel recruitment

explanation.summary: Unlimited replication reflects the hallmark of immortality, acquired late in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence through altered telomere function.
explanation.whyCorrect: Immortality is one of the eight fundamental hallmarks of cancer. In the classic colonic adenoma-carcinoma sequence, additional hallmarks such as immortality through altered telomere function and metastatic potential are acquired as the adenocarcinoma becomes increasingly aggressive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oncogenic KRAS encourages proliferation and prevents apoptosis earlier in the sequence, but evasion of apoptosis is a separate hallmark from unlimited replicative capacity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Evasion of the host immune response is a distinct hallmark unrelated to replicative lifespan.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Invasion of the lamina propria marks transformation to adenocarcinoma; it does not explain indefinite replication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sustained angiogenesis concerns blood supply to the tumor, not the number of divisions a cell can undergo.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: Whole-genome sequencing of a colorectal carcinoma identifies hundreds of somatic mutations. Functional analysis shows that one particular mutation confers no survival or proliferative advantage to the tumor cells, although it may add to the tumor's genomic instability. Which of the following terms best describes this mutation?

explanation.summary: Passenger mutations give no growth advantage but may contribute to genomic instability, raising the chance of further beneficial mutations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Passenger mutations are those mutations that do not give a growth advantage to the tumor but may contribute to genomic instability, thus increasing the likelihood of additional mutations that may be beneficial to cancer growth and survival. This contrasts with driver mutations, which contribute to a cancer hallmark and give a Darwinian growth advantage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Driver mutations contribute to a cancer hallmark and give the tumor a growth advantage, which this mutation lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A germline mutation is inherited through gametes and present in all cells; the stem describes an acquired somatic tumor mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The initiating mutation is the first driver mutation on the path to malignancy, so it by definition confers an advantage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A second hit knocks out the remaining allele of a tumor suppressor, which produces a growth advantage rather than none.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: Sequencing of tissue sampled from several different regions of a single large colorectal carcinoma reveals that the regions share an early APC mutation but otherwise carry distinct sets of additional mutations. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epigenetic silencing erased the shared driver mutations in some regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of the second APC allele restored genomic stability in some regions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passenger mutations are identical in every cell of a clonal tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Subclones evolved under Darwinian selection after a common initiating event

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor arose from several independent initiating mutations in unrelated cells

explanation.summary: Step-wise Darwinian progression from one initiating mutation produces a genetically heterogeneous cancer composed of competing subclones.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the initiating mutation, additional driver mutations are acquired in daughter cells that give a survival and proliferative advantage to certain subclones over others, exerting a Darwinian survival of the fittest selection. Different subclones can exist within the same tumor mass, all competing for the same nutrients and microenvironments. The end result of this step-wise progression is a genetically heterogeneous cancer that continues to evolve over time, which explains regions that share the early APC hit but differ in later mutations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epigenetic changes alter gene expression without changing the DNA sequence; they cannot erase a mutation from the genome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of the remaining APC allele removes tumor suppressor function and drives neoplasia; it does not restore genomic stability.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Passenger and driver mutations accumulate differently in different subclones; they are not identical across all cells of an evolving tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The shared APC mutation indicates a single clonal origin, not multiple independent initiating events in unrelated cells.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A tumor shows markedly reduced protein levels of a tumor suppressor. The gene's coding sequence is normal, its promoter CpG islands are unmethylated, and its mRNA is transcribed at normal levels, yet the message is not translated into protein. Which of the following epigenetic mechanisms best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: microRNA binding of mRNA silences the message at the level of translation without altering transcription or the DNA sequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Epigenetic changes affect gene expression without involving the DNA sequence itself and include DNA methylation, histone modification, and microRNA binding of mRNA. microRNA binding is a method of silencing mRNA messages for protein synthesis (translation), which matches a gene that is transcribed normally but yields little protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chromosomal instability is a genetic change involving the genome itself, and the stem specifies an intact coding sequence and normal transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Histone modification controls the activity of DNA-binding proteins and acts at the level of transcription, which is normal here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Promoter hypermethylation silences the promoter and blocks transcription, but this gene's promoter is unmethylated and mRNA is produced normally.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypomethylation de-represses a promoter and may allow aberrant expression of an oncogene; it does not reduce protein output from a normally transcribed gene.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A carcinoma overexpresses a proto-oncogene. Sequencing of the gene shows no mutation, amplification, or rearrangement, but analysis of the CpG islands in its promoter region reveals abnormally decreased methylation compared with normal tissue. Which of the following best explains the overexpression?

explanation.summary: DNA hypomethylation of a promoter removes normal silencing and may allow aberrant expression of an oncogene.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methyl groups at CpG islands (patterns of DNA with cytosine and guanine nucleotides) are normally used to silence gene promoter regions, preventing expression of the associated gene. DNA hypomethylation, meaning abnormally decreased methylation, may allow aberrant expression of an oncogene, which is the opposite of the hypermethylation that silences tumor suppressors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stem specifies the gene sequence carries no mutation, excluding an activating point mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The stem specifies there is no amplification of the gene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: microRNA binding silences mRNA translation and would lower, not raise, protein output.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypermethylation silences a promoter and would decrease expression, and the stem describes decreased rather than increased methylation.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A small benign colonic adenoma has already lost both APC alleles. It then acquires an oncogenic KRAS mutation. Which of the following is the most likely immediate effect of this new mutation on the lesion?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Further proliferation with resistance to apoptosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invasion of neoplastic epithelium into the lamina propria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of TP53 through chromosomal instability

explanation.summary: In the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, oncogenic KRAS further encourages proliferation and prevents apoptosis, so the adenoma grows into a larger polyp.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the first and second hits knock out APC and a small, non-invasive clonal adenoma emerges, acquisition of an oncogenic KRAS mutation further encourages proliferation and prevents apoptosis. The adenoma, seen grossly as a polyp on endoscopic examination, grows. It remains an adenoma at this stage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metastatic potential is acquired late as the adenocarcinoma becomes increasingly aggressive, well after the KRAS step.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Invasion marks the later transformation to malignant adenocarcinoma after further mutations accumulate, not the immediate effect of KRAS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of TP53 through chromosomal instability is the next classic step after KRAS, not a direct effect of the KRAS mutation itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: APC has already been lost, and KRAS acts in a separate pathway; it does not restore beta-catenin degradation.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A colonic polyp in a 58-year-old woman has been followed on serial endoscopies and has grown steadily. Molecular studies show loss of both APC alleles and an activating KRAS mutation. In the classic colonic adenoma-carcinoma sequence, which of the following molecular events is expected to occur next as the lesion progresses toward carcinoma?

explanation.summary: After APC loss and KRAS activation, chromosomal instability and mutations lead to loss of TP53, the guardian of the genome, as the adenoma progresses.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the classic sequence, APC is knocked out by first and second hits, an oncogenic KRAS mutation then enlarges the adenoma, and chromosomal instability and mutations next lead to loss of TP53, the guardian of the genome. More driver and passenger mutations then accumulate, subclones with survival advantage dominate, and the neoplasm eventually gains the ability to invade surrounding tissue as a malignant adenocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APC is a tumor suppressor that has already been lost in this lesion; it is not amplified during progression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NF1 loss underlies neurofibromatosis 1 and some sporadic neoplasms, not the colonic sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PTEN is a PI3K/AKT pathway tumor suppressor and is not the classic next step in this sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RB1 loss is the classic lesion of retinoblastoma and is not a step in the colonic adenoma-carcinoma sequence.

questions.topicName: Molecular Basis of Neoplasia: Oncogenes, Tumor Suppressor Genes, and Neoplastic Progression (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman is diagnosed with stage 4 pancreatic cancer. She has no significant medical history and is concerned about how her immune system became so weak. Her oncologist explains that the tumor secretes a cytokine in large quantities that broadly suppresses the activity of B cells, T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages. Which of the following substances is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: TGF-beta is a potent immunosuppressant cytokine that some tumors secrete to downregulate multiple immune lineages.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that TGF-beta is a potent immunosuppressant capable of suppressing the activities of B cells, T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages, and that some tumor cells secrete it in large quantities to suppress the immune system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FasL is a cell-surface protein that binds the Fas receptor on T cells to trigger apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells; it is not a secreted immunosuppressive cytokine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycocalyx is extracellular matrix material that masks surface antigens, not a cytokine that suppresses immune lineages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin-2 promotes T cell proliferation and activation, the opposite of immunosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha causes cachexia in malignancy and recruits white blood cells rather than broadly suppressing immune cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms allows tumor cells to evade immune detection specifically by masking their surface antigens?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of MHC class I molecules

explanation.summary: Antigen masking occurs when tumor cells coat themselves in excess extracellular matrix (glycocalyx).
explanation.whyCorrect: Many tumor cells secrete an excess of extracellular matrix material called glycocalyx. This thick coating masks the antigens on cancer cells, making it more difficult for immune cells to target them for destruction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Downregulating antigen expression is the outgrowth-of-antigen-variants mechanism, in which the antigen is lost rather than hidden.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of MHC class I removes the platform that displays antigen to cytotoxic T cells; it does not mask antigens with a coating.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta secretion broadly suppresses immune cells and does not physically mask antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PD-L1 upregulation engages the PD-1 checkpoint to inhibit T cells rather than masking antigens.

questions.stem: A tumor subclone continues to display abundant tumor antigen, yet cytotoxic CD8+ T cells can no longer recognize or kill it. Analysis shows the cells have acquired a mutation that eliminates a surface receptor normally present on all nucleated cells. Loss of which of the following molecules best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: Cytotoxic T cells identify targets via MHC class I; tumor loss of MHC class I prevents recognition.
explanation.whyCorrect: MHC class I is a receptor present on all cells that displays antigens on the cell surface. Some tumor subclones undergo mutations that cause loss of MHC molecules so they are no longer recognized by cytotoxic T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7 molecules are co-stimulatory ligands on antigen-presenting cells; they are not present on all nucleated cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 is a co-stimulatory receptor on T cells, not a molecule tumor cells lose to escape recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Fas receptor is on T cells and mediates apoptosis when engaged by tumor FasL; losing it would not affect antigen recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PD-1 is an inhibitory receptor on T cells, not a molecule displayed on tumor cells for recognition.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced lung cancer that has failed multiple rounds of chemotherapy is started on pembrolizumab (Keytruda). Which of the following best describes how this medication helps the immune system attack the tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It engineers the patient's T cells to target CD19

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is an antibody that binds PD-1 on T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It neutralizes secreted TGF-beta in the tumor microenvironment

choices.label: D
choices.text: It restores MHC class I expression on tumor cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies excess co-stimulatory signal directly to tumor cells

explanation.summary: Pembrolizumab is an anti-PD-1 antibody that blocks the inhibitory PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cells upregulate PD-L1 and PD-L2, which activate the PD-1 receptor on T cells and suppress them. Keytruda is an antibody that binds the PD-1 receptor on T cells, preventing it from interacting with PD-L1 on cancer cells, giving the immune system a fighting chance to eliminate the tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Engineering T cells to target CD19 describes CAR-T cell therapy, not a PD-1 antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutralizing TGF-beta is a different immunosuppression pathway and is not the mechanism of pembrolizumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pembrolizumab does not alter MHC class I expression on tumor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drug does not deliver co-stimulation to tumor cells; it removes an inhibitory checkpoint signal.

questions.stem: A tumor is found to upregulate an inhibitory receptor that binds the B7 molecules on antigen-presenting cells and thereby reduces engagement of the CD28 co-stimulatory receptor on T cells. Which of the following molecules is being upregulated?

explanation.summary: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for B7 ligands, dampening T cell co-stimulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cells can upregulate the inhibitory receptor CTLA-4, which binds its ligands, the B7 molecules, from antigen-presenting cells and reduces the engagement of the CD28 co-stimulatory receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FasL binds the Fas receptor to induce T cell apoptosis and has no role in B7/CD28 competition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MHC class II presents antigen to helper T cells and is not an inhibitory receptor for B7.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PD-L1 engages the PD-1 receptor on T cells; it does not bind B7 or block CD28.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta is a secreted immunosuppressive cytokine, not a receptor that competes for B7.

questions.stem: A melanoma expresses a cell-surface ligand that engages a death receptor on approaching cytotoxic T cells, causing those T cells to die via the extrinsic apoptosis pathway. Which of the following ligands is the tumor most likely expressing?

explanation.summary: Tumors such as melanoma and hepatocellular carcinoma express FasL, which triggers extrinsic-pathway apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor cells such as melanoma and hepatocellular carcinoma express FasL, which binds the Fas receptor on T cells, leading to apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells via the extrinsic pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7-1 is a co-stimulatory ligand that promotes T cell activation, not death.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 is a co-stimulatory receptor on T cells, not a tumor ligand that induces apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycocalyx is a physical coating that masks antigens and does not engage a death receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PD-L2 engages PD-1 to inhibit T cells but does not directly trigger extrinsic-pathway apoptosis through a death receptor.

questions.stem: A T cell encounters a tumor cell that presents antigen through MHC but fails to deliver a co-stimulatory second signal. Which of the following is the most likely fate of this T cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes anergic or undergoes apoptosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: It differentiates into a memory T cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: It proliferates into an activated effector clone

choices.label: D
choices.text: It secretes large amounts of TGF-beta

choices.label: E
choices.text: It upregulates MHC class I on the tumor cell

explanation.summary: T cells require two signals; antigen without co-stimulation leads to anergy or apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A T cell can only be activated after receiving two signals: antigen recognition (Signal 1) and a co-stimulatory signal from the antigen-presenting cell (Signal 2). If the co-stimulatory signal is not received, the T cell becomes unresponsive (anergic) or undergoes apoptosis, which tumor cells exploit to evade immunity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Memory differentiation follows productive activation, which does not occur without Signal 2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Effector proliferation requires both signals; without co-stimulation the T cell is not activated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta is secreted by tumor cells, not by T cells lacking co-stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A T cell does not restore MHC class I on the tumor cell; MHC expression is a tumor property.

questions.stem: A patient with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma initially responds to CAR-T cell therapy engineered against CD19, but later relapses. Biopsy of the recurrent tumor shows the malignant B cells no longer express CD19. Which of the following best explains the relapse?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The engineered T cells lost their MHC class I molecules

choices.label: B
choices.text: The engineered T cells were suppressed by CD28 co-stimulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tumor cells began secreting glycocalyx to physically block the CAR-T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tumor cells lost expression of the target antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor cells upregulated MHC class I to hide from the CAR-T cells

explanation.summary: Antigen escape occurs when tumor cells stop expressing the CAR-T target (CD19).
explanation.whyCorrect: In CAR-T therapy the patient's own T cells are engineered to target a specific antigen such as CD19 on B cells. A well-known challenge is that cancer cells may stop expressing CD19 on their surface, so there is no longer a target for the engineered T cells, allowing relapse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CAR-T cells recognize CD19 directly and do not depend on tumor MHC; loss of the T cells' own MHC does not explain relapse.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 co-stimulation promotes, rather than suppresses, T cell activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The biopsy shows loss of CD19, not a glycocalyx coating, as the cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CAR-T recognition of CD19 is MHC-independent, so upregulating MHC class I would not hide the tumor from CAR-T cells.

questions.stem: In a melanoma, highly immunogenic tumor subclones are eliminated by the host immune system, while other subclones that have lost or downregulated their surface antigens survive and expand. Which mechanism of immune evasion does this describe?

explanation.summary: Selective survival of antigen-negative subclones is the outgrowth of antigen variants.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a subclone is highly immunogenic it is eliminated, whereas some tumor subclones lose expression of a surface antigen or downregulate antigen expression so they are not recognized by immune cells. This has been observed in cancers such as melanoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigen masking hides antigens under a glycocalyx coat; here the antigens are actually lost, not covered.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PD-L1 checkpoint engagement inhibits T cells directly and does not describe subclone selection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TGF-beta immunosuppression is cytokine-mediated and does not involve selection of antigen-negative subclones.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lack of co-stimulation causes T cell anergy/apoptosis and is distinct from loss of tumor antigen.

questions.stem: A medical student reads that a normal function of the immune system is to constantly scan the body for emerging malignant cells and destroy them, and that avoiding this process is one of the hallmarks of cancer. This normal protective function is best described by which of the following terms?

explanation.summary: Immune surveillance is the immune system's continuous scanning for and destruction of malignant cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The term immune surveillance implies that a normal function of the immune system is to constantly scan the body for emerging malignant cells and destroy them; avoiding immune destruction is one of the hallmarks of cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anergy is an unresponsive state of T cells that lack co-stimulation, not immune scanning.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antigen masking is a tumor evasion strategy, not a normal immune function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cachexia is the wasting syndrome associated with TNF-alpha in malignancy, unrelated to immune scanning.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Checkpoint blockade is a therapy that uses antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1, not the normal scanning function.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced malignancy develops profound weight loss and muscle wasting. A cytokine elevated in this patient is known to cause cachexia in malignancy and to recruit white blood cells, and it is distinct from the immunosuppressive cytokine that tumors use to evade immunity. Which of the following cytokines is most likely responsible for the wasting?

explanation.summary: TNF-alpha causes cachexia in malignancy and recruits white blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that TNF-alpha causes cachexia in malignancy and leads to white blood cell recruitment, distinguishing it from TGF-beta, the immunosuppressant tumors secrete to evade immunity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FasL is a death-inducing surface ligand that triggers T cell apoptosis, not a cause of cachexia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Interleukin-2 activates and expands T cells and does not cause cachexia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PD-L1 is a checkpoint ligand on tumor cells, not a cytokine that causes wasting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta is the immunosuppressive cytokine that downregulates immune lineages; it is not the cause of cachexia described here.

questions.stem: A newer class of cancer therapy, described as checkpoint blockade, uses antibodies to restore T cell function against tumors. Against which of the following pairs of targets are these checkpoint-blockade antibodies directed?

choices.label: D
choices.text: MHC class I and MHC class II

explanation.summary: Checkpoint blockade uses antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1 to restore T cell function.
explanation.whyCorrect: New cancer therapy known as checkpoint blockade uses antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1 to restore T cell function; it is now approved for advanced-stage solid tumors and some forms of lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD28 and B7 are activating co-stimulatory molecules; blocking them would suppress, not restore, T cell function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fas and FasL mediate apoptosis and are not the targets of approved checkpoint-blockade therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class I and II present antigen and are not the targets of checkpoint-blockade antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta and TNF-alpha are cytokines and are not the checkpoint targets named for this therapy.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has a colon adenocarcinoma that, on molecular profiling, secretes large amounts of TGF-beta, expresses high levels of PD-L1, and has lost MHC class I in several subclones. Taken together, these adaptations best represent which of the following hallmarks of cancer?

explanation.summary: Immune evasion by tumors corresponds to the hallmark of cancer termed avoiding immune destruction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the hallmarks of cancer, one important tenet is the tumor's ability to evade the immune system, labeled avoiding immune destruction. Secreting the immunosuppressant TGF-beta, engaging the PD-1 checkpoint via PD-L1, and losing MHC molecules are all mechanisms by which cancer escapes immune surveillance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Enabling replicative immortality concerns unlimited cell division and has no relation to immune evasion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Evading growth suppressors is a separate hallmark concerning loss of anti-proliferative controls, not escape from immune cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resisting cell death refers to the tumor cell's own resistance to apoptosis, not to suppression of immune attack.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor-promoting inflammation is a distinct hallmark and is not what TGF-beta, PD-L1, and MHC loss describe.

questions.stem: A population of white blood cells fights infection and works to kill foreign cells and cancer cells. These cells identify their targets by looking for MHC class I molecules on the target cell surface. Which of the following cell types is being described?

explanation.summary: Cytotoxic T cells kill foreign and cancer cells and recognize targets through MHC class I.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytotoxic T cells are white blood cells that fight infection and work to kill foreign cells and cancer cells. They identify target cells by looking for MHC class I molecules, which display antigens on the cell surface; this is why tumor loss of MHC prevents their recognition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigen-presenting cells supply Signal 1 and Signal 2 to T cells rather than serving as the killers of cancer cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: B cells are among the lineages suppressed by TGF-beta but are not the cells that kill targets by scanning MHC class I.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dendritic cells present antigen and provide co-stimulation; they do not kill target cells by recognizing MHC class I.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Macrophages are suppressed by TGF-beta but are not described as killing targets by MHC class I recognition.

questions.stem: A tumor subclone acquires a mutation that eliminates its MHC molecules. Cytotoxic T cells specific for the tumor antigen accumulate around the subclone but cannot become activated against it. Which component of T cell activation is absent in this interaction?

explanation.summary: MHC displays antigen for the first activation signal; without MHC there is no antigen recognition (Signal 1).
explanation.whyCorrect: T cells require two signals: the first signal is antigen presented by MHC class I or class II molecules, and the second is co-stimulation from an antigen-presenting cell. MHC is the receptor that displays antigens on the cell surface, so a subclone that has lost MHC cannot deliver Signal 1, and the cytotoxic T cells no longer recognize it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CTLA-4 binding of B7 reduces co-stimulation; it is an inhibitory interaction, not the antigen-recognition signal lost when MHC is absent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fas receptor engagement by tumor FasL causes T cell apoptosis; it is not a component of T cell activation and is unrelated to MHC loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PD-1 engagement is an inhibitory checkpoint signal, not one of the two activating signals, and is not what MHC loss removes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Signal 2 is the co-stimulatory signal from the APC; the defect here is loss of the antigen-displaying MHC molecule, not loss of co-stimulation.

questions.stem: A T cell has recognized antigen displayed on an MHC molecule but has not yet been activated. The second signal required for its activation is delivered by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A co-stimulatory molecule on the antigen-presenting cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: FasL expressed on the surface of the tumor cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycocalyx coating the surface of the tumor cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: MHC class I molecules on the target cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: TGF-beta secreted by the surrounding tumor cells

explanation.summary: Signal 2 is a co-stimulatory signal delivered by the antigen-presenting cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: A T cell can only be activated after receiving two signals. The first is antigen presented by MHC class I or class II, and the second is a co-stimulatory signal from the antigen-presenting cell (APC), illustrated by the co-stimulatory molecule engaging the T cell alongside the T cell receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FasL binds the Fas receptor to induce T cell apoptosis, the opposite of an activating second signal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycocalyx masks tumor antigens and hinders immune targeting; it delivers no signal to the T cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class I displays antigen and provides Signal 1, not the second co-stimulatory signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta is an immunosuppressive cytokine that suppresses T cells; it does not provide an activating co-stimulatory signal.

questions.stem: A medical student learns that a T cell cannot be activated by antigen recognition alone and must also receive a co-stimulatory signal. Which of the following best explains the physiologic purpose of this two-signal requirement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allows T cells to recognize antigen without MHC molecules

choices.label: B
choices.text: It enables tumor cells to secrete immunosuppressive cytokines

choices.label: C
choices.text: It ensures cytotoxic T cells undergo apoptosis after killing a target

choices.label: D
choices.text: It ensures T cells do not destroy the body's own host cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It permits B cells to display antigen on MHC class I molecules

explanation.summary: The two-signal requirement is a safeguard that keeps T cells from destroying host cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: In general, a T cell can only be activated after receiving two signals, and this requirement ensures that T cells are not destroying host cells. Tumors exploit this safeguard by ridding themselves of the co-stimulatory signal so that antigen-recognizing T cells become anergic or apoptotic instead of activated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigen recognition (Signal 1) still requires MHC presentation; the two-signal rule does not bypass MHC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tumor cytokine secretion is a separate evasion mechanism and is not the purpose of requiring co-stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The two-signal model governs activation, not programmed death of T cells after a kill.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The requirement for co-stimulation has nothing to do with B cells displaying antigen on MHC class I.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with metastatic melanoma is treated with an antibody against CTLA-4. Which of the following best describes the site and step at which this antibody primarily restores T cell function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the circulation, by neutralizing secreted TGF-beta

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the lymph node, by allowing CD28 to engage B7 on the dendritic cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: In tumor tissue, by blocking FasL from binding the Fas receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: In tumor tissue, by preventing PD-L1 from inhibiting the CTL

choices.label: E
choices.text: On the tumor cell, by restoring expression of MHC class I

explanation.summary: CTLA-4 blockade acts during priming in the lymph node by restoring CD28 co-stimulation from B7 on dendritic cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: CTLA-4 binds its ligands, the B7 molecules, on antigen-presenting cells and reduces engagement of the CD28 co-stimulatory receptor. Blockade of CTLA-4 allows cytotoxic CD8+ T cells to engage B7 family co-receptors, leading to T cell activation; this occurs in the lymph node with the dendritic cell, producing a primed CTL capable of killing tumor cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neutralizing TGF-beta is not the action of an anti-CTLA-4 antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking FasL-Fas binding would address apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells, not the CTLA-4 checkpoint.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preventing PD-L1 from inhibiting the CTL in tumor tissue describes PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade, not anti-CTLA-4 therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-CTLA-4 antibodies do not restore MHC class I expression on tumor cells.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced lung cancer cannot receive pembrolizumab, an antibody against the PD-1 receptor. An antibody directed against which of the following would abrogate the same inhibitory signal that pembrolizumab blocks?

explanation.summary: Blocking either the PD-1 receptor or its ligand PD-L1 abrogates the same PD-1 inhibitory signal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blockade of the PD-1 receptor or of the PD-1 ligand by inhibitory antibodies abrogates the inhibitory signals transmitted by PD-1, again leading to activation of CTLs. Checkpoint blockade therefore uses antibodies against PD-L1 as well as against the receptor, since PD-L1 on cancer cells is what activates PD-1 on T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7-1 is a co-stimulatory ligand for CD28; an antibody against it would impair co-stimulation, not block PD-1 signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 is the co-stimulatory receptor; blocking it would reduce T cell activation rather than remove an inhibitory signal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CTLA-4 blockade restores T cell function through a different checkpoint, the competition with CD28 for B7, not the PD-1 signal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Fas receptor mediates FasL-induced apoptosis of T cells and is unrelated to the PD-1 checkpoint.

questions.stem: Cancer cells can upregulate cell-surface proteins that activate the programmed cell death (PD-1) receptor on T cells. Besides PD-L1, which of the following is a second such ligand?

explanation.summary: PD-L1 and PD-L2 are the two tumor cell-surface ligands that activate PD-1 on T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cells can upregulate PD-L1 and PD-L2, cell-surface proteins that activate the programmed cell death (PD-1) receptor on T cells, thereby engaging a negative regulatory checkpoint that suppresses the immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7-2 is a ligand on antigen-presenting cells for CD28 and CTLA-4, not for PD-1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 is the co-stimulatory receptor on T cells and does not engage PD-1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CTLA-4 is an inhibitory receptor that binds B7 molecules; it is not a ligand for PD-1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FasL binds the Fas receptor on T cells to trigger apoptosis; it does not activate PD-1.

questions.stem: A patient with an advanced solid tumor receives an anti-PD-1 antibody. In the tumor tissue, previously inhibited cytotoxic T lymphocytes become activated and kill tumor cells. The activated CTL destroys the tumor cell by releasing which of the following?

explanation.summary: Once PD-1 inhibition is removed, the activated CTL kills the tumor cell by releasing cytotoxic granules.
explanation.whyCorrect: In tumor tissue, PD-1 on the CTL engaged by PD-1 ligand on the tumor cell keeps the CTL inhibited. When anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-1 ligand antibodies block this interaction, the activated CD8+ CTL releases cytotoxic granules, leading to killing of the tumor cell.
