whyWrongByChoice.A: B7 molecules are co-stimulatory ligands on antigen-presenting cells, not effector molecules released by CTLs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycocalyx is extracellular matrix secreted by tumor cells to mask antigens; T cells do not release it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PD-L2 is a tumor cell-surface ligand that inhibits T cells; it is not released by the CTL to kill targets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta is an immunosuppressive cytokine secreted by tumor cells, not the CTL's killing mechanism.

questions.stem: Several tumor immune-evasion mechanisms depend on molecules the tumor cell displays on its own surface. Which of the following mechanisms is instead mediated by a soluble factor secreted into the tumor microenvironment?

choices.label: B
choices.text: FasL-induced apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of MHC class I molecules

choices.label: D
choices.text: PD-L1 activation of the PD-1 receptor

explanation.summary: TGF-beta is a secreted cytokine; the other listed mechanisms involve surface molecules.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytokines are small proteins that function as signaling molecules. Some tumor cells secrete TGF-beta in large quantities, and this secreted growth factor suppresses B cells, T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages, which distinguishes it from evasion mechanisms based on cell-surface proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CTLA-4 is an inhibitory cell-surface receptor that binds B7 molecules on antigen-presenting cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FasL is a cell-surface protein present on some tumor cells that binds the Fas receptor on T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of MHC class I is a change in the tumor cell's own surface receptors, not secretion of a soluble factor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PD-L1 is a cell-surface protein on cancer cells that activates the PD-1 receptor on T cells.

questions.stem: A pathologist describes one subclone within a melanoma as highly immunogenic. Which of the following best characterizes this subclone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It expresses FasL on its cell surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has lost expression of its MHC molecules

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is coated by a thick layer of glycocalyx

choices.label: D
choices.text: It readily presents as foreign to host immune cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It secretes large quantities of the cytokine TGF-beta

explanation.summary: A highly immunogenic subclone easily presents as foreign to host immune cells and is eliminated.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a subclone of tumor cells is highly immunogenic, meaning it can easily present as foreign to host immune cells, the subclone group will be eliminated. Subclones that survive are those that lose or downregulate surface antigen expression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FasL expression kills approaching T cells and promotes evasion rather than immunogenicity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of MHC molecules prevents recognition by cytotoxic T cells, making the subclone less immunogenic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A glycocalyx coat masks antigens and hinders immune targeting, the opposite of being highly immunogenic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secreting TGF-beta suppresses immune cells and would help a subclone evade, not make it immunogenic.

questions.stem: Tumor cells from a resected carcinoma are shown by permeabilized staining to express both MHC class I and abundant tumor antigen, yet co-cultured cytotoxic T cells fail to recognize them. After enzymatic digestion of a thick extracellular matrix layer surrounding the cells, the same T cells recognize and kill them. Which of the following evasion mechanisms was operating?

explanation.summary: When antigen and MHC are present but hidden under a removable extracellular coat, the mechanism is antigen masking.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many tumor cells secrete an excess of extracellular matrix material called glycocalyx; this thick coating masks the antigens on cancer cells so immune cells have difficulty targeting them. Because the antigen and MHC are still expressed and recognition returns once the coat is removed, the antigens were masked rather than lost.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunosuppression is mediated by secreted TGF-beta, not by a physical coating whose removal restores recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lack of co-stimulation causes anergy or apoptosis of T cells and would not be reversed by digesting an extracellular coat.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class I is documented as present, so loss of MHC molecules cannot explain the failed recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: In outgrowth of antigen variants the tumor loses or downregulates the antigen itself; here the antigen is abundantly present.

questions.stem: A patient with B-lymphoblastic leukemia relapses after CAR-T cell therapy directed at CD19, and the relapsed cells no longer express CD19. This therapeutic escape is most analogous to which of the following naturally occurring mechanisms of tumor immune evasion?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of MHC class I molecules

explanation.summary: Losing the targeted antigen after CAR-T therapy parallels outgrowth of antigen variants.
explanation.whyCorrect: The phenomenon of tumor subclones losing or downregulating a surface antigen so they are no longer recognized extends into cancer immunotherapy. In CAR-T therapy against CD19, a well-known challenge is that cancer cells may stop expressing CD19, leaving no target for the engineered T cells, exactly as antigen-loss variants escape natural immunity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigen masking hides antigen beneath a glycocalyx coat; the relapsed cells have actually stopped expressing CD19.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunosuppression by secreted TGF-beta suppresses immune cells and does not involve loss of the target antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lack of co-stimulation renders T cells anergic or apoptotic; it does not describe the disappearance of a target antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CAR-T cells target CD19 directly, and the escape described involves loss of CD19, not of MHC molecules.

questions.stem: CAR-T cell therapy in which the patient's own T cells are engineered to target CD19 has emerged as a potential treatment for which of the following malignancies?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Non-small cell carcinoma of the lung

explanation.summary: CD19-directed CAR-T therapy is used for B-cell malignancies such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: CAR-T (chimeric antigen receptor T-cell) therapy has emerged as a potential treatment for several malignancies including B-cell malignancies, such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, because CD19 is an antigen on B cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatocellular carcinoma is cited for FasL-mediated T cell apoptosis, not for CD19-directed CAR-T treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Melanoma is noted for FasL expression and antigen-variant outgrowth, not as a target of CD19 CAR-T therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lung cancer is the setting for PD-1 checkpoint blockade, not CD19 CAR-T therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatic cancer is not a B-cell malignancy and does not express the B cell antigen CD19.

questions.stem: A patient with a B-cell malignancy asks how chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy works. Which of the following best describes this treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A cytokine infusion that activates B cells against the tumor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibodies that bind the PD-1 receptor on the patient's T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Donor T cells selected to recognize the tumor's MHC class I

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patient's own T cells engineered to target a specific antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor cells modified to express co-stimulatory molecules

explanation.summary: CAR-T therapy engineers the patient's own T cells to target a chosen antigen such as CD19.
explanation.whyCorrect: In CAR-T therapy, the patient's own T-cells are engineered to target a specific antigen, like CD19 on B cells. Because the engineered cells depend on that antigen, loss of CD19 expression by the cancer cells removes their target.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CAR-T is a cellular therapy of engineered T cells, not a cytokine infusion acting on B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies binding PD-1 on T cells describe checkpoint blockade such as pembrolizumab, not CAR-T therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CAR-T cells are the patient's own cells engineered against a specific antigen, not donor cells recognizing MHC class I.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CAR-T modifies the patient's T cells, not the tumor cells, and does not add co-stimulatory molecules to tumors.

questions.stem: A melanoma expresses a surface ligand that induces apoptosis of tumor-infiltrating cytotoxic T cells through the extrinsic pathway. Which of the following receptors on the T cell is engaged by this tumor ligand?

explanation.summary: Tumor FasL binds the Fas receptor on T cells to trigger extrinsic-pathway apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor cells such as melanoma and hepatocellular carcinoma express FasL, which binds to the Fas receptor on T cells, leading to apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells via the extrinsic pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD28 is the co-stimulatory receptor engaged by B7 molecules; it promotes activation rather than apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CTLA-4 is an inhibitory receptor that binds B7 molecules and reduces co-stimulation; it is not engaged by FasL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PD-1 is engaged by PD-L1/PD-L2 and inhibits T cell activation; it is not the death receptor bound by FasL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The T cell receptor recognizes antigen on MHC (Signal 1) and is not the receptor through which FasL kills T cells.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with a large liver mass is found to have a tumor whose cells express FasL, causing apoptosis of infiltrating cytotoxic T cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Hepatocellular carcinoma and melanoma are the tumors noted to express FasL and kill cytotoxic T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor cells such as melanoma and hepatocellular carcinoma express FasL, which binds the Fas receptor on T cells and leads to apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells via the extrinsic pathway. A FasL-expressing primary liver tumor is therefore most consistent with hepatocellular carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B-lymphoblastic leukemia is a CAR-T target and would not present as a solid liver mass expressing FasL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is a B-cell malignancy treated with CD19 CAR-T therapy; it is not the FasL-expressing tumor described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lung cancer is the setting for PD-1 blockade with pembrolizumab, not the tumor cited for FasL-mediated T cell apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatic cancer is presented as an example of TGF-beta-mediated immunosuppression, not FasL expression.

questions.stem: An oncologist explains that checkpoint blockade, using antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1, is a newer form of cancer therapy. This treatment has been approved for which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Advanced-stage solid tumors and some forms of lymphoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: All hematologic malignancies regardless of stage

choices.label: C
choices.text: B-lymphoblastic leukemia that has lost CD19 expression

choices.label: D
choices.text: Early-stage solid tumors before surgical resection only

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumors that have lost MHC class I molecules only

explanation.summary: Checkpoint blockade is approved for advanced-stage solid tumors and some lymphomas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Knowing the checkpoint mechanisms, a new cancer therapy known as checkpoint blockade uses antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1 to restore T cell function. This treatment has now been approved for patients with advanced-stage solid tumors and some forms of lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Approval covers some forms of lymphoma, not all hematologic malignancies regardless of stage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD19-negative B-lymphoblastic leukemia relates to CAR-T escape, not to checkpoint blockade approval.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Approval is described for advanced-stage disease, not for early-stage tumors before resection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Checkpoint blockade restores T cell function via CTLA-4 and PD-L1 and is not restricted to MHC class I-deficient tumors.

questions.stem: CTLA-4 and PD-1 are both negative regulatory checkpoints that tumors exploit to suppress T cells. Which of the following correctly distinguishes the PD-1 pathway from the CTLA-4 pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PD-1 blockade restores priming in the node, not killing in tumor tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: PD-1 is engaged by PD-L1/PD-L2 on tumor cells, not by B7 on APCs

choices.label: C
choices.text: PD-1 is expressed on tumor cells rather than on T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: CTLA-4 is a secreted cytokine whereas PD-1 is a surface receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: CTLA-4 is engaged by ligands displayed on the tumor cell itself

explanation.summary: PD-1 on T cells is activated by PD-L1/PD-L2 on cancer cells, whereas CTLA-4 binds B7 on antigen-presenting cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cells upregulate PD-L1 and PD-L2, cell-surface proteins that activate the PD-1 receptor on T cells in tumor tissue. In contrast, CTLA-4 binds its ligands, the B7 molecules, from antigen-presenting cells and reduces engagement of the CD28 co-stimulatory receptor during priming.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PD-1 blockade acts in tumor tissue to allow CTL killing; it is CTLA-4 blockade that restores priming in the lymph node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PD-1 is the receptor on T cells; the tumor cell expresses its ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CTLA-4 is an inhibitory cell-surface receptor, not a secreted cytokine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CTLA-4's ligands are the B7 molecules on antigen-presenting cells, not molecules displayed by the tumor cell.

questions.stem: The immune response is regulated by a class of molecules that includes TGF-beta. Which of the following best describes cytokines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies that block inhibitory checkpoint receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell-surface receptors that display antigens to T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Engineered receptors placed on a patient's own T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Extracellular matrix material that coats the surface of tumor cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small proteins that function as signaling molecules

explanation.summary: Cytokines are small proteins that act as signaling molecules regulating the immune response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The immune response is regulated by cytokines, which are small proteins that function as signaling molecules. TGF-beta is one such cytokine, a potent immunosuppressant that some tumor cells secrete in large quantities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies against checkpoint receptors describe checkpoint blockade therapy, not cytokines.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cell-surface receptors that display antigens are MHC molecules, not cytokines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Engineered receptors on a patient's own T cells describe CAR-T therapy, not cytokines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Extracellular matrix coating tumor cells describes glycocalyx used for antigen masking, not cytokines.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic melanoma is given an antibody that blocks CTLA-4. Which of the following is the expected direct consequence of this treatment at the interface between the antigen-presenting cell and the T cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased expression of PD-L1 on tumor cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased binding of CTLA-4 to B7 molecules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased engagement of CD28 by B7-1/B7-2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased secretion of TGF-beta by tumor cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced MHC class I display on tumor cells

explanation.summary: Blocking CTLA-4 frees B7 molecules to engage the CD28 co-stimulatory receptor, activating the T cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: CTLA-4 binds the B7 molecules from antigen-presenting cells and reduces engagement of the CD28 co-stimulatory receptor, keeping the T cell inactive. When CTLA-4 is blocked with an antibody, B7-1/B7-2 can engage CD28, the T cell becomes active, and it can kill tumor cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CTLA-4 blockade acts on the APC-T cell interaction and does not change tumor PD-L1 expression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An anti-CTLA-4 antibody prevents, rather than increases, CTLA-4 binding to B7.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking CTLA-4 has no described effect on tumor TGF-beta secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MHC class I display on tumor cells is not altered by anti-CTLA-4 therapy.

questions.stem: In a lymph node, an antigen is presented to a T cell by an immature, unactivated antigen-presenting cell, and the T cell becomes unresponsive. Which property of the antigen-presenting cell determines whether antigen presentation activates a T cell rather than rendering it anergic?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expression of the death ligand FasL

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expression of MHC class I and II molecules

choices.label: D
choices.text: Expression of the inhibitory PD-1 receptor

explanation.summary: Only an APC that provides the co-stimulatory Signal 2 activates the T cell; antigen alone yields anergy or apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: T cell activation requires antigen recognition plus a co-stimulatory signal from the APC. An immature or unactivated APC presenting antigen without the co-stimulatory molecule produces unresponsive (anergic) or apoptotic T cells, whereas an APC displaying the co-stimulatory molecule generates activated T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FasL on tumor cells induces T cell apoptosis via Fas; it is not the APC feature that determines activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MHC presentation supplies Signal 1, which is present in both outcomes; it does not decide activation versus anergy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PD-1 is an inhibitory receptor on T cells, not a property of the antigen-presenting cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta is secreted by tumor cells as an immunosuppressant and is not the APC property governing co-stimulation.

questions.stem: A patient with an advanced-stage solid tumor is started on checkpoint blockade therapy. Which of the following tumor immune-evasion strategies is this therapy specifically designed to counteract?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Engagement of inhibitory T cell checkpoints

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of MHC molecules by mutated tumor subclones

explanation.summary: Checkpoint blockade reverses tumor engagement of negative regulatory checkpoints that inhibit T cell activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor cells may inhibit tumor immunity by upregulating negative regulatory checkpoints such as CTLA-4 and PD-L1/PD-L2 that suppress the immune response. Checkpoint blockade uses antibodies against CTLA-4 and PD-L1 to abrogate these inhibitory signals and restore T cell function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Checkpoint antibodies do not remove the glycocalyx coat that masks antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Checkpoint blockade targets checkpoint receptors and ligands, not the secreted cytokine TGF-beta.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Checkpoint blockade cannot restore MHC molecules lost through tumor mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antibodies against CTLA-4 or PD-L1 do not re-express antigens lost by antigen-negative variants.

questions.stem: In an experimental model of melanoma, tumor-infiltrating cytotoxic T cells consistently undergo apoptosis through the extrinsic pathway shortly after contacting tumor cells. Which of the following changes in the tumor cells would be expected to restore survival of these T cells?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of MHC class I expression

explanation.summary: Melanoma kills T cells via FasL binding Fas; removing tumor FasL prevents this extrinsic apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor cells such as melanoma express FasL, which binds the Fas receptor on T cells and leads to apoptosis of cytotoxic T cells via the extrinsic pathway. Eliminating FasL from the tumor removes the death signal, so the T cells would no longer be driven into apoptosis on contact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased PD-L1 would further inhibit T cells through PD-1 rather than protect them from extrinsic apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased glycocalyx would mask antigens but would not stop FasL from engaging Fas on T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased TGF-beta would suppress T cells further and does nothing to block Fas-mediated death.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of MHC class I would prevent T cell recognition of the tumor but does not remove the FasL death signal killing the T cells.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to a dermatology clinic with extensive freckling over the face and neck but very few freckles on the shoulders. He develops severe sunburn after only a few minutes of sun exposure, and two lesions removed from his face were squamous cell carcinomas. A defect in which of the following DNA repair mechanisms most likely underlies his condition?

explanation.summary: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from a defect in nucleotide excision repair (NER).
explanation.whyCorrect: The photosensitivity, freckling limited to sun-exposed areas, and early squamous cell carcinomas describe xeroderma pigmentosum, caused by inherited loss-of-function of NER. NER normally removes and replaces oligonucleotides containing UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, and because humans lack photolyase, NER is the key mechanism for repairing this damage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes this photosensitive skin-cancer syndrome to defective nucleotide excision repair, not base excision repair.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defective homologous recombination underlies BRCA1/2-associated breast and ovarian cancers, not xeroderma pigmentosum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defective mismatch repair causes Lynch syndrome with gastrointestinal and endometrial cancer, not photosensitive skin cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defective nonhomologous end joining is linked to severe combined immunodeficiency and ataxia telangiectasia.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with an adenocarcinoma of the cecum. His mother and a maternal uncle had colorectal cancer, and a sister had endometrial cancer, with several relatives diagnosed before age 50. Molecular testing of the tumor shows microsatellite instability. A defect in which of the following processes is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome is caused by defective mismatch repair, producing microsatellite instability.
explanation.whyCorrect: The family pattern of colorectal and endometrial cancer with early onset, plus microsatellite instability, indicates Lynch syndrome. Defective mismatch repair fails to correct replication errors, so microsatellites (tandem repeats of 1-6 nucleotides) become unstable in length.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Direct reversal is not the pathway the brick links to microsatellite instability or Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defective homologous recombination is associated with BRCA-related breast and ovarian cancer, not microsatellite instability.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defective nonhomologous end joining causes immunodeficiency and ataxia telangiectasia, not this colorectal cancer syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Defective nucleotide excision repair causes xeroderma pigmentosum, a UV-sensitive skin disorder.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with a strong family history of breast and ovarian cancer is found to carry a germline BRCA1 mutation. The protein encoded by this gene normally participates in which of the following DNA repair processes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mismatch repair of errors made during replication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining of broken double-strand DNA ends

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair of ultraviolet pyrimidine dimers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proofreading of new strands by DNA polymerase

explanation.summary: BRCA1 functions in homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Individuals with BRCA1 mutations have defective homologous recombination and are at elevated risk of breast and ovarian cancer. Homologous recombination uses a homologous chromosome as a template to accurately repair double-strand breaks without loss of nucleotides.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome, not BRCA-associated cancers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonhomologous end joining directly fuses DNA ends without homology and is not the BRCA1 pathway; its defects cause immunodeficiency and ataxia telangiectasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nucleotide excision repair addresses helix-distorting lesions such as UV pyrimidine dimers, and its defect causes xeroderma pigmentosum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polymerase proofreading is a replication fidelity function, not the homologous recombination role of BRCA1.

questions.stem: A young child has a history of severe combined immunodeficiency and later develops gait ataxia, choreoathetosis, and dilated blood vessels visible in the conjunctivae and skin. A defect in which of the following DNA repair mechanisms best explains this combination of findings?

explanation.summary: Defective nonhomologous end joining underlies both severe combined immunodeficiency and ataxia telangiectasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nonhomologous end joining is normally harnessed during V(D)J recombination in B cells; its defects can cause severe combined immunodeficiency. The brick also lists ataxia telangiectasia, with ataxia and telangiectasias of skin and eyes, as a clinical consequence of defective NHEJ.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Base excision repair is not the pathway the brick associates with these findings.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defective homologous recombination causes BRCA-related cancers and Fanconi anemia, not this immunodeficiency-plus-ataxia picture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defective mismatch repair causes Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Defective nucleotide excision repair causes xeroderma pigmentosum.

questions.stem: Immunohistochemical staining of a colorectal tumor shows loss of MLH1 and PMS2 nuclear staining in the malignant glands, while MSH2 and MSH6 staining remain intact. This pattern most strongly indicates a primary defect in which of the following genes?

explanation.summary: Simultaneous loss of MLH1 and PMS2 points to a primary MLH1 defect.
explanation.whyCorrect: MLH1 and PMS2 form a functional heterodimer, so a defect in MLH1 destabilizes and leads to loss of PMS2 as well. Seeing both proteins absent therefore indicates a primary problem with the MLH1 gene.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BRCA1 acts in homologous recombination and is unrelated to this mismatch repair immunohistochemistry pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MSH2 staining is intact, so it is not the defective gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PMS2 is lost secondarily because it is destabilized when its MLH1 partner is defective, so it is not the primary problem here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MSH6 staining is intact, so it is not the defective gene.

questions.stem: A pathology report on a colon cancer notes that tandem repeats of 1-6 nucleotides scattered throughout the tumor genome have become unstable and vary in length compared with normal tissue. This finding is a direct hallmark of a defect in which of the following?

explanation.summary: Microsatellite instability is a hallmark of defective mismatch repair.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microsatellites are tandem repeats of 1-6 nucleotides whose length normally stays constant. When mismatch repair is defective, these repeats become unstable and change in length, a state termed microsatellite instability.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Homologous recombination defects cause BRCA-related and Fanconi phenotypes, not microsatellite instability.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonhomologous end joining defects cause immunodeficiency and translocations, not microsatellite length changes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nucleotide excision repair defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Telomerase maintains chromosome ends and is unrelated to microsatellite instability.

questions.stem: A physician is evaluating a family for possible Lynch syndrome. Which of the following findings would be most suspicious for the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A family history limited to pancreatic cancer in three relatives of a single generation

choices.label: B
choices.text: An isolated case of childhood leukemia in one relative of a single generation

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least three relatives with breast cancer only, spanning two successive generations of the family

choices.label: D
choices.text: At least three relatives with colorectal or endometrial cancer across two successive generations

choices.label: E
choices.text: One relative in a single generation diagnosed with colorectal cancer after age 70

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome is suggested by multiple relatives with colorectal or endometrial cancer, successive generations, and early onset.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clinical signs of possible Lynch syndrome include at least three relatives with a Lynch-associated cancer such as colorectal or endometrial cancer (one a first-degree relative of the other two), at least two successive generations affected, and at least one diagnosed before age 50.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A family history of only pancreatic cancer is not immediately suspicious for Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isolated childhood leukemia is not part of the Lynch syndrome clinical criteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The prototypical cancers are colorectal and endometrial, not breast cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Colorectal cancer diagnosed after age 70 is less likely to be inherited; early onset (before 50) is more suspicious.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child has short stature, absent thumbs and other skeletal abnormalities, and progressive pancytopenia. Cultured cells show marked chromosomal breakage when exposed to DNA cross-linking agents, and the condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. A defect in which of the following repair processes best explains this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Homologous recombination repair of DNA cross-links

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mismatch repair of base-base replication errors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining of broken DNA ends

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair of ultraviolet pyrimidine dimers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proofreading by DNA polymerase during replication

explanation.summary: Fanconi anemia results from defective homologous recombination repair of DNA cross-links.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in genes encoding proteins that repair DNA cross-links through homologous recombination. It is characterized by developmental abnormalities such as short stature and skeletal defects, hypersensitivity to cross-linking agents, bone marrow failure, and increased leukemia risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome, not this marrow failure syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonhomologous end joining defects cause immunodeficiency and ataxia telangiectasia, not cross-link hypersensitivity with marrow failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nucleotide excision repair defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polymerase proofreading is a replication fidelity mechanism, not the cross-link repair pathway defective in Fanconi anemia.

questions.stem: Nucleotide excision repair is described as particularly important for correcting ultraviolet-light-induced pyrimidine dimers in humans. Which of the following best explains why humans rely on NER for this purpose?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyrimidine dimers are repaired only during mitosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyrimidine dimers cannot be recognized by any repair system

explanation.summary: Humans lack photolyase, so NER is the key mechanism for repairing UV pyrimidine dimers.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that because humans lack photolyase, NER is an important mechanism to repair pyrimidine dimers. NER recognizes the helix-distorting dimer and removes and replaces the oligonucleotide containing it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Humans have DNA ligase, which in fact seals the gap during NER.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of proofreading is not the reason NER is needed for UV dimers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick does not restrict pyrimidine dimer repair to mitosis; the point is the absence of photolyase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyrimidine dimers are recognized precisely by NER as helix-distorting lesions.

questions.stem: The error-prone nature of nonhomologous end joining, which can fuse any two DNA ends without requiring homology, is physiologically harnessed by the immune system for which of the following processes?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Somatic mismatch repair in T cells

explanation.summary: NHEJ is used physiologically for V(D)J recombination to generate antibody and receptor diversity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the inaccuracy of NHEJ has physiological utility, allowing B cells to undergo V(D)J recombination, the process by which novel antibodies and receptors are generated to detect foreign antigens. This is why NHEJ defects can cause severe combined immunodeficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Meiotic recombination uses homologous recombination, not the error-prone NHEJ pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nucleotide excision repair is unrelated to immune receptor diversity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: V(D)J recombination, not mismatch repair, is the NHEJ-dependent immune process described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Telomere elongation depends on telomerase, not NHEJ.

questions.stem: During a review of genomic instability, a student is asked to name the most commonly mutated gene in cancer, often called the guardian of the genome. Which of the following is the correct answer?

explanation.summary: TP53 (p53) is the most commonly mutated gene in cancer and is called the guardian of the genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's review prompt identifies the most commonly mutated gene in cancer, also known as the guardian of the genome, as p53 (TP53). It guards genomic integrity by halting the cell cycle for repair or triggering apoptosis when damage is excessive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BRCA1 mutations cause defective homologous recombination and breast/ovarian cancer but are not the guardian of the genome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MLH1 is a mismatch repair gene linked to Lynch syndrome, not the guardian of the genome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MSH2 is a mismatch repair gene involved in Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PMS2 is a mismatch repair gene, lost secondarily with MLH1, not the guardian of the genome.

questions.stem: A cell in late S/G2 phase sustains a double-strand DNA break and has an intact homologous chromosome available. It repairs the break by reconnecting the complementary strands without the loss of any nucleotide sequence. Which of the following repair mechanisms was used, and why is it favored over the alternative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Base excision repair, because it excises a single damaged base without losing sequence

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homologous recombination, because it uses a homologous chromosome as a template

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mismatch repair, because it corrects errors left behind by replication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining, because it never introduces mutations at the break

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair, because it removes bulky helix-distorting adducts

explanation.summary: Homologous recombination accurately repairs double-strand breaks using a homologous chromosome as template.
explanation.whyCorrect: Homologous recombination uses a homologous chromosome as a template to reconnect severed strands without loss of nucleotide sequence, making it the accurate double-strand break repair pathway. It is preferred over nonhomologous end joining, which is error-prone and can even cause chromosomal translocations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Base excision repair removes single damaged bases and does not repair double-strand breaks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mismatch repair corrects replication mismatches, not double-strand breaks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nonhomologous end joining is error-prone and can introduce mutations and translocations, so this reasoning is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleotide excision repair removes helix-distorting single-strand lesions, not double-strand breaks.

questions.stem: A tumor biology lecture presents the hallmarks of cancer as a wheel of ten linked capabilities. One segment is described as an increased propensity for mutations, including DNA base changes and structural alterations, that fuels the acquisition of the other hallmarks. Which of the following terms best names this hallmark?

explanation.summary: Genomic instability, also labeled the mutator phenotype, is the hallmark defined by an increased propensity for mutations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genomic instability refers to an increased propensity for mutations, including DNA base changes and structural alterations, in the genomic DNA. In the hallmarks-of-neoplasia wheel it is labeled genomic instability (mutator phenotype), and people with deficient DNA repair or increased exposure to sources of genetic damage have more of it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deregulated energetics refers to altered cellular metabolism, not DNA base changes and structural alterations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Replicative immortality concerns unlimited cell division, not an increased mutation rate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Evading growth suppressors describes loss of anti-proliferative controls, not a mutator phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor-promoting inflammation is a separate hallmark on the wheel and does not define an increased mutation propensity.

questions.stem: It is estimated that every one of the 30-50 trillion cells in the human body incurs around 70,000 sites of DNA damage per day, which may take the form of a strand break, base modification, base deletion, or base insertion. Which of the following is the broad term for any such site of damage within a polynucleotide?

explanation.summary: A DNA lesion is any site of damage within a polynucleotide, and cells sustain about 70,000 of them daily.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA is far more fragile than one might expect: every cell incurs around 70,000 DNA lesions per day. A DNA lesion is the broad term for any site of damage within a polynucleotide, which may result in a strand break, base modification, base deletion, or base insertion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A checkpoint is a cell-cycle point at which the genome is assessed for damage, not the damage itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A microsatellite is a tandem repeat of 1-6 nucleotides found throughout the genome, not a site of damage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A mutation is what results only when a lesion is not corrected and causes a change in the DNA base sequence; the damage site itself is a lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A translocation is a chromosomal rearrangement that can follow error-prone repair of double-strand breaks, not the general term for damage.

questions.stem: A dividing epithelial cell sustains a base modification that escapes all repair mechanisms and produces a permanent change in the DNA base sequence. Which of the following best describes the fate of this change in the cell's descendants?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is converted back into a lesion by DNA polymerase during replication

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is removed by repair enzymes at the next S-phase checkpoint

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is retained in all subsequent generations of the cell's lineage

choices.label: D
choices.text: It persists only in the original cell and is not inherited by its progeny

choices.label: E
choices.text: It triggers obligatory apoptosis before the next cell division occurs

explanation.summary: An uncorrected lesion that changes the base sequence is a mutation, and a mutation is retained in all subsequent generations of the cell's lineage.
explanation.whyCorrect: When a DNA lesion is not corrected and causes a change in the DNA base sequence, it is referred to as a mutation. Unlike a lesion, which repair mechanisms can still fix, a mutation is copied faithfully and retained in every descendant of that cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA polymerase copies the altered sequence; it does not revert a mutation into a lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Checkpoints detect DNA damage and halt division for repair; a sequence change that has already been fixed into the genome is not recognized as damage to be removed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mutations are heritable within the lineage; that is what distinguishes them from transient lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Apoptosis is activated when too much damage is sustained, not automatically after a single uncorrected base change.

questions.stem: A replicating cell conducts a global assessment of its genome and detects a high level of DNA damage. It halts division and attempts repair, but the amount of damage proves too great to correct. Which of the following is the expected outcome, and at what point in the cell cycle are such assessments especially concentrated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apoptosis; assessments occur especially before and after S phase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continued division; assessments occur only during mitosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Microsatellite instability; assessments occur only in G0

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining; assessments occur only during cytokinesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Permanent arrest without death; assessments occur only in G1

explanation.summary: Checkpoints before and after DNA replication halt division for repair, and excessive damage triggers apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cells have dedicated times when they conduct global assessments of their genome: checkpoints are established within all replicating cells, especially before and after DNA replication (S phase). Cells halt division if a high level of damage is detected and attempt repair; if too much damage has been sustained, special mechanisms for apoptosis (programmed cell death) are activated.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A cell with excessive damage does not continue dividing; it undergoes apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Microsatellite instability is a consequence of defective mismatch repair, not the checkpoint response to excessive damage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NHEJ is a repair mechanism, not the outcome of failed repair, and checkpoints are not restricted to cytokinesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick describes apoptosis, not permanent arrest, as the response to damage that cannot be repaired, and checkpoints flank S phase rather than sitting only in G1.

questions.stem: During nucleotide excision repair of a UV-damaged strand, the phosphodiester backbone is cut both upstream and downstream of the lesion so that the damaged segment can be removed. Which of the following enzymes performs these cuts?

explanation.summary: NER relies on special endonucleases to sever the phosphodiester backbone on both sides of the lesion.
explanation.whyCorrect: NER is a remove-and-replace mechanism. It relies on special endonucleases to sever the phosphodiester backbone upstream and downstream of the lesion, after which helicase removes the segment, DNA polymerase fills the gap, and ligase seals it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA ligase seals the gap at the final step; it does not cut the backbone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA polymerase fills the gap after the damaged segment has been removed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Helicase removes the excised segment after the endonuclease cuts have been made.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Photolyase directly reverses pyrimidine dimers in some organisms, but humans lack photolyase and it is not part of NER.

questions.stem: A researcher compares DNA repair pathways by the size of the segment each removes. One pathway is described as a remove-and-replace mechanism that recognizes a broad range of helix-distorting single-strand lesions and excises a stretch of nucleotides containing the lesion rather than a single base. Which of the following pathways is being described?

explanation.summary: NER removes an entire oligonucleotide stretch containing a helix-distorting single-strand lesion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nucleotide excision repair is a remove-and-replace mechanism capable of recognizing a broader range of helix-distorting single-strand lesions. Instead of a single base, a stretch of nucleotides containing the lesion is removed, and the resulting gap is filled and sealed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Homologous recombination repairs double-strand breaks using a homologous chromosome as template; it is not a single-strand remove-and-replace pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mismatch repair corrects incorrectly incorporated bases in newly synthesized strands after replication, not helix-distorting lesions in general.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonhomologous end joining fuses the ends of two DNA fragments after a double-strand break.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Proofreading is a DNA polymerase function during replication and is explicitly described as imperfect, which is why mismatch repair exists.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with xeroderma pigmentosum is counseled about lifelong risks related to sun exposure. Beyond squamous cell carcinoma and basal cell carcinoma, which of the following malignancies is also associated with chronic sun exposure and therefore of particular concern in this patient?

explanation.summary: Squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and melanoma are the skin cancers associated with chronic sun exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical correlation accompanying xeroderma pigmentosum lists squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and melanoma as skin cancers associated with chronic sun exposure. Because NER-deficient individuals cannot repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, they carry a significantly increased risk of these skin cancers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leukemia is a risk in Fanconi anemia and ataxia telangiectasia, not a consequence of chronic sun exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: B-lymphocyte malignancies are listed among BRCA2-associated cancers, not sun-related cancers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Colorectal cancer is the prototypical malignancy of Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair), not a sun-exposure cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endometrial cancer is a Lynch-associated cancer and is not linked to sunlight.

questions.stem: During DNA replication a polymerase incorporates guanine opposite thymine in the newly synthesized strand. Before the error can be excised, it must first be identified. Which of the following protein complexes is responsible for recognizing the mismatch?

explanation.summary: The MSH2-MSH6 complex identifies mismatches in newly synthesized DNA; MLH1-PMS2 then excises them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Incorrect bases incorporated into newly synthesized strands are recognized by the Mut class proteins that recruit endonucleases. The MSH2-MSH6 complex identifies the error in newly synthesized DNA, MLH1-PMS2 excises the incorrect base, and the excised strand is filled in by DNA polymerase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BRCA1 and BRCA2 function in homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks, not mismatch recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A ligase complex fuses DNA ends in nonhomologous end joining; it does not detect mismatches.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MLH1-PMS2 performs excision of the incorrect base after recognition has already occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NER endonucleases cut around helix-distorting lesions in nucleotide excision repair, a different pathway.

questions.stem: Mismatch repair is designed to catch errors that DNA polymerases make despite their proofreading capabilities. Because of the type of error it corrects, this pathway is most active during which of the following phases of the cell cycle?

explanation.summary: Mismatch repair corrects replication errors and therefore occurs primarily in S phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mismatch repair is designed to correct errors in DNA replication, when incorrect bases are incorporated into newly synthesized strands. The brick summarizes that mismatch repair catches errors in DNA replication and occurs primarily in the S phase, the phase in which DNA is replicated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and is not when replication errors arise.
whyWrongByChoice.B: G0 is a quiescent state without DNA replication, so no new replication errors are being generated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G1 precedes DNA synthesis; the newly synthesized strands that mismatch repair scans do not yet exist.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitosis involves chromosome segregation, not DNA synthesis.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman is diagnosed with Lynch syndrome after genetic testing reveals a germline mutation in MSH2. She asks about the risk to her children. Which of the following inheritance patterns applies to this disorder?

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a germline mismatch repair gene mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lynch syndrome is the most common inherited colorectal cancer susceptibility syndrome. It is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a germline mutation in one of several DNA mismatch repair genes: MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal recessive inheritance describes Fanconi anemia, not Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial inheritance is not involved; the causative genes are nuclear mismatch repair genes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lynch syndrome is autosomal, not X-linked.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mismatch repair genes in Lynch syndrome are not X-linked.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with no family history of cancer is found to have an adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. Molecular testing of the tumor shows microsatellite instability, but germline testing for mutations in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 is negative. Which of the following best explains the tumor's molecular findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A germline BRCA2 mutation causing defective homologous recombination repair

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defective nonhomologous end joining causing chromosomal translocations

choices.label: C
choices.text: Defective nucleotide excision repair of ultraviolet pyrimidine dimers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sporadic loss of mismatch repair, seen in 10-15% of sporadic colon cancers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unrecognized Lynch syndrome inherited from an unaffected parent

explanation.summary: Microsatellite instability is not exclusive to Lynch syndrome; 10-15% of sporadic colon cancers also have it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microsatellite instability is a hallmark of defective mismatch repair, but the brick notes that 10-15% of sporadic colon cancer cases have microsatellite instability. In an elderly patient with no family history and negative germline testing, a sporadic mismatch repair defect confined to the tumor is the best explanation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BRCA2 defects impair homologous recombination and are linked to breast, ovarian, prostate, pancreatic, and other cancers, not to microsatellite instability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defective nonhomologous end joining leads to immunodeficiency and ataxia telangiectasia; it does not produce microsatellite instability.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defective nucleotide excision repair causes xeroderma pigmentosum and skin cancer, not microsatellite instability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lynch syndrome is defined by a germline mismatch repair mutation, which was excluded, and the late age and absent family history argue against it.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman with a confirmed germline MLH1 mutation undergoes surveillance colonoscopy. Based on the typical distribution of tumors in her syndrome, which of the following regions of the gastrointestinal tract carries the greatest risk of harboring a cancer?

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome cancers arise predominantly in the cecum and proximal colon.
explanation.whyCorrect: Individuals with Lynch syndrome have a significantly increased risk of cancer within the gastrointestinal tract, predominantly in the cecum and proximal colon. Surveillance should therefore give particular attention to the right side of the colon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The anal canal is not the region the brick associates with Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The esophagus is not the site emphasized for Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The stomach is listed among BRCA2-associated cancer sites, not the predominant Lynch site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rectosigmoid is not the predominant site described for Lynch syndrome tumors; the syndrome favors the proximal colon.

questions.stem: A pathology resident reads an older report that describes a patient's condition as hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC). Which of the following is the current name for this syndrome?

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome was formerly called hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC).
explanation.whyCorrect: Defective mismatch repair is a key etiology of Lynch syndrome, formerly called hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC). It is the most common inherited colorectal cancer susceptibility syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ataxia telangiectasia is a consequence of NHEJ defects, with neurologic findings and telangiectasias.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive cross-link repair disorder with marrow failure, not a colorectal cancer syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Severe combined immunodeficiency results from NHEJ defects impairing V(D)J recombination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Xeroderma pigmentosum is the NER-deficiency skin disorder.

questions.stem: A cell is exposed to ionizing radiation that severs both strands of a chromosome. Neither of the two available repair pathways is able to reconnect the severed strands. Which of the following is the most likely fate of this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It enters G0 and persists indefinitely with the break

choices.label: B
choices.text: It repairs the break with photolyase

choices.label: C
choices.text: It replicates the broken chromosome normally

choices.label: D
choices.text: It survives with a stable microsatellite expansion

explanation.summary: An uncorrected double-strand break is potentially fatal, and the cell will almost certainly undergo apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA helices can sustain damage that severs both strands. These lesions are potentially fatal for a cell; if not corrected, the cell will almost certainly undergo apoptosis. Cells have two main mechanisms, homologous recombination and nonhomologous end joining, that attempt to reconnect the severed strands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick does not describe indefinite survival with a double-strand break; the lesion is potentially fatal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Humans lack photolyase, and photolyase addresses pyrimidine dimers, not double-strand breaks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A severed chromosome cannot be replicated normally; uncorrected, the break leads to cell death.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Microsatellite instability is a product of defective mismatch repair, not of an unrepaired double-strand break.

questions.stem: A cell in G1 phase sustains a double-strand break. Because no homologous template is available at this point in the cell cycle, the cell falls back on a pathway that uses a special ligase complex to directly fuse the two DNA ends. Which of the following best characterizes this pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It corrects mismatched bases in the newly synthesized strand

choices.label: B
choices.text: It excises a single damaged base and replaces it

choices.label: C
choices.text: It joins any two ends regardless of homology and risks genetic integrity

choices.label: D
choices.text: It removes a stretch of nucleotides around a helix-distorting lesion

choices.label: E
choices.text: It uses a homologous chromosome as template and is highly accurate

explanation.summary: Nonhomologous end joining directly fuses DNA ends with a ligase complex, prioritizing reconnection over accuracy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nonhomologous end joining uses a special ligase complex to directly fuse the ends of two DNA fragments. When homologous recombination is not possible, because of the degree of damage or the current status of the cell cycle, the cell's higher priority is to use NHEJ to reconnect the severed strands, even at the risk of jeopardizing some genetic integrity, since it connects any two severed strands without requiring homology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correcting replication mismatches is mismatch repair, not a double-strand break pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Single-base removal does not describe how a double-strand break is reconnected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Removing an oligonucleotide around a helix-distorting lesion is nucleotide excision repair.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Template-directed accurate repair describes homologous recombination, which is precisely the pathway unavailable in this scenario.

questions.stem: A leukemia cell line is found to carry a fusion of segments from two different chromosomes. Analysis shows that both chromosomes had sustained double-strand breaks at about the same time and that the broken ends were joined to each other rather than to their original partners. Which of the following repair mechanisms most likely produced this rearrangement?

explanation.summary: NHEJ can join breaks from separate chromosomes, producing translocations that contribute to cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because NHEJ connects any two severed strands it can find, without requiring homology, it is error-prone. If multiple double-strand breaks occur in separate chromosomes, NHEJ can result in translocations, and this contributes to the pathophysiology of cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Proofreading removes misincorporated nucleotides during synthesis and is unrelated to rejoining chromosome fragments.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Homologous recombination uses a homologous chromosome as template and reconnects complementary strands without loss of sequence; it does not fuse unrelated chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mismatch repair corrects replication errors and does not join chromosome ends.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleotide excision repair addresses single-strand helix-distorting lesions and cannot produce a translocation.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is diagnosed with breast cancer. His father died of pancreatic cancer, and a brother was treated for prostate cancer at age 52. Genetic testing is most likely to reveal a germline mutation in which of the following genes?

explanation.summary: BRCA2 mutations are associated with breast cancer in men as well as prostate, pancreatic, and other cancers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mutations in BRCA2 (breast cancer gene 2) are associated with breast cancer in men and women as well as cancers of the ovary, prostate, pancreas, bile ducts, stomach, melanocytes, and B lymphocytes. About 1.8-7.1% of men with mutated BRCA2 develop breast cancer by age 70, compared with 0.1% of men in the general population.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MLH1 is a mismatch repair gene of Lynch syndrome, whose prototypical cancers are colorectal and endometrial.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MSH2 defects cause Lynch syndrome, not male breast, prostate, and pancreatic cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PMS2 is a mismatch repair gene; its loss is typically secondary to MLH1 defects in Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MSH6 is a Lynch syndrome mismatch repair gene, not a homologous recombination gene linked to this cancer spectrum.

questions.stem: Two sisters undergo genetic testing after their mother dies of ovarian cancer. One carries a harmful BRCA1 variant and the other a harmful BRCA2 variant. Compared with the 1.1% lifetime ovarian cancer risk of women in the general population, which of the following best describes the sisters' relative risks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both have roughly the same 13% lifetime risk

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neither has a meaningfully elevated ovarian risk

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only the BRCA2 carrier has an elevated ovarian risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: The BRCA1 carrier has the higher risk, about 39-58%

choices.label: E
choices.text: The BRCA2 carrier has the higher risk, about 39-58%

explanation.summary: Lifetime ovarian cancer risk is about 39-58% with BRCA1 and 13-29% with BRCA2, versus 1.1% in the general population.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 39-58% of women with mutated BRCA1 and 13-29% of women with mutated BRCA2 develop ovarian cancer during their lifetime, in contrast to 1.1% of women in the general population. Both sisters have a markedly elevated risk, but the BRCA1 carrier's is higher.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 13% figure is the general-population lifetime breast cancer risk, and the two genes confer different ovarian risks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both variants confer a substantially elevated ovarian cancer risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations raise ovarian cancer risk well above the 1.1% baseline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 39-58% ovarian risk range belongs to BRCA1 carriers; BRCA2 carriers have a 13-29% risk.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman who completed treatment for right-sided breast cancer 3 years ago is found to carry a germline BRCA1 mutation. Compared with breast cancer survivors without such a mutation, she is at increased risk for which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A new cancer in the contralateral breast

choices.label: E
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of sun-exposed skin

explanation.summary: Breast cancer patients with BRCA1/2 mutations have an increased risk of cancer in the opposite (contralateral) breast.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among women who have been diagnosed with breast cancer, those with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations have an increased risk of developing cancer in the opposite (contralateral) breast in the future. This is one reason prophylactic mastectomy may be offered to lower cancer risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow failure is a feature of Fanconi anemia, not of BRCA1 carriers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cecal and proximal colon cancers are the hallmark of Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair), not BRCA1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Microsatellite instability results from defective mismatch repair, not from defective homologous recombination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sun-related skin cancers are the consequence of defective nucleotide excision repair in xeroderma pigmentosum.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with a germline BRCA1 mutation has completed childbearing and wishes to reduce her risk of ovarian cancer as much as possible. Which of the following risk-reducing procedures addresses this goal?

explanation.summary: Women with BRCA1/2 may undergo prophylactic salpingo-oophorectomy to lower ovarian cancer risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Women with BRCA1/2 may receive prophylactic mastectomy (removal of the breast) or salpingo-oophorectomy (removal of the Fallopian tubes and ovaries) to lower the risk of cancer. For a patient whose concern is ovarian cancer, removal of the tubes and ovaries is the relevant procedure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mastectomy lowers breast cancer risk but does nothing for the ovaries.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Removal of the uterus alone leaves the ovaries and Fallopian tubes in place; the brick specifies salpingo-oophorectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Colectomy would address colorectal cancer risk, which is the concern in Lynch syndrome, not BRCA-associated ovarian cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gastrectomy is not a described risk-reducing procedure for BRCA carriers.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with short stature and radial-ray skeletal anomalies has an established diagnosis of Fanconi anemia and is followed for progressive marrow aplasia. In addition to bone marrow failure, this disorder places him at increased risk for which of the following malignancies?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of sun-exposed skin

explanation.summary: Fanconi anemia carries an increased risk of bone marrow failure (aplasia) and leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that may be caused by mutations in more than a dozen different genes, each encoding a protein in the pathway that repairs DNA cross-links through homologous recombination. It is characterized by developmental abnormalities, hypersensitivity to cross-linking agents, and increased risk of bone marrow failure (aplasia) and leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colorectal cancer is the hallmark of Lynch syndrome, not Fanconi anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ovarian cancer risk is tied to BRCA1/2 mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostate cancer is listed among BRCA2-associated cancers, not Fanconi anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sun-exposed skin cancers are the consequence of xeroderma pigmentosum and defective NER.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl develops progressive gait ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, and peripheral neuropathy, and dilated blood vessels are noted on the bulbar conjunctivae and skin. In addition to these neurologic and cutaneous findings, this condition predisposes her to which of the following malignancies?

explanation.summary: Ataxia telangiectasia predisposes to leukemia and lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Individuals with ataxia telangiectasia develop ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, and neuropathy, usually with onset before the age of 5 years, along with benign blood vessel engorgement in the skin and eyes (telangiectasia). Ataxia telangiectasia, a clinical consequence of NHEJ defects, also predisposes to cancer such as leukemia and lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basal cell carcinoma is a sun-exposure skin cancer of concern in xeroderma pigmentosum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Colorectal cancer is the prototypical Lynch syndrome malignancy from defective mismatch repair.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ovarian cancer is associated with BRCA1/2 mutations and defective homologous recombination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatic cancer is among the BRCA2-associated cancers, not ataxia telangiectasia.

questions.stem: A family with multiple cases of early-onset colorectal and endometrial cancer undergoes germline testing for Lynch syndrome. A pathogenic mutation in which of the following genes would confirm the diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome is caused by a germline mutation in a mismatch repair gene: MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a germline mutation in one of several DNA mismatch repair genes: MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2. MSH6 partners with MSH2 to recognize mismatches in newly synthesized DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fanconi anemia genes repair DNA cross-links through homologous recombination and cause marrow failure, not Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BRCA1 mutations impair homologous recombination and cause breast and ovarian cancer risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: BRCA2 functions in homologous recombination and is associated with breast, ovarian, prostate, pancreatic, and other cancers, not Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TP53 is the most commonly mutated gene in cancer overall but is not one of the mismatch repair genes that define Lynch syndrome.

questions.stem: A genetic counselor explains lifetime breast cancer risk to a 30-year-old woman who has just tested positive for a harmful BRCA1 variant. Which of the following most accurately compares her risk with that of women in the general population?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 0.2-1.2%, versus 0.1% in the general population

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 1.1%, versus 13% in the general population

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 13%, the same as the general population

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 39-58%, versus 1.1% in the general population

choices.label: E
choices.text: More than 60%, versus 13% in the general population

explanation.summary: More than 60% of women with a harmful BRCA1 or BRCA2 change develop breast cancer, versus 13% of women in general.
explanation.whyCorrect: More than 60% of women who inherit a harmful change in BRCA1 or BRCA2 will develop breast cancer during their lifetime, in contrast to 13% of women in the general population. This large difference is why prophylactic mastectomy may be offered.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.2-1.2% versus 0.1% are the male breast cancer figures for BRCA1 carriers versus men in general.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 1.1% is the general-population lifetime risk of ovarian cancer, not breast cancer, and a carrier's risk is not below baseline.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 13% is the general-population figure; a BRCA1 carrier's risk is far higher.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 39-58% versus 1.1% describes ovarian cancer risk in BRCA1 carriers, not breast cancer risk.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her roommate, who reports that she has been acting bizarrely and had flu-like symptoms a few days earlier. She is admitted, and about a week later she develops unstable blood pressure, fever, involuntary facial movements, and becomes obtunded. Assuming all of these findings are attributable to a single underlying cancer, which of the following malignancies is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis presents with a psychiatric/flu-like prodrome followed by autonomic instability and is most strongly associated with ovarian teratoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is the classic biphasic course of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (ANRE): an initial phase dominated by psychiatric symptoms and seizures, followed roughly a week later by decreased consciousness, dyskinesia, and autonomic instability (labile blood pressure, arrhythmia, hyperthermia). ANRE is caused by autoantibodies against NMDA receptors, and the tumor most commonly associated with it is ovarian teratoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with acanthosis nigricans and the sign of Leser-Trelat, not with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphoma can cause calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia but is not the tumor linked to anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Small cell lung cancer is linked to many paraneoplastic syndromes but is not the typical tumor behind anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis, not anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is evaluated for progressive weight loss and epigastric pain. On examination, he has thickened, velvety, hyperpigmented plaques over the back of his neck and in both axillae that developed over the past several months. He is not obese and has no history of diabetes. Which of the following malignancies is most likely underlying his skin findings?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

explanation.summary: Paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans in a non-obese, non-diabetic adult is most commonly associated with gastric adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acanthosis nigricans is thickened, black or brown, velvety hyperpigmentation, most commonly on the neck and axilla. Although most cases are linked to obesity or diabetes, roughly 20% are paraneoplastic, and when so, the most commonly associated tumor is gastric adenocarcinoma. These tumors are thought to secrete growth factors that stimulate the characteristic skin changes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ovarian teratoma is associated with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, not acanthosis nigricans.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Small cell lung cancer is associated with LEMS, limbic encephalitis, Cushing syndrome, and SIADH rather than acanthosis nigricans.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is the classic PTHrP-secreting tumor causing hypercalcemia, not acanthosis nigricans.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis, not with paraneoplastic skin hyperpigmentation.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman with known breast cancer presents with headache, fatigue, constipation, depression, and forgetfulness. A routine metabolic panel is drawn. Which of the following abnormalities is most likely responsible for her symptoms?

explanation.summary: The constellation of stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones in a cancer patient points to paraneoplastic hypercalcemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Her constipation (groans), depression and forgetfulness (psychiatric overtones), and fatigue are classic manifestations of hypercalcemia. In a patient with malignancy, symptomatic hypercalcemia is most often paraneoplastic, typically driven by tumor secretion of PTHrP. Breast carcinoma is among the carcinomas that cause PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypernatremia is not a paraneoplastic syndrome of breast cancer and typically causes intense thirst and confusion, not this symptom pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypokalemia can cause constipation and weakness, but paralysis would predominate and it is not a feature of paraneoplastic syndromes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyponatremia is seen in SIADH and causes neurologic findings such as decreased consciousness; it is most associated with small cell lung cancer, not breast cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Isolated hypophosphatemia does not produce this symptom complex; low phosphate accompanies PTHrP-driven hypercalcemia but the calcium elevation drives symptoms.

questions.stem: A man with a 45-pack-year smoking history presents with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. On history he reports persistent pain in his knees and ankles, and examination reveals digital clubbing with bilateral swelling of the knees and ankles. In addition to treating the exacerbation, evaluation for which of the following conditions is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: New-onset digital clubbing with joint swelling and pain is hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, which is most commonly paraneoplastic and associated with lung cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is characterized by digital clubbing, synovial effusions, and joint pain, and about 90% of cases are paraneoplastic. Lung cancer of any type is the most commonly associated malignancy, so sudden-onset clubbing should always prompt a work-up for an underlying lung malignancy. The mechanism involves subperiosteal bone formation along the phalanges.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colon adenocarcinoma may be associated with acanthosis nigricans but not with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric adenocarcinoma is linked to acanthosis nigricans and the sign of Leser-Trelat, not hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymphoma may cause calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia but is not associated with hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal cell carcinoma can cause hypercalcemia but is not the tumor behind hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.

questions.stem: Parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) is most commonly produced by which of the following cancers?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Small cell carcinoma of the lung

choices.label: E
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung

explanation.summary: PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia is most commonly caused by squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most malignant tumors that cause hypercalcemia do so by secreting PTHrP, which raises serum calcium and lowers serum phosphate. The cancers most commonly responsible are squamous cell carcinomas of the lung and head and neck, along with carcinomas of the breast, ovary, kidney, and bladder. Of the listed options, squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is the classic PTHrP producer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with acanthosis nigricans and the sign of Leser-Trelat, not PTHrP production.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphoma can on occasion produce calcitriol, but it is not known to produce PTHrP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ovarian teratoma is associated with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, not PTHrP production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Small cell lung cancer produces ACTH and ADH (causing Cushing syndrome and SIADH) but is not the typical PTHrP producer.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man reports drooping eyelids and progressive muscle weakness that worsens as the day goes on and with repetitive activity. Imaging reveals an anterior mediastinal mass. His symptoms are attributable to a paraneoplastic process. Antibodies against which of the following are most likely responsible?

choices.label: B
choices.text: NMDA receptors in the central nervous system

explanation.summary: Myasthenia gravis with a thymoma is driven by antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction targeting postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, producing weakness that worsens with repetitive use. When paraneoplastic, it is most commonly associated with thymoma (an anterior mediastinal mass), where an immune response against a thymoma epitope cross-reacts with neuromuscular junction components sharing that epitope.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-Hu antibodies mediate limbic encephalitis associated with small cell lung cancer, not myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies to NMDA receptors cause anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, associated with ovarian teratoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels cause Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, in which weakness improves with use and which is linked to small cell lung cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Voltage-gated potassium channel antibodies are not the mechanism described for this thymoma-associated presentation.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with a long smoking history reports proximal leg weakness that seems to improve slightly after a few minutes of activity. Work-up reveals a lung mass consistent with small cell lung cancer. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of his weakness?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein

explanation.summary: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome results from antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels and is most commonly associated with small cell lung cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is caused by autoantibodies against presynaptic calcium channels on motor neurons, so patients present with weakness that can improve as the muscle is used. As a paraneoplastic syndrome it is most commonly associated with small cell lung cancer, arising from cross-reactivity between epitopes on the cancer cells and the calcium channels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors cause myasthenia gravis, in which weakness worsens with use and which is linked to thymoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ectopic ACTH secretion causes paraneoplastic Cushing syndrome, not muscle weakness of this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ectopic ADH secretion causes SIADH with hyponatremia, not calcium-channel-mediated weakness.
