questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman requests advice on colorectal cancer screening. Her mother was diagnosed with sporadic colorectal adenocarcinoma at age 50; there is no known cancer syndrome in the family. At what age should this patient begin screening?

explanation.summary: With a family history of sporadic colorectal cancer, screening begins at 40 or 10 years before the relative's onset.
explanation.whyCorrect: Screening is based on individualized risk. Patients with a family history of sporadic colorectal adenocarcinoma should begin screening at 40 years or 10 years before the onset of the cancer in the family member. With the mother's diagnosis at 50, both rules point to age 40.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Age 21 is the general starting age for Pap smears in average-risk women, not colorectal screening.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Age 30 is the threshold before which BRCA1/2 carriers begin breast MRI screening; it is not a colorectal screening age.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Age 45 is the starting age for healthy individuals without a family history; her family history moves it earlier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting until the mother's age at diagnosis would miss the 10-year lead time recommended for family history.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with no family history of cancer asks her physician what her chance is of developing breast cancer over the course of her life. Which of the following best approximates the current lifetime risk of breast cancer in a woman?

explanation.summary: A woman's lifetime risk of breast cancer is about 1 in 8.
explanation.whyCorrect: Breast cancer arises in the ducts and lobules of the breast and is more prevalent in women than men. The current lifetime risk of breast cancer in a woman is 1 in 8, making it the most frequently diagnosed cancer in women.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 50% lifetime risk greatly overstates the figure; even BRCA carriers are counseled differently from this population estimate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: One in twenty understates the risk; breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in women.
whyWrongByChoice.C: One in four overstates the population lifetime risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: One in six is higher than the stated lifetime risk.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. Her father died of a brain tumor at 38, her brother had a sarcoma at 15, and her paternal aunt had breast cancer at 33. Genetic testing reveals a germline mutation in a tumor suppressor gene. Which of the following genes is most likely mutated?

explanation.summary: Breast cancer in a multi-tumor family points to Li-Fraumeni syndrome from germline TP53 mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hereditary cancers are caused by gene mutations passed from parent to child, and tumor predisposition syndromes arise from inherited mutations of tumor suppressor genes. Breast cancer may arise in the context of germline TP53 mutations in Li-Fraumeni syndrome; hereditary cancers tend to manifest earlier and act more aggressively than sporadic counterparts, as in this family.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Germline APC mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis with near-certain colorectal adenocarcinoma, not this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV is an infectious agent that causes cervical cancer, not an inherited tumor suppressor gene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NF1 mutation causes neurofibromatosis 1 with cafe-au-lait macules and neurofibromas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RB1 mutation causes retinoblastoma tumor predisposition syndrome, a childhood eye tumor.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman undergoes screening mammography, which reveals a cluster of microcalcifications. Biopsy of the area shows neoplastic cells expanding a duct without invasion past the basement membrane, with chunky purple microcalcifications within the lesion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Invasive breast carcinoma with lymph node metastasis

explanation.summary: Microcalcifications on mammography with neoplastic cells confined to a duct indicate ductal carcinoma in situ.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mammography screening detects suspicious breast lesions, such as those showing microcalcifications, that need biopsy. The goal is to identify and treat developing cancers, such as ductal carcinoma in situ, before they progress to invasive or metastatic disease; DCIS shows neoplastic cells expanding a duct without invasion past the basement membrane.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lesion contains neoplastic cells, so it is not a benign calcification.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSIL is a cervical cytology finding on Pap smear, not a breast biopsy diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Invasion past the basement membrane is absent, so this is not invasive carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A metastasis would not be confined within a native breast duct behind an intact basement membrane.

questions.stem: A public health officer is asked to prioritize interventions based on the estimated share of cancer deaths attributable to identifiable factors. Smoking accounts for the largest share. Which of the following factors accounts for the second-largest share of estimated cancer deaths?

explanation.summary: After smoking (33%), obesity (25%) accounts for the largest share of estimated cancer deaths.
explanation.whyCorrect: Estimated cancer deaths by identifiable factors are led by smoking at 33%, followed by obesity at 25%. Diet, infectious agents, occupational agents, family history, and miscellaneous factors each account for about 5%, alcohol and reproductive factors about 3% each, and 11% remain unknown, showing that environmental factors far outweigh genetic ones.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alcohol consumption accounts for about 3%.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diet accounts for about 5% of estimated cancer deaths.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Family history is a notably small slice, about 5%.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Infectious agents account for about 5% of estimated cancer deaths in this breakdown.

questions.stem: Epidemiologic studies show that breast cancer is much more common in the United States than in Japan. When women emigrate from Japan to the United States, their risk of breast cancer increases, and in subsequent generations the risk approaches that of native-born US citizens. Which of the following is the best interpretation of these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Breast cancer in the United States is primarily infectious in origin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Environmental factors play a much bigger role than genetic factors in breast cancer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Japanese women are protected by inherited tumor suppressor variants that are lost on migration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migration induces new germline mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2

choices.label: E
choices.text: The difference reflects only greater use of mammography in the United States

explanation.summary: Migration studies show environmental factors outweigh genetics for most cancers.
explanation.whyCorrect: For most cancers and patients, environmental factors play a much bigger role than genetic factors. Much of this understanding comes from epidemiologic studies showing specific cancers are more common in some parts of the world, and that risk changes when people emigrate, as with Japanese women moving to the United States.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Infectious agents cause about 15% of cancers worldwide, but breast cancer risk here is tied to environmental factors such as lifestyle, not infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inherited genes do not change on migration; the rise in risk across generations indicates environmental, not genetic, causes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Moving between countries does not create inherited mutations; the rising risk reflects a new environment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mammography raises apparent incidence by earlier detection, but the migration pattern is presented as evidence of environmental risk, not a screening artifact.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with a 45 pack-year smoking history presents with painless hematuria. Cystoscopy reveals a mass, and biopsy confirms carcinoma. Besides lung cancer, cigarette smoking is a major risk factor for cancer of which of the following sites?

explanation.summary: Smoking is a major risk factor for cancers of the mouth, esophagus, pancreas, and bladder, not just lung.
explanation.whyCorrect: Smoking causes more premature deaths in the United States than any other environmental factor, many from myocardial infarction and stroke. It is also a major risk factor for many cancers: lung cancer, of course, but also cancers of the mouth, esophagus, pancreas, and bladder, many of which have a high mortality rate. Bladder cancer is a classic sporadic, induced cancer from carcinogen exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to vinyl chloride exposure, not smoking.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mesothelioma of the pleura is caused by asbestos exposure, not smoking.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Retinoblastoma is a childhood cancer associated with RB1 mutation, not smoking.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thyroid cancer is not among the smoking-associated cancers listed; it is notable for its excellent prognosis.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man eats a diet high in refined carbohydrates and fat and consumes processed red meats nearly every day. He has no family history of cancer. This dietary pattern is a well-studied, widely accepted risk factor for which of the following cancers?

explanation.summary: Excess refined carbohydrates, fat, and processed red meat raise colorectal cancer risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The list of dietary factors that may raise cancer risk is long and changing, but some are well-studied and widely accepted as definite risk factors. Excessive amounts of refined carbohydrates and fat, as well as processed red meats, are associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute myeloid leukemia is linked to occupational benzene exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cervical cancer is caused by high-risk strains of HPV, a sexually transmitted infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to vinyl chloride exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mesothelioma is linked to occupational asbestos exposure, not diet.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with a 30-year history of heavy alcohol abuse and known alcoholic cirrhosis presents with right upper quadrant pain and weight loss. Imaging shows a new mass arising within the cirrhotic liver. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Alcoholic cirrhosis predisposes to hepatocellular carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many patients with long-standing alcohol abuse develop alcoholic cirrhosis of the liver, a condition that predisposes the patient to developing hepatocellular carcinoma, or cancer of liver cells. A new mass in a cirrhotic liver in a heavy drinker is most likely hepatocellular carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alcohol raises the risk of esophageal cancer, but a primary mass within a cirrhotic liver is best explained by hepatocellular carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatic angiosarcoma is a vascular tumor linked to occupational vinyl chloride exposure, not alcoholic cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MALT lymphoma is associated with Helicobacter pylori in the stomach, not with cirrhosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatic cancer is linked to smoking; a mass arising within a cirrhotic liver points to a primary liver cell cancer.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman with a body mass index of 44 kg/m2 presents with abnormal uterine bleeding. Endometrial biopsy shows endometrial carcinoma. Which of the following best explains the link between her obesity and this cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Obesity increases dietary intake of processed red meat, which damages endometrial DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Obesity leads to excessive estrogen exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obesity promotes chronic Helicobacter pylori colonization of the endometrium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Obesity raises progesterone, which stimulates endometrial proliferation

explanation.summary: Obesity raises estrogen exposure, increasing the risk of breast and endometrial cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Obesity is increasing at an alarming rate in the United States and worldwide. In women, obesity leads to excessive estrogen exposure, which increases the risk of breast and endometrial cancer. The effect is not trivial: rates of cancer death in patients with morbid obesity are more than 50% higher than in the rest of the population, and obesity also contributes to cancer deaths in men.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Processed red meat is a dietary risk factor for colorectal cancer; the obesity-endometrium link is hormonal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Radon is an occupational and residential carcinogen linked to lung cancer, unrelated to obesity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: H. pylori is causally related to gastric carcinoma and MALT lymphoma, not endometrial cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progesterone counterbalances estrogen and gives reprieve from estrogen stimulation; it is estrogen, not progesterone, that drives this risk.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman who received radiation therapy for a childhood cancer develops a second malignancy within the previously irradiated field. Her brother, a lifelong outdoor worker, was recently treated for a skin cancer attributed to sun exposure. Which of the following best describes the shared mechanism by which therapeutic radiation and the sun's ultraviolet rays increase cancer risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both damage cellular DNA, producing mutations that pave the way for cancer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both inactivate inherited tumor suppressor genes carried in the germline

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both promote infection with oncogenic viruses such as HPV and EBV

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both raise circulating estrogen levels and stimulate epithelial proliferation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Both suppress the immune surveillance that eliminates neoplastic cells

explanation.summary: Therapeutic radiation and UV light both cause DNA damage and mutations that lead to cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Whether from therapeutic interventional procedures (such as radiation treatments for cancer) or from the sun's UV rays, radiation significantly increases the risk of cancer. Both types of radiation may damage the cell's DNA, leading to genetic mutations that can pave the way for the development of cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Radiation induces acquired mutations in somatic cells (sporadic, induced cancers), not inherited germline mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Radiation is a direct DNA-damaging carcinogen and does not act by promoting viral infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Estrogen-driven proliferation is the mechanism for luminal breast and endometrial cancer, not for radiation carcinogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mechanism described is direct DNA damage with mutation, not immune suppression.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician with fatigue, pallor, and easy bruising, and is found to have a malignancy. In counseling the parents, the physician notes that although most cancers occur in older adults, children develop cancers that are often distinct from those in adults. Which of the following categories of cancer is most common in pediatric patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute leukemias and neoplasms of the central nervous system

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma and endometrial adenocarcinoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Malignant mesothelioma and hepatic angiosarcoma from occupational exposure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prostate adenocarcinoma and invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast

explanation.summary: Pediatric cancers are most commonly acute leukemias and CNS neoplasms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Age is an important risk factor, and most cancers occur in patients over 55 years of age. Pediatric patients, however, develop cancers that are often distinct from those in adults, most commonly acute leukemias and neoplasms of the central nervous system. Common infant and childhood cancers include neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, retinoblastoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and rhabdomyosarcoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cervical and endometrial carcinomas are adult cancers tied to HPV infection and estrogen exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lung and colorectal carcinomas are adult cancers, mostly occurring after age 50 and associated with carcinogen exposure and diet.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mesothelioma and hepatic angiosarcoma are occupational cancers of adults exposed to asbestos and vinyl chloride.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostate and breast cancers are the most common cancers in adult men and women, respectively.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history is diagnosed with bladder cancer. He has no family history of cancer, and genetic testing reveals no inherited mutation; the tumor cells contain a series of somatic mutations acquired over his lifetime. Which of the following best classifies this cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hereditary cancer from a tumor predisposition syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hereditary cancer transmitted through the somatic cell line

choices.label: C
choices.text: Induced sporadic cancer resulting from carcinogen exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infection-related cancer caused by a viral agent

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spontaneous sporadic cancer arising without carcinogen exposure

explanation.summary: Smoking-related bladder cancer is a sporadic, induced cancer from carcinogen exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancers are inherited or sporadic (arising de novo). Sporadic cancers can be further classified as spontaneous cancers, which arise without carcinogen exposure, and induced cancers, which result from carcinogen exposure. Sporadic cancers arise from acquired somatic mutations that are not passed to the next generation; lung and bladder cancers are examples of sporadic cancers due to carcinogen exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hereditary cancers come from germline mutations passed from parent to child; no inherited mutation was found.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The somatic cell line is not passed to the next generation; somatic mutations define sporadic, not hereditary, cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Infectious agents cause about 15% of cancers, but bladder cancer in a heavy smoker is attributed to carcinogen exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A spontaneous sporadic cancer arises without carcinogen exposure, but this patient has a heavy smoking exposure.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man is diagnosed with colon cancer. His father and paternal grandmother were both diagnosed with colon cancer in their 20s and 30s, and he is found to have Lynch syndrome. Compared with sporadic colon cancer, which of the following best characterizes the hereditary form of this disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It appears after age 50 and has a relatively good prognosis if detected early

choices.label: B
choices.text: It arises from carcinogen-induced somatic mutations that are not passed to offspring

choices.label: C
choices.text: It can occur as early as age 20 and typically has a poorer prognosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is caused by a germline APC mutation producing hundreds of adenomatous polyps

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is prevented by beginning colonoscopy at age 45 and repeating every 10 years

explanation.summary: Hereditary colon cancers such as Lynch syndrome present earlier and behave more aggressively than sporadic cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hereditary cancers tend to manifest earlier and act more aggressively than their sporadic counterparts. Sporadic colon cancer usually appears after age 50 and, if detected early, typically has a relatively good prognosis, whereas hereditary forms such as those in patients with Lynch syndrome can occur as early as age 20 and typically have a poorer prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Onset after 50 with a good prognosis when detected early describes sporadic colon cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carcinogen-induced somatic mutations define sporadic, induced cancers; Lynch syndrome is inherited.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hundreds of adenomatous polyps from a germline APC mutation describes familial adenomatous polyposis, a different syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Age 45 with 10-year repeat is the average-risk screening schedule; it does not apply to a hereditary syndrome with onset in the 20s.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy whose family recently emigrated from Uganda is brought to clinic with a rapidly enlarging mass of the mandible. Biopsy shows sheets of monomorphic, mitotically active B cells with interspersed tingible body macrophages producing a "starry sky" appearance. Which of the following pathogens is most strongly associated with this child's tumor?

explanation.summary: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma classically presents as a pediatric jaw mass in Africa and is strongly associated with EBV.
explanation.whyCorrect: The African (endemic) subtype of Burkitt lymphoma typically presents in children as a large mandibular mass and is virtually always EBV-positive (EBV identified in >90% of endemic cases). The "starry sky" histology of neoplastic B cells with tingible body macrophages is characteristic.

whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori is associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma of the stomach, not a pediatric jaw mass.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV causes squamous lesions such as warts and squamous cell carcinomas, not Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, a malignancy of CD4+ T cells, not a B-cell jaw tumor in children.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. haematobium is associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, not lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man reports abdominal pain after meals, nausea, frequent burping, and unintentional weight loss. Testing confirms infection with a curved gram-negative rod that, if left untreated, can progress to gastric cancer. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this organism promotes neoplastic transformation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Altered regulation of vascular endothelial growth factor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosa

explanation.summary: H. pylori drives gastric carcinogenesis through longstanding chronic inflammation of the mucosa.
explanation.whyCorrect: Conflict between H. pylori and the host immune system produces chronic gastritis; this longstanding inflammatory damage and resultant epithelial proliferation lead to a step-wise cascade toward gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Altered VEGF regulation is the mechanism of HHV-8 in Kaposi sarcoma, not of H. pylori.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E6 inactivation of p53 is a mechanism of high-risk HPV, not H. pylori.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E7 inactivation of Rb is a mechanism of high-risk HPV, not H. pylori.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The Tax oncoprotein is implicated in HTLV-1-driven adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.

questions.stem: A pathologist reviews sequential gastric biopsies from a patient with chronic H. pylori infection to document the precancerous cascade. Which of the following histologic changes occurs immediately before the development of invasive gastric adenocarcinoma?

explanation.summary: Dysplasia is the pre-malignant step that directly precedes invasive gastric adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the H. pylori cascade, chronic gastritis leads to atrophic gastritis, then intestinal metaplasia, then dysplasia (enlarged, hyperchromatic, crowded nuclei). When dysplastic cells invade surrounding tissue, invasive gastric adenocarcinoma is formed, so dysplasia is the last step before invasion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atrophic gastritis occurs earlier in the cascade, before intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperplasia is not the identified step in this cascade and does not directly precede invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypertrophy is not a step described in the gastric precancerous cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intestinal metaplasia (goblet and Paneth cells) precedes dysplasia, not invasion directly.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has an abnormal Pap smear, and cervical biopsy reveals non-keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. The lesion is driven by a virus that produces two oncoproteins not made by low-risk serotypes. Which of the following best describes the action of these oncoproteins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They inactivate p53 and Rb, removing the G1-to-S checkpoint

choices.label: B
choices.text: They incorporate viral DNA directly into the hepatocyte genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: They inhibit apoptosis while driving CD4+ T-cell proliferation

choices.label: D
choices.text: They stimulate transcription of viral RNA to expand T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: They upregulate VEGF to promote angiogenesis

explanation.summary: High-risk HPV E6 and E7 oncoproteins inactivate p53 and Rb, permitting uncontrolled proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-risk HPV serotypes (16, 18, 31, 33) produce E6 and E7 oncoproteins. E6 inactivates p53 and E7 inactivates Rb; without normal p53 and Rb function the cell cycle proceeds through the G1-to-S transition unchecked, permitting uncontrolled proliferation that, with accumulated mutations, progresses to carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Incorporation of viral DNA into hepatocytes describes HBV, not HPV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting apoptosis while driving CD4+ T-cell proliferation describes the HTLV-1 HBZ protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stimulating transcription of viral RNA to expand T cells describes the HTLV-1 Tax protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VEGF upregulation and angiogenesis is the HHV-8/Kaposi sarcoma mechanism.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man receiving antiretroviral therapy for HIV presents with multiple red-violet, raised plaques on his arms that continue to grow. Biopsy shows a proliferation of neoplastic vascular channels. The causative virus promotes this tumor primarily by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of the CD21 surface marker on resting B lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic inflammation of the bladder urothelial epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Continuous activation of vascular endothelial growth factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inactivation of p53 by the E6 oncoprotein of the virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Integration of viral DNA into the host hepatocyte genome

explanation.summary: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma by deregulating VEGF, driving angiogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8, which alters regulation of VEGF. VEGF drives angiogenesis, and its continuous activation leads to proliferating mesenchymal/endothelial cells that form a vascular sarcoma, appearing as red-violet skin lesions, especially in immunosuppressed patients with AIDS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD21 binding on B lymphocytes describes EBV, not HHV-8.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic bladder inflammation describes Schistosoma haematobium, not HHV-8.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E6 inactivation of p53 is a high-risk HPV mechanism, not HHV-8.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Integration of viral DNA into hepatocytes describes HBV in hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with painless, enlarging cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy shows large malignant cells with a bilobed nucleus and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli described as "owl eye" cells. Which of the following viruses is most commonly associated with this malignancy?

explanation.summary: Reed-Sternberg 'owl eye' cells indicate classic Hodgkin lymphoma, ~50% of which are EBV-associated.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bilobed "owl eye" Reed-Sternberg cell is the key histologic finding of classic Hodgkin lymphoma, which typically presents with painless supradiaphragmatic lymphadenopathy. Approximately 50% of classic Hodgkin lymphoma cases are related to EBV infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HBV is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HCV is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not Reed-Sternberg cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV causes squamous lesions and carcinomas, not Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, which shows a flower-shaped nucleus, not owl eye cells.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man from southern Japan develops fatigue, hypercalcemia, and lymphadenopathy. A peripheral smear shows malignant CD4+ T cells, some with a characteristic multi-lobated, flower-shaped nucleus. Which of the following viruses is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: A flower-shaped nucleus in a malignancy of CD4+ T cells signals HTLV-1-associated adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: HTLV-1 is a retrovirus endemic to regions including Japan that shows tropism for CD4+ T cells. It causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL); in the acute phase, a characteristic multi-lobated, flower-shaped nucleus may be seen. Neoplastic transformation is linked to the viral Tax and HBZ proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EBV is associated with Hodgkin lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not the flower cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori is a bacterium associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma, not ATLL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma, not ATLL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV causes squamous lesions and carcinomas, not a T-cell leukemia.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use has chronic hepatitis progressing to cirrhosis. Imaging reveals a liver mass, and biopsy shows plump, eosinophilic polygonal cells with nuclear atypia that resemble hepatocytes. Which of the following best explains the development of this malignancy?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tropism of the virus for CD4+ T cells

explanation.summary: Chronic HCV (or HBV) infection causes hepatocellular carcinoma through longstanding inflammatory damage and cirrhosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: HCV is transmitted commonly by IV drug use, and about 60-80% of infections become chronic. Long-term inflammation and cellular injury evolve to cirrhosis and damage cellular DNA, with reactive oxygen species and increased hepatocyte proliferation, resulting in hepatocellular carcinoma composed of plump, eosinophilic malignant hepatocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacterial-driven intestinal metaplasia describes H. pylori in the stomach, not HCV in the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.B: VEGF deregulation is the HHV-8/Kaposi sarcoma mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E7 inactivation of Rb is a high-risk HPV mechanism, not a hepatitis virus mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropism for CD4+ T cells describes HTLV-1, not a hepatitis virus.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man who spent years in North Africa presents with painless hematuria. Cystoscopy shows a bladder mass, and biopsy reveals squamous cell carcinoma with adjacent parasitic eggs bearing a terminal spine. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: S. haematobium has an affinity for the bladder and causes squamous cell carcinoma via chronic inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Schistosoma haematobium is a parasitic flatworm that has an affinity for the bladder, where it causes urinary schistosomiasis. Cyclical infection and immune response drive chronic inflammation and reactive oxygen species that damage DNA; over time the bladder epithelium undergoes metaplasia, dysplasia, and finally squamous cell carcinoma. Its eggs are recognized by a terminal spine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EBV is associated with lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not bladder cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori affects the stomach (adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma), not the bladder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HBV causes hepatocellular carcinoma, not bladder squamous cell carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: While HPV causes squamous carcinomas at other sites, the parasitic eggs with a terminal spine identify Schistosoma.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman has epigastric discomfort, and gastric biopsy shows an increased population of small, neoplastic B cells consistent with extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. Testing is positive for H. pylori. Which of the following statements about her condition is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A substantial proportion of cases are cured following H. pylori eradication

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lesion characteristically shows binucleate Reed-Sternberg cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: The malignant cells are CD4+ T cells with multi-lobated nuclei

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tumor arises from neoplastic vascular endothelial channels driven by HHV-8

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor is driven by the E6 and E7 oncoproteins of high-risk HPV

explanation.summary: Gastric MALT lymphoma is H. pylori-associated, and many cases regress after antibiotic eradication.
explanation.whyCorrect: Extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma of the stomach is associated with H. pylori infection secondary to chronic bacterial-driven immune stimulation. Histology shows an increased population of small neoplastic B cells, and a substantial proportion of H. pylori-associated MALT lymphoma cases are cured following H. pylori eradication with antibiotics.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reed-Sternberg cells characterize Hodgkin lymphoma, not MALT lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MALT lymphoma is a B-cell neoplasm; CD4+ T-cell malignancy describes HTLV-1-associated ATLL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neoplastic vascular channels describe Kaposi sarcoma, not MALT lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: E6 and E7 oncoproteins drive high-risk HPV carcinomas, not gastric MALT lymphoma.

questions.stem: A pediatric oncologist confirms Burkitt lymphoma in a young patient, noting a highly proliferative B-cell tumor. Which of the following chromosomal translocations is classically associated with this lymphoma?

explanation.summary: Burkitt lymphoma is classically driven by the t(8;14) translocation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Burkitt lymphoma is a highly mitotically active non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma classically associated with the t(8;14) translocation, which places the MYC oncogene under the influence of the immunoglobulin heavy-chain promoter, driving the aggressive proliferation seen on the "starry sky" histology.

whyWrongByChoice.B: t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, is associated with chronic myeloid leukemia, not Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: t(11;22) is associated with Ewing sarcoma, not Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: t(14;18) is associated with follicular lymphoma (BCL2), not Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: t(15;17) is associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia, not Burkitt lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old sexually active man presents with soft, cauliflower-like growths on the genitals. Biopsy shows a benign papillary proliferation of squamous epithelium without invasion. Which of the following HPV serotypes are most likely responsible for these lesions?

explanation.summary: Low-risk HPV serotypes 6 and 11 cause genital warts (condyloma acuminata) that do not commonly progress to cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low-risk HPV serotypes 6 and 11 cause genital warts (condyloma acuminata) and squamous papillomas of the larynx (laryngeal papillomatosis). These are composed of a benign papillary proliferation of squamous epithelium and do not commonly progress to cancer because they do not produce the E6 and E7 oncoproteins.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk serotypes that produce E6/E7 and cause squamous cell carcinomas, not benign genital warts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV 16 and 31 are both high-risk carcinogenic serotypes, not the cause of benign genital warts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV 18 and 33 are both high-risk carcinogenic serotypes, not the cause of benign genital warts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV 31 and 33 are high-risk serotypes associated with carcinoma, not benign condyloma acuminata.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student presents with fever, sore throat, and swollen cervical lymph nodes. A peripheral smear shows atypical lymphocytosis, and her roommate had a similar illness after they shared drinks. The causative virus establishes latency by binding a specific surface marker on its target cell. Which of the following is that marker?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rb protein on squamous epithelial cells

explanation.summary: EBV, the cause of mononucleosis, targets B lymphocytes by binding the CD21 surface marker.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, and atypical lymphocytosis in a young adult who shared oral secretions is classic mononucleosis, the "kissing disease" caused by EBV (HHV-4). EBV targets B lymphocytes by binding the CD21 surface cell marker, then remains latent in those cells for a long time while stimulating their proliferation and survival.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4+ T cells are the target of HTLV-1 (and HIV), not of the virus that causes mononucleosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EBV shows tropism for B cells via CD21, not for CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rb is an intracellular tumor suppressor inactivated by HPV E7, not a surface marker bound by EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VEGF signaling is deregulated by HHV-8 in Kaposi sarcoma; it is not the entry marker for EBV.

questions.stem: A researcher studies how a latent herpesvirus in B lymphocytes drives the cells to proliferate and survive for years, eventually predisposing to B-cell lymphomas. She identifies viral genes that stimulate the normal cellular machinery of the infected cell. Which of the following pairs of viral oncogenes is she most likely studying?

explanation.summary: EBV induces proliferation and survival of latently infected B cells through viral oncogenes such as LMP-1 and EBNA-2.
explanation.whyCorrect: EBV remains latent in B cells for a long time and induces the proliferation and survival of virus-infected cells by stimulating the normal cellular machinery through viral oncogenes such as LMP-1 and EBNA-2. Under this stimulation the cells acquire additional genetic alterations over time, increasing the risk of B-cell lymphomas such as Hodgkin and Burkitt lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CagA is a bacterial gene of H. pylori associated with gastric adenocarcinoma risk, not a viral oncogene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E6 and E7 are the oncoproteins of high-risk HPV that inactivate p53 and Rb in squamous epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MYC and BCL2 are cellular genes, not viral oncogenes carried by a herpesvirus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tax and HBZ are the HTLV-1 proteins linked to transformation of CD4+ T cells, not a herpesvirus infecting B cells.

questions.stem: A hematologist reviews the age distribution of patients diagnosed with classic Hodgkin lymphoma at her center over 20 years. Which of the following patterns is she most likely to observe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single peak in children under 10 years of age

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single peak in patients between 40 and 50 years of age

choices.label: C
choices.text: A steady rise in incidence with each decade of life

choices.label: D
choices.text: A uniform distribution across all age groups

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two peaks, one in young adults and one after age 60

explanation.summary: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma shows a bimodal age distribution with a first peak in young adults and a second in patients over 60.
explanation.whyCorrect: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma typically shows two peaks in incidence: the first in young adults and the second in patients over 60 years of age. Approximately 50% of cases are related to EBV infection, and other risk factors include immunosuppression and a family history of the disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hodgkin lymphoma does not peak in young children; the first peak occurs in young adults.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Middle age falls between the two described peaks rather than being the single peak.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The distribution is bimodal, not a steady rise with age.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The disease has a distinctly bimodal pattern, not a uniform distribution.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy in the United States with no known immunodeficiency presents with a rapidly enlarging abdominal mass. Biopsy shows sheets of monomorphic, highly mitotically active B cells with interspersed tingible body macrophages. Which of the following best describes the relationship between this tumor and Epstein-Barr virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: EBV is identified in about 15% of cases of this subtype

choices.label: B
choices.text: EBV is identified in about 90% of cases of this subtype

choices.label: C
choices.text: EBV is identified in about half of cases of this subtype

choices.label: D
choices.text: EBV is identified in essentially all cases of this subtype

choices.label: E
choices.text: EBV is never identified in cases of this subtype

explanation.summary: Sporadic (non-endemic) Burkitt lymphoma presents as a fast-growing abdominal mass in children and is EBV-positive in only about 15% of cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: A "starry sky" B-cell tumor presenting as a fast-growing abdominal mass in a child outside an endemic region and without immunodeficiency is the sporadic subtype of Burkitt lymphoma. EBV is identified in >90% of endemic (African) cases, but only 15% of sporadic cases and 25% of HIV-associated cases.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The >90% figure applies to endemic Burkitt lymphoma, not sporadic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 50% EBV association describes classic Hodgkin lymphoma, not sporadic Burkitt lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Near-universal EBV positivity characterizes the endemic African subtype, which presents as a jaw mass, not the sporadic subtype.
whyWrongByChoice.E: EBV is identified in a minority (15%) of sporadic cases; it is not absent.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with poorly controlled HIV infection develops an aggressive B-cell lymphoma whose histology shows a "starry sky" pattern of neoplastic cells and tingible body macrophages. Compared with the endemic African form of this lymphoma, which of the following is most accurate regarding this patient's subtype?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is composed of neoplastic CD4+ T cells rather than B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is EBV-positive in roughly one quarter of cases

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is more strongly associated with EBV than the endemic form

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lacks the t(8;14) translocation seen in the endemic form

choices.label: E
choices.text: It typically presents as a large mandibular mass

explanation.summary: Immunodeficiency-associated Burkitt lymphoma occurs in the setting of HIV and is EBV-positive in about 25% of cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Burkitt lymphoma may occur in the setting of immunosuppression, such as HIV infection. EBV is identified in >90% of endemic cases, 15% of sporadic cases, and 25% of HIV-associated cases, so the immunodeficiency-associated subtype is EBV-positive in roughly one quarter of cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Burkitt lymphoma in every subtype is a non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma; CD4+ T-cell malignancy describes HTLV-1-associated ATLL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The endemic form is virtually always EBV-positive (>90%), a far stronger association than the 25% seen with HIV-associated disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Burkitt lymphoma is classically associated with the t(8;14) translocation regardless of subtype.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A large mandibular (jaw) mass is the classic presentation of the endemic African subtype, not the immunodeficiency-associated form.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man who emigrated from Southern China presents with nasal obstruction and a neck mass. Biopsy of a nasopharyngeal lesion shows neoplastic epithelial cells intimately admixed with a dense lymphocytic infiltrate. Which of the following pathogens is most strongly associated with this neoplasm?

explanation.summary: Non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma with a dense lymphocytic infiltrate is strongly associated with EBV and is more common in Southern China.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a rare malignancy with increased frequency in Southern China, northern Africa, and some Inuit populations of Alaska and Canada. EBV is strongly associated with the neoplasm, though the exact etiology likely also involves environmental and genetic factors. The non-keratinizing subtype shows neoplastic epithelial cells typically associated with a dense lymphocytic infiltrate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori is associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma, not a nasopharyngeal neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma, not an epithelial nasopharyngeal tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: High-risk HPV causes squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix, vulva, penis, anus, and oropharynx, not nasopharyngeal carcinoma with this epidemiology.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, a T-cell malignancy, not a nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

questions.stem: A public health nurse counsels a patient about the virus responsible for Kaposi sarcoma. Which of the following is the most common route of transmission of this virus?

explanation.summary: HHV-8, the Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, is transmitted by bodily fluids, most commonly through salivary contact.
explanation.whyCorrect: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, is transmitted by bodily fluids, most commonly through salivary contact. It alters regulation of VEGF, leading to the vascular sarcoma seen especially in immunosuppressed patients with AIDS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Breast milk is a route of HTLV-1 transmission, not the most common route for HHV-8.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Needle stick injury is a common route for hepatitis C virus, not the primary route for HHV-8.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Skin penetration from contaminated water is how Schistosoma haematobium enters the body.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transplacental transmission is described as an uncommon route for HCV, not the main route for HHV-8.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with advanced HIV infection presents with progressive dyspnea. Imaging shows a large pleural effusion without a discrete mass. Cytology of the fluid reveals a population of large malignant B cells. Which of the following viruses is the cause of this rare lymphoma?

explanation.summary: Primary effusion lymphoma is a rare HHV-8-driven B-cell lymphoma presenting as a malignant effusion in HIV-associated immunosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to its endothelial tropism in Kaposi sarcoma, HHV-8 has affinity for B cells and is implicated in certain lymphomas and lymphoproliferative disorders. HHV-8 is the cause of primary effusion lymphoma, a rare B-cell lymphoma that presents as an effusion of malignant B cells in the context of HIV-associated immunosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HBV targets hepatocytes and is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, not a B-cell effusion lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HCV is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma through cirrhosis, not primary effusion lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV 18 is a high-risk serotype causing squamous cell carcinomas, not lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, a malignancy of CD4+ T cells, not B cells.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old nurse sustains a needle stick injury from a patient known to carry a hepatitis virus that is transmitted commonly by IV drug use and occupational exposure and only uncommonly by sexual intercourse. She asks about her long-term prognosis if she becomes infected. Approximately what proportion of infections with this virus become chronic?

explanation.summary: About 60-80% of hepatitis C infections become chronic, which is where the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma begins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The transmission pattern described (IV drug use, needle stick injury, uncommon sexual and transplacental spread) is that of hepatitis C virus. About 60%-80% of HCV infections become chronic, causing chronic inflammatory cells to accumulate in the liver (hepatitis); long-term inflammation can evolve to cirrhosis and damage cellular DNA, resulting in hepatocellular carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 10-15% is the estimated share of all cancers caused by viruses, not the HCV chronicity rate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 25-40% substantially underestimates the proportion of HCV infections that become chronic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Not all HCV infections become chronic; roughly 20-40% clear.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronicity is the rule rather than the exception with HCV; far more than 5% become chronic.

questions.stem: A hospital's occupational health office requires all newly hired nurses and physicians to document immunity to a hepatitis virus before starting work. The virus in question is transmitted sexually, through IV drug use, and from mother to child during childbirth. Which of the following viruses is the target of this requirement?

explanation.summary: Health professionals with increased risk of blood exposure are required to receive the HBV vaccine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatitis B virus is transmitted sexually, through IV drug use, and from mother to child during childbirth. Professionals with an increased risk of being exposed to blood with HBV, such as health professionals (especially nurses and doctors), are required to get the HBV vaccine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EBV is spread by oral secretions and causes mononucleosis; it is not the subject of a workplace vaccine requirement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HCV is also a bloodborne hepatitis virus, but improved screening rather than vaccination is what reduced transfusion-related HCV; the vaccine requirement applies to HBV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-8 is transmitted mainly through salivary contact and is not the subject of a vaccine requirement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HTLV-1 is transmitted mother to neonate and through blood, but there is no described vaccine requirement for health workers.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B infection and cirrhosis develops hepatocellular carcinoma. A student notes that this virus is capable of incorporating some of its DNA into the DNA of host hepatocytes. Which of the following best describes the currently accepted major driver of carcinogenesis in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Integration of viral DNA adjacent to cellular oncogenes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Viral inhibition of apoptosis in infected hepatocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral stimulation of hepatocyte growth factor transcription

explanation.summary: Although HBV can integrate DNA into hepatocytes, longstanding inflammation-mediated damage is thought to be the major player in HBV carcinogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: HBV is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma. Though HBV can incorporate some of its DNA into the DNA of a host hepatocyte, the longstanding inflammation-mediated cellular damage is currently thought to be the major player in carcinogenesis. Chronic infection results in cirrhosis, and continued inflammatory damage such as from reactive oxygen species, in the context of increased hepatocyte proliferation, leads to hepatocellular carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA integration by HBV does occur, but it is not considered the major driver; chronic inflammation is.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibition of apoptosis is attributed to the HTLV-1 HBZ protein, not to HBV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oncoprotein-mediated p53 inactivation is the mechanism of high-risk HPV E6, not of HBV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral stimulation of a growth factor is the HHV-8/VEGF mechanism in Kaposi sarcoma, not HBV.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with a 30-year history of heavy alcohol use and known cirrhosis develops a liver mass. Serologic testing for hepatitis B and hepatitis C is negative. Biopsy shows plump, eosinophilic polygonal cells with nuclear atypia resembling hepatocytes. Which of the following best explains his diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alcohol directly integrates into hepatocyte DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Longstanding hepatic injury of any cause can lead to this tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Occult infection with an oncogenic virus must be present

choices.label: D
choices.text: The histology indicates a vascular rather than hepatocellular origin

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor is most likely a metastasis rather than a primary liver cancer

explanation.summary: Hepatocellular carcinoma is not limited to viral hepatitis; other causes of longstanding hepatic injury, such as alcohol use disorder, also lead to it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatocellular carcinoma is not limited to patients with HBV and HCV infections but can also be seen in other contexts of longstanding hepatic injury, such as certain metabolic diseases and alcohol use disorder. Regardless of cause, hepatocellular carcinoma is composed of malignant hepatocytes that often appear as plump, eosinophilic, polygonal epithelial cells with nuclear atypia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alcohol does not integrate into DNA; it causes longstanding hepatic injury and inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A viral cause is not required; alcohol-related cirrhosis is a recognized non-viral pathway to hepatocellular carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plump eosinophilic cells resembling hepatocytes indicate hepatocellular origin; a vascular tumor would show neoplastic vascular channels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cells resembling hepatocytes arising in a cirrhotic liver indicate primary hepatocellular carcinoma, not a metastasis.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl has several rough, vegetated papules on the dorsum of her fingers. Biopsy of one lesion shows a benign proliferation of hyperkeratotic squamous epithelium. Which of the following HPV serotypes is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Common warts (verruca vulgaris) on the hands of children are benign squamous papillomas caused by HPV serotypes 1, 2, 4, and 7.
explanation.whyCorrect: Warts, also known as verruca vulgaris, are commonly seen on the hands in children and young adults and correspond to a benign proliferation of hyperkeratotic squamous epithelium. These benign squamous papillomas are caused by HPV serotypes 1, 2, 4, and 7.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV 16 is a high-risk serotype associated with squamous cell carcinoma, not benign hand warts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV 18 is a high-risk carcinogenic serotype, not a cause of verruca vulgaris.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV 31 is a high-risk serotype producing E6 and E7, not a cause of common warts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV 33 is a high-risk serotype implicated in carcinogenesis, not verruca vulgaris.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has progressive hoarseness and stridor. Laryngoscopy reveals multiple exophytic growths on the vocal cords that recur after excision. Histology shows a papillary proliferation of squamous epithelium. Which of the following best characterizes these lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Benign squamous papillomas that do not commonly progress to cancer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dysplastic epithelium that will progress to invasive carcinoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neoplastic B-cell proliferation within the laryngeal mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma driven by E6 and E7 oncoproteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vascular neoplasm driven by deregulated VEGF

explanation.summary: Recurrent laryngeal papillomatosis is caused by low-risk HPV 6 and 11 and consists of benign squamous papillomas that do not commonly progress to cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low-risk HPV serotypes 6 and 11 cause genital warts and squamous papillomas of the larynx (laryngeal papillomatosis) that do not commonly progress to cancer. Histologically they are composed of a papillary proliferation of squamous epithelium similar to other warts. Low-risk serotypes do not produce the E6 and E7 oncoproteins.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These lesions are benign papillomas, not dysplasia; low-risk HPV lesions do not commonly progress to carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A papillary squamous proliferation is epithelial; it is not a lymphoid neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E6 and E7 are produced by high-risk serotypes (16, 18, 31, 33), not the low-risk types that cause laryngeal papillomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A VEGF-driven vascular neoplasm describes Kaposi sarcoma caused by HHV-8, not squamous papillomas.

questions.stem: A student reviewing high-risk HPV pathogenesis notes that the viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 inactivate the products of the TP53 and Rb genes, allowing the cell cycle to proceed without checks at the G1-to-S transition. Which of the following best classifies TP53 and Rb?

explanation.summary: p53 and Rb are tumor suppressors whose inactivation by HPV E6 and E7 removes the G1-to-S checkpoint.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-risk HPV E6 and E7 oncoproteins inhibit the tumor suppressive actions of p53 and Rb, respectively. Without normal p53 and Rb function the cell cycle can continue without any checks from the G1 to S phase transition, permitting uncontrolled proliferation that progresses to carcinoma with the acquisition of oncogenic mutations over time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TP53 and Rb are described here as cell-cycle checkpoint regulators, not as DNA repair enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neither p53 nor Rb is a growth factor receptor; they are checkpoint tumor suppressors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proto-oncogenes promote growth when activated; p53 and Rb instead restrain the cell cycle and are lost in cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: E6 and E7 are the viral oncogenes; TP53 and Rb are host cellular genes.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man presents with a painless mass at the base of the tongue and a level II neck node. Biopsy reveals non-keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. He has never smoked. Which of the following pathogens is most likely implicated in this tumor?

explanation.summary: High-risk HPV serotypes such as HPV 16 cause squamous cell carcinoma of the oropharynx in addition to anogenital sites.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-risk HPV serotypes, including HPV 16, 18, 31, and 33, are implicated in carcinogenesis, particularly squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix, vulva, penis, anus, and oropharynx. These serotypes produce E6 and E7 oncoproteins that inactivate p53 and Rb, permitting uncontrolled proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular tumor, not oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV 11 is a low-risk serotype that does not produce E6 and E7 and is not implicated in carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV 6 is a low-risk serotype causing condyloma acuminata and laryngeal papillomas, which do not commonly progress to cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, not an epithelial carcinoma of the oropharynx.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman born in the Caribbean is diagnosed with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. She has no history of IV drug use, transfusion, or high-risk sexual behavior. Which of the following is the most likely route by which she acquired the causative virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ingestion of contaminated food or drinking water

choices.label: B
choices.text: Needle stick injury in an occupational setting

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salivary contact with an infected household member

choices.label: D
choices.text: Skin penetration by a parasite in fresh water

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vertical transmission from her mother at birth

explanation.summary: HTLV-1 is most commonly transmitted from mother to neonate at birth, and exposure may precede ATLL by several decades.
explanation.whyCorrect: HTLV-1 is a retrovirus endemic to certain regions including Japan, Africa, the Caribbean, and South America. It is transmitted from mother to neonate at birth (most common), sexually, through IV drug use, by blood contact, and via breast milk. The exposure can occur several decades before clinical features of ATLL appear, which fits a patient diagnosed in her 50s without adult risk behaviors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HTLV-1 is not described as foodborne; its routes are perinatal, sexual, blood, and breast milk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Needle stick injury is a route for HCV and can transmit HTLV-1 via blood, but the patient has no such exposure and it is not the most common route.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Salivary contact is the most common route for HHV-8 (and oral secretions for EBV), not for HTLV-1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Skin penetration from contaminated water is the entry route of Schistosoma haematobium, not a retrovirus.

questions.stem: A virologist studying HTLV-1-infected CD4+ T cells characterizes two viral proteins implicated in neoplastic transformation. One stimulates transcription of viral RNA and activates pathways related to T-cell proliferation. Which of the following best describes the action of the other protein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds CD21 to allow viral entry into the cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: It drives T-cell proliferation and inhibits apoptosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inactivates Rb to remove the G1-to-S checkpoint

choices.label: D
choices.text: It induces pro-inflammatory cytokine release from the host

choices.label: E
choices.text: It upregulates VEGF to promote angiogenesis

explanation.summary: HTLV-1 transformation is linked to Tax, which stimulates viral transcription and T-cell proliferation pathways, and HBZ, which drives T-cell proliferation and inhibits apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Though the exact mechanism of HTLV-1 tumorigenesis is unknown, neoplastic transformation is thought to be related to two viral proteins. Tax stimulates transcription of viral RNA and activates pathways related to T-cell proliferation (the protein described in the stem). HBZ drives T-cell proliferation and inhibits apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD21 binding is how EBV enters B lymphocytes; HTLV-1 targets CD4+ T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rb inactivation is the action of the HPV E7 oncoprotein, not an HTLV-1 protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Induction of pro-inflammatory cytokines describes CagA-expressing H. pylori strains in the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VEGF upregulation and angiogenesis is the mechanism of HHV-8 in Kaposi sarcoma.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman from southern Japan is found to be seropositive for HTLV-1 during blood donor screening. She is asymptomatic. Which of the following statements best describes her prognosis with respect to adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATLL develops only if she is also co-infected with HIV or another retrovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: ATLL will develop only after the virus integrates into the DNA of hepatocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most infected individuals develop ATLL within a few years of acquiring the virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only a small portion of infected patients develop ATLL, often decades after exposure

choices.label: E
choices.text: She cannot develop ATLL because she acquired the virus as an adult rather than at birth

explanation.summary: Only a small portion of HTLV-1-infected patients develop ATLL, and exposure can precede disease by several decades.
explanation.whyCorrect: HTLV-1 is a retrovirus like HIV that is endemic to regions including Japan. Only a small portion of patients infected with HTLV-1 develop ATLL, a disease of malignant CD4+ T cells, and the exposure can occur several decades before clinical features appear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HIV co-infection is not a requirement for ATLL; HTLV-1 alone, via Tax and HBZ, is linked to transformation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HTLV-1 shows tropism for CD4+ T cells, not hepatocytes; hepatocyte DNA integration is a feature of HBV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The opposite is true: most infected individuals never develop ATLL, and when it occurs it follows a latency of decades.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Timing of acquisition is not described as protective; HTLV-1 is acquired perinatally most commonly but also sexually and via blood in adults.

questions.stem: A gastroenterologist evaluates two patients with chronic H. pylori gastritis. Molecular typing shows that one patient's strain expresses a particular bacterial gene whose products induce pro-inflammatory cytokines and drive atrophy and intestinal metaplasia. Which of the following genes confers the highest risk of gastric adenocarcinoma?

explanation.summary: H. pylori strains expressing the CagA gene carry the highest risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The highest risk for gastric adenocarcinoma occurs with H. pylori expressing the CagA gene. These strains induce pro-inflammatory cytokines and effectively induce atrophy and intestinal metaplasia before the development of dysplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: E6 is a high-risk HPV oncoprotein that inactivates p53 in squamous epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EBNA-2 is an EBV viral oncogene, not a gene carried by H. pylori.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HBZ is an HTLV-1 protein that drives T-cell proliferation and inhibits apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: LMP-1 is an EBV viral oncogene that stimulates B-cell proliferation, not a bacterial gene.

questions.stem: A public health researcher compares gastric adenocarcinoma trends across countries. Which of the following observations is most consistent with what is known about this cancer's relationship to H. pylori?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endoscopic screening programs in high-incidence countries such as Japan have failed to improve outcomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: H. pylori colonizes fewer than 5% of the world's population, making it a rare infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incidence in the United States has decreased significantly as H. pylori infection rates have fallen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incidence is essentially uniform worldwide regardless of regional H. pylori prevalence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Japan has among the lowest incidences of gastric adenocarcinoma anywhere in the world

explanation.summary: Gastric adenocarcinoma incidence tracks H. pylori prevalence, and it has fallen significantly in the United States as infection rates have declined.
explanation.whyCorrect: The incidence of gastric adenocarcinoma varies considerably across the globe, with a higher incidence in Japan and parts of Central and South America. In the United States, incidence has decreased significantly with reduced rates of H. pylori infection. In high-incidence areas like Japan, endoscopic screening programs have positively affected public health through early detection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endoscopic screening in Japan has positively affected public health through early detection of gastric cancers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: By some estimates H. pylori colonizes half the world's population.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Incidence varies considerably across the globe, being higher in Japan and parts of Central and South America.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Japan is a high-incidence country for gastric adenocarcinoma, not a low-incidence one.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with longstanding untreated H. pylori infection undergoes gastric biopsy. The mucosa contains cells with clear, round mucinous vacuoles and cells with prominent red cytoplasmic granules that are not normally found in the stomach. Which of the following stages of the precancerous cascade does this biopsy represent?

explanation.summary: Intestinal metaplasia in the stomach is identified by goblet cells with clear mucinous vacuoles and Paneth cells with red granules.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the H. pylori cascade, the mucosa eventually undergoes intestinal metaplasia in an attempt to withstand the harsh inflammatory environment. Intestinal metaplasia is identified by the presence of goblet cells with clear, round, mucinous vacuoles and Paneth cells with red granules, neither of which belongs in normal gastric mucosa.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MALT lymphoma shows an increased population of small neoplastic B cells, not metaplastic epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dysplasia is identified by enlarged, hyperchromatic, crowded nuclei rather than by intestinal-type cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Invasive adenocarcinoma is defined by dysplastic cells invading surrounding tissue, which is not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronic gastritis is identified by increased lymphocytes and plasma cells, not by goblet and Paneth cells.

questions.stem: Serial gastric biopsies are obtained from a patient with chronic H. pylori infection. The first biopsy shows chronic gastritis with abundant lymphocytes and plasma cells. A later biopsy shows a reduced number of gastric glands with fibrotic changes but no goblet cells. Which of the following best describes the later biopsy?

explanation.summary: After chronic gastritis, the gastric mucosa atrophies, seen as fewer glands and fibrotic changes, before intestinal metaplasia develops.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the step-wise cascade, H. pylori first induces chronic gastritis with increased lymphocytes and plasma cells. Next, the gastric mucosa atrophies in the context of the inflammation, seen as fewer glands along with fibrotic changes. Only afterward does the mucosa undergo intestinal metaplasia, marked by goblet and Paneth cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MALT lymphoma is an increased population of small neoplastic B cells, not loss of glands.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dysplasia is defined by enlarged, hyperchromatic, crowded nuclei, not by gland loss and fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intestinal metaplasia requires goblet cells and Paneth cells, which are explicitly absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Normal antral mucosa has a full complement of glands without fibrosis or chronic inflammation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old aid worker develops an intensely itchy rash shortly after wading in a freshwater lake in Egypt. Years later, she is found to have parasite eggs with terminal spines in her bladder wall. Which of the following organisms is the intermediate host required for this parasite to complete its life cycle?

explanation.summary: Schistosoma haematobium enters through the skin (swimmer's itch), matures in the liver, and its eggs pass into water where a snail serves as the intermediate host.
explanation.whyCorrect: Schistosoma haematobium is a free-living, aquatic, parasitic flatworm. The immature parasite enters the human body via the skin and may present as an itchy rash known as "swimmer's itch." It travels through the bloodstream to the liver, matures, mates, and the eggs exit the body by urine and defecation into the water, where a snail becomes the intermediate host until an immature organism develops that can infect another human.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fish are not described as hosts; the eggs develop in a snail intermediate host.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mosquitoes are not part of the schistosome life cycle; the parasite is acquired directly from water through the skin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pigs play no role in the S. haematobium life cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ticks are not vectors or hosts for this aquatic helminth.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with colon adenocarcinoma is being staged. Imaging reveals a 4-cm primary tumor invading the muscularis propria, three positive regional lymph nodes, and multiple lesions in the liver consistent with metastases. Which of the following components of the TNM system most adversely affects his prognosis?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Number of involved regional lymph nodes (N)

explanation.summary: Distant metastasis (M1) is the single most adverse prognostic component of the TNM system and defines Stage IV disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the TNM system, distant metastasis (M1) generally carries the greatest negative prognostic weight and places the patient at Stage IV, which has the poorest outcome and is usually not curable. The liver lesions represent distant spread, which dominates staging over local and nodal factors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Depth of local invasion refines the T category but is outweighed by the presence of distant metastasis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Grade is a histologic prognostic factor but does not define anatomic stage; distant metastasis is the dominant factor here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nodal involvement (N) worsens prognosis but is less adverse than distant metastatic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primary tumor size contributes to the T category but is far less decisive than distant spread once metastasis is present.

questions.stem: A pathologist explains that two patients with the same type of carcinoma can have very different expected outcomes. For most solid tumors, which of the following is generally the strongest predictor of prognosis?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patient age at the time of diagnosis

explanation.summary: For most solid tumors, anatomic stage is a stronger predictor of outcome than grade or individual histologic features.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stage reflects the anatomic extent of disease (tumor size, nodal involvement, and metastasis) and usually correlates more closely with survival than grade for most solid tumors. Widespread disease overrides favorable histology.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Nuclear pleomorphism is a grading feature and is subordinate to overall stage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Grade is an important prognostic factor but is generally less predictive than stage for most solid tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitotic rate is one component of grade, not the overall dominant prognostic factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Age can influence treatment tolerance but is not the strongest predictor of tumor-specific outcome.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman undergoes cervical biopsy after an abnormal Pap smear. Histology shows severely atypical squamous cells occupying the full thickness of the epithelium, but the basement membrane is intact and there is no stromal invasion. Which of the following best describes this lesion's stage and prognostic significance?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stage I, with a moderate risk of nodal spread

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stage II, with local extension beyond the organ of origin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stage IV, because high-grade atypia implies distant spread

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unstageable, because grade and stage cannot be assessed on biopsy

explanation.summary: Carcinoma in situ (Tis) is Stage 0: malignant cells confined above the basement membrane, with excellent prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Full-thickness atypia without breach of the basement membrane defines carcinoma in situ (Tis), classified as Stage 0. Because there is no invasion, there is no access to lymphatics or vessels, so metastasis cannot occur and the lesion is highly curable by complete excision.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Stage I requires invasive tumor; an intact basement membrane means the lesion is in situ, not invasive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stage II implies local extension of invasive disease, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: High-grade cytology does not equal metastasis; without invasion there is no distant spread.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lesion is readily classified as carcinoma in situ; it is not unstageable.

questions.stem: A high-grade sarcoma specimen is described by the pathologist as showing marked variation in cell and nuclear size, tumor giant cells, and numerous abnormal (tripolar) mitotic figures, with no resemblance to any normal tissue. This lack of differentiation is best termed which of the following?

explanation.summary: Anaplasia is the complete lack of differentiation and is a histologic hallmark of malignancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anaplasia describes tumor cells that have lost differentiation and show marked pleomorphism, tumor giant cells, bizarre nuclei, and abnormal mitoses. It corresponds to the highest histologic grade and is a defining feature of aggressive malignancy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dysplasia is disordered but still differentiated growth, typically pre-invasive and less extreme than anaplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number in a controlled, differentiated tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size without loss of differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metaplasia is reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another, not a lack of differentiation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma completes chemotherapy. Follow-up PET/CT and physical examination show no detectable tumor. His oncologist emphasizes that this does not necessarily mean he is cured. Which of the following best describes his current status?

explanation.summary: Complete remission is the disappearance of all detectable disease, which is not synonymous with cure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complete remission means no tumor is detectable by clinical exam or imaging. However, microscopic residual disease may remain below detection limits, so recurrence can occur; cure can only be inferred later after prolonged disease-free follow-up.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cure requires prolonged absence of disease with recurrence risk approaching baseline and cannot be declared at this point.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Partial remission requires a measurable reduction with tumor still detectable, but disease is no longer detectable here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progressive disease means growth or new lesions, the opposite of this scenario.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stable disease means the tumor is present and unchanged, which is not the case.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman receiving therapy for metastatic breast cancer has restaging scans showing that the sum of her target lesion diameters has decreased by 45%, though several lesions remain measurable. Which of the following terms best describes her treatment response?

explanation.summary: Partial remission is at least a 30% reduction in measurable tumor burden with disease still detectable.
explanation.whyCorrect: A 45% reduction in tumor burden with residual measurable lesions meets the definition of partial remission (conventionally a decrease of about 30% or more). The response is meaningful, but disease persists.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complete remission requires disappearance of all detectable disease, but measurable lesions remain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cure requires prolonged absence of disease and cannot be applied to persistent measurable tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progressive disease means tumor growth or new lesions, the opposite of shrinkage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stable disease means little change in size, whereas a 45% decrease is a clear reduction.

questions.stem: Two patients each have an invasive ductal carcinoma of the same size and stage. Patient 1's tumor is well differentiated with tubule formation and rare mitoses; Patient 2's tumor is poorly differentiated with marked nuclear pleomorphism and frequent mitoses. Which statement about grade is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grade and stage always change together in the same direction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grade is determined by the presence of distant metastases

choices.label: C
