choices.text: Grade reflects the anatomic extent of spread of the tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patient 1's well-differentiated tumor generally carries a better prognosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patient 2's poorly differentiated tumor generally carries a better prognosis

explanation.summary: Lower-grade, well-differentiated tumors resemble normal tissue and generally have a better prognosis than high-grade tumors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Grade reflects how closely tumor cells resemble their tissue of origin. Well-differentiated (low-grade) tumors like Patient 1's tend to be less aggressive and carry a better prognosis than poorly differentiated (high-grade) tumors, when stage is held constant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Grade and stage are independent measures and do not necessarily move together.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Distant metastasis is part of staging (M), not grading.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anatomic extent of spread is described by stage, not grade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Poorly differentiated tumors are more aggressive and carry a worse, not better, prognosis.

questions.stem: A tumor board is deciding how to describe a newly diagnosed gastric carcinoma. One member wants to communicate the degree of histologic differentiation of the tumor cells, and another wants to communicate the anatomic extent of the disease. Which pairing correctly matches concept to term?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both differentiation and anatomic extent = grading

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both differentiation and anatomic extent = staging

explanation.summary: Grading describes histologic differentiation; staging describes the anatomic extent of spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: Grade is a microscopic assessment of how well tumor cells are differentiated, while stage (TNM) describes the anatomic extent of disease including local size, nodal involvement, and distant metastasis. These are complementary but distinct measures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anatomic extent is captured by staging, not grading.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Differentiation is captured by grading, not staging.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Remission refers to treatment response, not to histologic differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the definitions of grading and staging.

questions.stem: A patient reads that a particular cancer has a 5-year survival rate of 90%. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this statistic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 90% of patients are alive 5 years after diagnosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: 90% of patients are permanently cured of the disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: 90% of patients will have a recurrence within 5 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: The average patient will live exactly 5 more years

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cancer has spread to distant sites in 90% of patients

explanation.summary: The 5-year survival rate is the percentage of patients still alive 5 years after diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 5-year survival rate is a statistical benchmark defined as the proportion of patients alive 5 years after diagnosis. It is used to compare prognosis across cancers but does not by itself equate to cure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Being alive at 5 years is not the same as being cured; some patients still have or later develop disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The statistic describes survival, not recurrence rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It is a proportion surviving, not a prediction of an exact lifespan for individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The statistic does not describe the frequency of distant spread.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with newly diagnosed non-small cell lung cancer has limited disease that appears resectable, but he is bedridden more than half of each day and cannot care for himself. His oncologist notes that this factor independently predicts poorer outcomes and limits treatment options. Which prognostic factor is being described?

explanation.summary: Performance status measures a patient's functional ability and independently predicts prognosis and treatment tolerance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Performance status quantifies how well a patient can carry out daily activities. Poor performance status (e.g., bedridden more than half the day) independently predicts worse outcomes and often limits eligibility for aggressive therapy, separate from the anatomic characteristics of the tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carcinoma in situ describes a non-invasive lesion, unrelated to functional status.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Disease-free survival is an outcome measure over time, not the patient's current functional status.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stage describes anatomic extent of disease, which here is limited and resectable.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Grade describes histologic differentiation, not the patient's functional capacity.

questions.stem: In a clinical trial, investigators want an endpoint that captures how long patients remain alive without any detectable return of their cancer after treatment. Which of the following measures best fits this definition?

explanation.summary: Disease-free survival measures the time patients remain alive without detectable disease after treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Disease-free survival specifically measures the interval after treatment during which no disease is detectable, capturing the durability of a response. It reflects how long remission is maintained before any recurrence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 5-year survival rate is a fixed-timepoint survival proportion, not a measure of disease-free interval.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complete remission rate is the proportion achieving no detectable disease at a point in time, not a duration measure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Overall survival measures time to death from any cause and does not track recurrence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor grade distribution describes histology across patients, not a survival endpoint.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer has restaging scans after three cycles of chemotherapy. Compared with baseline, the target lesions have enlarged and two new peritoneal nodules have appeared. Which of the following best characterizes her response, and what does it indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete remission, indicating no detectable disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Partial remission, indicating a favorable response

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stable disease, indicating no meaningful change

explanation.summary: Growth of existing lesions or appearance of new lesions defines progressive disease and signals treatment failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Progressive disease is defined by an increase in tumor burden or the development of new lesions. Enlarging target lesions plus new peritoneal nodules meet this definition and indicate that the current therapy is failing, prompting a change in management.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complete remission requires no detectable disease, but the tumor has grown.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cure requires prolonged absence of disease and is incompatible with growing tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Partial remission requires tumor shrinkage, the opposite of what occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stable disease requires little change; here the disease has clearly worsened.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with acute lymphoblastic leukemia begins an induction regimen that includes a folate antagonist. The drug reduces the pool of reduced folates, thereby impairing purine and thymidylic acid synthesis and blocking progression of cells from G1 into S phase. Which of the following enzymes does this agent most directly inhibit?

explanation.summary: Methotrexate is an S-phase antimetabolite that blocks folate metabolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methotrexate binds and inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (and thymidylate synthetase), preventing formation of reduced folates. This blocks purine and thymidylic acid synthesis, interfering with DNA synthesis, repair, and replication and preventing the G1-to-S transition.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibition of DNA polymerase is the primary action of the pyrimidine analog cytarabine, not methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Topoisomerase I is the target of irinotecan, which prevents relegation of cleaved DNA strands.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcriptase is an antiviral target and is unrelated to cytotoxic chemotherapy mechanisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Interference with tubulin/microtubule dynamics describes vinca alkaloids and taxanes, not a folate antagonist.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia has been receiving induction chemotherapy that includes vincristine. Several weeks into treatment he develops difficulty walking, frequent tripping, and tingling and numbness of his fingers and toes. Examination shows decreased deep tendon reflexes, mild foot drop, and reduced grip strength. Which of the following adverse effects best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: Vinca alkaloids characteristically cause peripheral neuropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vincristine inhibits microtubule formation and affects rapidly turning-over and nerve cells, producing peripheral neuropathy. Tingling, numbness, decreased deep tendon reflexes, and foot drop are classic; caught early, it can be managed with dose reduction and monitoring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiotoxicity is the signature toxicity of doxorubicin (anthracyclines), not vinca alkaloids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemorrhagic cystitis is associated with cyclophosphamide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary fibrosis is characteristic of bleomycin and busulfan.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nephrotoxicity is a hallmark toxicity of the platinum agents cisplatin and carboplatin.

questions.stem: A researcher studies why some cancer cells continue to divide despite carrying extensive DNA damage. In normal cells, a series of surveillance points halts progression when DNA is damaged or the environment is unfavorable. Which of the following best describes the normal function of these cell cycle checkpoints?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They accelerate division of cells with damaged DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: They halt the cycle and trigger apoptosis in damaged cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: They mark tumor cells for destruction by monoclonal antibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: They replicate chromosomal DNA during S phase

choices.label: E
choices.text: They synthesize the microtubules of the mitotic spindle

explanation.summary: Checkpoints arrest the cycle and drive apoptosis of cells with damaged DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The G1/S, G2/M, and metaphase/anaphase checkpoints ensure a cell is ready to divide. DNA damage or an unfavorable environment halts the cycle and drives apoptosis, eliminating 'bad' cells. In cancer these checkpoints are often broken, permitting uncontrolled division.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Checkpoints restrain, not accelerate, division of damaged cells; loss of this restraint is what characterizes cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marking tumor cells for immune destruction describes monoclonal antibodies, not intrinsic checkpoints.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DNA replication is the defining event of S phase, not the function of a checkpoint.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microtubule synthesis occurs in G2 phase and is not the role of a checkpoint.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer develops progressive dyspnea and fatigue. Echocardiography shows a decline in left ventricular ejection fraction. Which of the following chemotherapeutic agents is most likely responsible for this toxicity?

explanation.summary: Doxorubicin (an anthracycline) is the classic cause of cardiotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Doxorubicin, an anthracycline that cross-links DNA independently of the cell cycle, is characteristically associated with cardiotoxicity, which can manifest as declining ejection fraction and heart failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytarabine is associated with keratitis and conjunctivitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irinotecan is associated with severe acute and delayed diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate's signature toxicity is myelosuppression, not cardiotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine is associated with peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man being treated for lymphoma develops dysuria and gross hematuria. Cystoscopy shows diffuse bladder mucosal inflammation and bleeding. Which of the following chemotherapeutic agents most likely caused this finding?

explanation.summary: Cyclophosphamide characteristically causes hemorrhagic cystitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent whose signature toxicity is hemorrhagic cystitis, presenting with dysuria and hematuria from bladder mucosal injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleomycin is associated with pulmonary fibrosis, not bladder toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cisplatin causes nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity rather than hemorrhagic cystitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxorubicin causes cardiotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man treated for testicular cancer develops a gradually worsening dry cough and dyspnea. Pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern with reduced diffusing capacity, and imaging suggests interstitial fibrosis. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Bleomycin is the classic cause of pulmonary fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bleomycin, a G2-phase agent that binds DNA and causes strand breaks, characteristically produces pulmonary fibrosis, presenting as progressive dyspnea and a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytarabine causes keratitis and conjunctivitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irinotecan is associated with severe diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate's signature toxicity is myelosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man undergoing chemotherapy develops a rising serum creatinine and new bilateral high-frequency hearing loss confirmed on audiometry. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible for both findings?

explanation.summary: Platinum agents such as cisplatin cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cisplatin is a platinum agent that cross-links DNA independently of the cell cycle; its signature toxicities include both nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, explaining the rising creatinine and hearing loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cyclophosphamide characteristically causes hemorrhagic cystitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxorubicin causes cardiotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methotrexate causes myelosuppression.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with non-Hodgkin lymphoma is started on a monoclonal antibody that binds an antigen on the surface of B cells, rendering them more susceptible to destruction by the immune system. Which of the following is the target of this agent?

explanation.summary: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rituximab acts on CD20 receptors on B cells, making them more susceptible to immune-mediated attack. It is used for B-cell malignancies such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HER2 is the target of trastuzumab, used in HER2-positive breast cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Topoisomerase I is inhibited by irinotecan, a cytotoxic agent rather than an antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tubulin is targeted by microtubule inhibitors (vinca alkaloids, taxanes), not a monoclonal antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VEGF is bound by bevacizumab to inhibit angiogenesis.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic colorectal cancer receives a monoclonal antibody intended to cut off the tumor's blood supply. The drug binds a circulating growth factor, inhibiting the abnormal blood vessel proliferation that accompanies tumor growth. Which of the following is the molecular target of this agent?

choices.label: C
choices.text: HER2 receptor on tumor cell membranes

explanation.summary: Bevacizumab binds VEGF to inhibit angiogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bevacizumab binds vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), inhibiting the angiogenesis that accompanies tumor growth. Without a vascular supply, the cancer cells die.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD20 is the target of rituximab on B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The CD3 receptor is the T-cell component onto which CAR-T constructs are fused, not a bevacizumab target.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HER2 is the target of trastuzumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate, a cytotoxic antimetabolite.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman has a breast tumor that overexpresses HER2. Her oncologist recommends a monoclonal antibody that binds this receptor to block downstream growth signaling and mark the cells for immune-mediated destruction. Which of the following agents is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Trastuzumab targets HER2-positive breast cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trastuzumab binds HER2 receptors on tumor cells, blocking the signaling pathways that drive growth and marking the cells for immune-mediated destruction. It is used primarily for HER2-positive breast cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bevacizumab binds VEGF to inhibit angiogenesis, not the HER2 receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Doxorubicin is a cytotoxic anthracycline that cross-links DNA, not a HER2-directed antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells for B-cell malignancies, not HER2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator used in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, a different target.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer is treated with irinotecan. The agent and its active metabolite bind reversibly to a DNA-associated enzyme, preventing relegation of the cleaved DNA strand and producing double-strand breaks during S phase. Which of the following enzymes does this agent inhibit?

explanation.summary: Irinotecan is a topoisomerase I inhibitor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Irinotecan and its active metabolite bind reversibly to the topoisomerase I-DNA complex, preventing relegation of the cleaved strand. This produces double-strand breaks that cells cannot efficiently repair, causing S-phase-specific cell death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA polymerase is the primary target of cytarabine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thymidylate synthetase is inhibited by methotrexate, not irinotecan.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tubulin is bound by microtubule inhibitors such as the vinca alkaloids and taxanes.

questions.stem: A patient with acute myeloid leukemia receives cytarabine. This agent is incorporated into DNA, but its primary action is inhibition of an enzyme required for DNA synthesis and repair, and it is specific for the S phase. Which of the following best describes cytarabine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A monoclonal antibody directed against CD20

choices.label: B
choices.text: A pyrimidine analog that inhibits DNA polymerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: A taxane that stabilizes microtubules and blocks disassembly

choices.label: D
choices.text: A vinca alkaloid that binds tubulin and arrests metaphase

choices.label: E
choices.text: An alkylating agent that cross-links DNA independently of the cycle

explanation.summary: Cytarabine is an S-phase pyrimidine analog that inhibits DNA polymerase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytarabine is a pyrimidine analog incorporated into DNA, but its primary action is inhibition of DNA polymerase, resulting in decreased DNA synthesis and repair. It is an S-phase-specific antimetabolite.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A CD20-directed monoclonal antibody describes rituximab, not a cytotoxic antimetabolite.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stabilizing microtubules and blocking their disassembly describes taxanes, which act in the M phase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Binding tubulin to arrest metaphase describes vinca alkaloids, which act in the M phase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cross-linking DNA independently of the cell cycle describes alkylating and platinum agents.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer is prescribed tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator. Within the broad classification of cancer pharmacotherapy, which of the following categories best describes this treatment?

explanation.summary: Tamoxifen is a SERM used as hormone (endocrine) therapy for ER-positive breast cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Medical treatment of cancer includes traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy, molecularly targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and hormone (endocrine) therapy. Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator used in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, is the brick's example of hormone therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cell therapy such as CAR-T uses genetically modified autologous T cells, not a drug acting on hormone receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunotherapy uses the body's own immune system to fight cancer; tamoxifen does not work through the immune system.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Molecularly targeted antibody therapy refers to monoclonal antibodies such as rituximab, bevacizumab, and trastuzumab, not a SERM.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytotoxic chemotherapy agents (antimetabolites, alkylating agents, microtubule inhibitors, and others) interrupt the cell cycle; tamoxifen acts on the estrogen receptor instead.

questions.stem: A histology student compares the proliferative behavior of cells from several tissues. Cells from which of the following tissues stay more or less permanently in the G0 phase of the cell cycle?

explanation.summary: Skeletal muscle and brain cells remain more or less permanently in G0.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nondividing cells are in the G0 phase. Some cells, like those in skeletal muscle and the brain, stay more or less permanently in G0, whereas others regularly re-enter the cell cycle in interphase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Malignant B cells divide uncontrolled because their checkpoints are broken; they are not resting in G0.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow cells turn over rapidly, which is why chemotherapy produces myelosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epidermal cells are the brick's example of cells that regularly enter the cell cycle in interphase rather than remaining in G0.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastric mucosa cells divide rapidly, which is why chemotherapy causes nausea and vomiting.

questions.stem: A cell in the epidermis leaves the G0 phase and enters interphase. Before it can replicate its chromosomal DNA, it must first synthesize messenger RNA and the proteins required for the remainder of the cycle. In which of the following phases does this synthesis occur?

explanation.summary: In G1 the cell synthesizes mRNA and proteins needed for the rest of the cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Interphase includes G1, S, and G2. In the first gap (G1) phase, the cell synthesizes messenger RNA and proteins required for the remainder of the cycle, before chromosomal DNA is replicated in S phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: G0 is the nondividing resting state; the cell in the stem has already left G0.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G2 is when the cell synthesizes more protein, including microtubules for the mitotic spindle, after DNA replication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M phase is mitosis, which is not part of interphase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S phase is when chromosomal DNA is replicated, which occurs after the G1 preparation described.

questions.stem: A dividing cell has just completed replication of its chromosomal DNA. Before it can undergo mitosis, it synthesizes additional protein, including the microtubules that will be required for the mitotic spindle. Which of the following phases of the cell cycle is this cell in?

explanation.summary: G2 is the second gap phase in which microtubules for the mitotic spindle are made.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the second gap (G2) phase, which follows S phase, the cell synthesizes more protein, including microtubules, which are required for the mitotic spindle. The cell then undergoes mitosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytokinesis is the division of the cell at the end of M phase, not a preparatory interphase step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: G0 is the nondividing state and involves no preparation for mitosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G1 precedes DNA replication and is when messenger RNA and proteins for the remainder of the cycle are made.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S phase is the period of DNA replication that the cell has just completed.

questions.stem: During mitosis, a surveillance mechanism confirms that all chromosomes are attached to the spindle before the cell is allowed to trigger anaphase and proceed to cytokinesis. Which of the following cell cycle checkpoints performs this function?

explanation.summary: The metaphase/anaphase checkpoint verifies spindle attachment before anaphase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The three main checkpoints are G1/S, G2/M, and metaphase/anaphase. The metaphase/anaphase checkpoint asks whether all chromosomes are attached to the spindle; if so, anaphase is triggered and the cell proceeds to cytokinesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: G0 is the nondividing resting phase, not one of the three main checkpoints.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The G1/S checkpoint asks whether the environment is favorable for entering the cell cycle and proceeding to S phase; it occurs before DNA replication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The G2/M checkpoint asks whether all DNA is replicated and the environment is favorable before entering the mitotic phase, not whether chromosomes are attached to the spindle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An S checkpoint is not one of the three main checkpoints the brick describes.

questions.stem: A cultured cell is found to have incompletely replicated chromosomal DNA. Rather than proceeding into the mitotic phase, the cell halts its cycle and undergoes apoptosis. Which of the following checkpoints is most directly responsible for detecting this problem?

explanation.summary: The G2/M checkpoint asks whether all DNA has been replicated before mitosis begins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The G2/M checkpoint asks two questions: Is all DNA replicated? Is the environment favorable? Only if both are satisfied does the cell enter the mitotic phase. Incomplete replication halts the cycle and drives apoptosis, ridding the body of a 'bad' cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytokinesis follows anaphase and is not a checkpoint that evaluates DNA replication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick does not describe a G0 exit checkpoint; the three main checkpoints are G1/S, G2/M, and metaphase/anaphase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The G1/S checkpoint asks whether the environment is favorable to enter the cell cycle and proceed to S phase; DNA replication has not yet occurred at that point.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The metaphase/anaphase checkpoint asks whether all chromosomes are attached to the spindle, a question about mitosis rather than DNA replication.

questions.stem: A tumor is found to have loss-of-function mutations in both Rb and p53. Based on the roles of these proteins in the cell cycle, which of the following control points is most directly compromised in these cancer cells?

explanation.summary: Rb and p53 modulate the G1 restriction point.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rb and p53 modulate the G1 restriction point, the control point at which a cell in G1 commits to entering the cell cycle and proceeding to DNA synthesis. In cancerous cells, many checkpoints are broken, allowing uncontrolled division of cells with damaged DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytokinesis is the final division of the cell after anaphase and is not governed by Rb and p53.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA replication is the activity of S phase; Rb and p53 act at the G1 restriction point before S phase is entered.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Microtubule synthesis is a G2 event that supplies the mitotic spindle; it is not the point modulated by Rb and p53.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spindle attachment is evaluated at the metaphase/anaphase checkpoint, not by Rb and p53 at G1.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with breast cancer receives a taxane. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this drug interferes with cell replication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds tubulin and prevents microtubule formation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cross-links DNA chains independent of the cycle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits DNA polymerase during S phase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stabilizes microtubules and inhibits their disassembly

explanation.summary: Taxanes stabilize microtubules and block their disassembly, unlike vinca alkaloids.
explanation.whyCorrect: Taxanes promote microtubule assembly by enhancing the action of tubulin dimers, stabilizing existing microtubules, and inhibiting their disassembly. This interferes with the mitotic phase and inhibits cell replication. The vinca alkaloids act on the same structure in the opposite direction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding tubulin to inhibit microtubule formation is the mechanism of the vinca alkaloids, not the taxanes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cross-linking DNA independent of the cell cycle describes alkylating and platinum agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibition of DNA polymerase is the primary action of the pyrimidine analog cytarabine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preventing relegation of the cleaved DNA strand describes irinotecan, a topoisomerase I inhibitor.

questions.stem: A chemotherapeutic agent inhibits DNA synthesis by binding DNA and producing single- and double-strand breaks; to a lesser degree it also inhibits RNA and protein synthesis. The agent is classified as specific for the phase in which the cell makes the microtubules needed for the mitotic spindle. Which of the following is this agent?

explanation.summary: Bleomycin is the G2-phase agent that causes DNA strand breaks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bleomycin is classified as a G2-phase drug. It inhibits DNA synthesis, binds to DNA leading to single- and double-strand breaks, and also inhibits (to a lesser degree) RNA and protein synthesis. G2 is the phase in which microtubules for the mitotic spindle are synthesized.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytarabine is an S-phase pyrimidine analog whose primary action is inhibition of DNA polymerase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irinotecan is a topoisomerase I inhibitor acting in S phase, producing double-strand breaks through failed relegation rather than direct DNA binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate is an S-phase antimetabolite that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine is an M-phase microtubule inhibitor that binds tubulin.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man is started on busulfan, an alkylating agent, as part of his cancer regimen. Based on this drug's characteristic toxicity, which of the following adverse effects should be monitored for most closely during treatment?

explanation.summary: Busulfan, like bleomycin, is associated with pulmonary fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the ChemoMan summary, both bleomycin and busulfan are linked to pulmonary fibrosis. Busulfan is an alkylating agent that cross-links DNA independently of the cell cycle, but its signature toxicity is pulmonary rather than bladder, ear, eye, or heart.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiotoxicity is characteristic of doxorubicin and the anthracyclines.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemorrhagic cystitis is the signature toxicity of cyclophosphamide, a different alkylating agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Keratitis and conjunctivitis are associated with cytarabine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ototoxicity is characteristic of the platinum agents cisplatin and carboplatin.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man receives a nitrosourea as part of his chemotherapy regimen. This class of agent cross-links DNA chains and operates independently of the cell cycle. Which of the following adverse effects is most characteristically associated with this class?

explanation.summary: Nitrosoureas are associated with neurotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitrosoureas are cell cycle-independent alkylating agents (alongside busulfan and cyclophosphamide). In the ChemoMan summary of adverse effects, nitrosoureas are linked to neurotoxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Keratitis and conjunctivitis are associated with cytarabine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemorrhagic cystitis is the toxicity of cyclophosphamide, a different alkylating agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nephrotoxicity is characteristic of the platinum agents cisplatin and carboplatin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Severe acute and delayed diarrhea is the toxicity of irinotecan.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with lung cancer is treated with carboplatin. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds tubulin and arrests cells in metaphase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cross-links DNA chains independent of cell cycle phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase during S phase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits DNA polymerase after incorporation into DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prevents relegation of topoisomerase I-cleaved DNA

explanation.summary: Platinum agents cross-link DNA and act independently of the cell cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carboplatin and cisplatin are platinum agents. Like the alkylating agents, they cross-link DNA chains and cause them to break, inhibiting DNA replication and transcription, and they operate independently of the cell cycle. These drugs are used in many cancers including breast, bladder, leukemias/lymphomas, and lung cancers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding tubulin and arresting cells at metaphase describes the vinca alkaloids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase is the mechanism of methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Incorporation into DNA with inhibition of DNA polymerase describes cytarabine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Preventing relegation of the cleaved DNA strand describes irinotecan.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia develops bilateral eye pain, redness, tearing, and photophobia. Examination shows keratitis and conjunctivitis. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Cytarabine is associated with keratitis and conjunctivitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the ChemoMan summary, cytarabine (the 'CY' on the eyes) is linked to keratitis and conjunctivitis. Cytarabine is an S-phase pyrimidine analog used in leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irinotecan causes severe acute and delayed diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate's signature toxicity is myelosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer develops profuse watery diarrhea within hours of a chemotherapy infusion and then again about a week later. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Irinotecan causes severe acute and delayed diarrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: Irinotecan, a topoisomerase I inhibitor, is characteristically associated with severe acute and delayed diarrhea, as shown in the ChemoMan summary of adverse effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cisplatin causes nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cyclophosphamide causes hemorrhagic cystitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytarabine causes keratitis and conjunctivitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxorubicin causes cardiotoxicity.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with acute lymphoblastic leukemia is receiving methotrexate. Which of the following adverse effects is most characteristically associated with this drug and should be anticipated with routine monitoring?

explanation.summary: Methotrexate's signature toxicity is myelosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells, drugs that affect bone marrow cells result in myelosuppression. Methotrexate is the ChemoMan agent linked to myelosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemorrhagic cystitis is the toxicity of cyclophosphamide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ototoxicity is characteristic of cisplatin and carboplatin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peripheral neuropathy is characteristic of the vinca alkaloids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulmonary fibrosis is characteristic of bleomycin and busulfan.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy receiving vincristine for acute lymphoblastic leukemia is brought to clinic several weeks into treatment because his parents promptly noticed new tingling and numbness in his fingers and toes and some tripping. Examination confirms early peripheral neuropathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a platinum agent to the regimen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the vincristine dose to overcome tolerance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reassure the parents that the symptoms are unrelated

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduce the vincristine dose and continue monitoring

explanation.summary: Early-reported vincristine neuropathy is managed by dose reduction and continued monitoring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vincristine affects cells in the nerves, causing the peripheral neuropathy that produces tingling, numbness, and tripping. Because the parents reported it early, it can be managed with reduced doses and continued monitoring rather than abandoning treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding a platinum agent would introduce nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity and does nothing to address the vincristine neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increasing the dose would worsen the microtubule-mediated nerve injury.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Early neuropathy does not require permanently stopping the entire induction regimen; dose reduction with monitoring is the described approach.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The symptoms are a recognized adverse effect of vincristine, so reassurance that they are unrelated would be incorrect.

questions.stem: A medical student reviewing a formulary notices that several newer anticancer drugs have generic names ending in the suffix -mab. Which of the following best describes what this suffix indicates about a drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a modified autologous cell product

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a therapeutic monoclonal antibody

explanation.summary: The suffix -mab denotes a therapeutic monoclonal antibody.
explanation.whyCorrect: Any drug that ends in the suffix -mab is a therapeutic monoclonal antibody, which targets specific cell surface molecules. Examples in the brick are rituximab, bevacizumab, and trastuzumab.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CAR-T is a cell therapy rather than a drug and is not named with the -mab suffix.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The topoisomerase inhibitor in the brick is irinotecan, which does not carry the -mab suffix.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alkylating agents such as busulfan and cyclophosphamide are small-molecule cytotoxic drugs, not antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antimetabolites such as methotrexate and cytarabine are S-phase cytotoxic drugs, not antibodies.

questions.stem: A researcher studies why tumor cells, which are 'foreign' and should stimulate an immune response, often escape recognition and elimination. She finds that the cancer cells exploit inhibitory signaling pathways to 'turn off' the antitumor immune response. Which of the following terms best describes these pathways?

explanation.summary: Immune checkpoints are inhibitory pathways cancer cells use to turn off antitumor immunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The immune system plays an essential role in recognizing and eliminating tumor cells. However, cancer cells can use inhibitory signaling pathways called immune checkpoints to 'turn off' the antitumor immune response. Many immunotherapy drugs target these areas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angiogenesis is the abnormal blood vessel proliferation that accompanies tumor growth, targeted by bevacizumab.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Apoptosis is programmed cell death triggered when checkpoints detect damaged DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cell cycle checkpoints (G1/S, G2/M, metaphase/anaphase) verify readiness to divide; they are not immune-evasion pathways.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chimeric antigen receptors are engineered onto a patient's T cells in CAR-T therapy; they are a treatment, not a tumor evasion pathway.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with a B-cell malignancy undergoes a treatment in which his own T cells are collected, genetically modified to express a receptor specific for a cancer antigen, and then injected back into him. Which of the following best categorizes this treatment?

explanation.summary: CAR-T is a cell therapy using the patient's own (autologous) genetically modified T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chimeric antigen-receptor T cells (CAR-T) are a cell therapy rather than a drug. CAR-T cells are genetically modified autologous (belonging to the patient) T cells that, once modified and injected back, carry a specific receptor for the tumor cells, making it much easier for them to target the cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antiangiogenic therapy refers to bevacizumab binding VEGF, not modified T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytotoxic chemotherapy consists of drugs that interrupt the cell cycle, not reinfused cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hormone therapy such as tamoxifen acts on hormone receptors and involves no cell modification.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Monoclonal antibody therapy (e.g., rituximab against CD20) infuses an antibody drug, not modified cells.

questions.stem: In manufacturing chimeric antigen-receptor T cells, the antigen-binding domain from a B-cell receptor specific for a cancer antigen is fused onto a native receptor on the patient's T cells, creating a receptor with structures from different cell origins. Onto which of the following T-cell structures is the antigen-binding domain fused?

explanation.summary: The B-cell antigen-binding domain is fused to the T-cell CD3 receptor to form the chimeric receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: CAR-T cells are altered by taking the antigen-binding domain from a B-cell receptor specific for a cancer antigen and fusing it onto the patient's T-cell CD3 receptor. This creates a 'chimeric' receptor, meaning it has structures from different cell origins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD20 is a B-cell surface antigen targeted by rituximab; it is not the T-cell structure used in the fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HER2 is a tumor-cell receptor targeted by trastuzumab, not a T-cell receptor component.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tubulin is the target of microtubule inhibitors and has no role in the CAR-T construct.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VEGF is a circulating growth factor bound by bevacizumab; it is not a T-cell structure.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy develops nausea and vomiting after each treatment cycle. Which of the following best explains why cytotoxic agents commonly produce this adverse effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They activate immune checkpoints on T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: They bind circulating vascular endothelial growth factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: They cross-link DNA in cardiac myocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: They kill rapidly dividing cells of the gastric mucosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: They stabilize microtubules in peripheral nerves

explanation.summary: Chemotherapy kills any rapidly dividing cell, including gastric mucosa, causing nausea and vomiting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most chemotherapeutic drugs target any rapidly dividing cell, not just cancer cells, so they also kill normal cells that turn over rapidly. Drugs that affect the gastric mucosa lead to nausea and vomiting, just as drugs that affect bone marrow cells cause myelosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immune checkpoints are pathways cancer cells use to turn off immunity; they are not the cause of chemotherapy-induced nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Binding VEGF is the targeted action of bevacizumab and does not explain gastrointestinal toxicity of cytotoxic drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA damage in the heart relates to the cardiotoxicity of doxorubicin, not to nausea and vomiting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Effects on nerve cells explain the peripheral neuropathy of vinca alkaloids, not gastrointestinal symptoms.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with HER2-positive breast cancer asks why the monoclonal antibody in her regimen is expected to cause fewer and less intense adverse effects than the traditional cytotoxic drugs she previously received. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acts only on cells resting in G0

choices.label: B
choices.text: It cross-links DNA independent of the cell cycle

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits DNA polymerase only in tumor cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reacts against cancer cells in a more targeted way

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stabilizes microtubules only in tumor cells

explanation.summary: Monoclonal antibodies act more specifically on cancer cells, reducing adverse effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The more specific agents like monoclonal antibodies react against the cancer cells in a more targeted way, which reduces the number and intensity of adverse effects compared with cytotoxic drugs that attack any rapidly dividing cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nondividing G0 cells have minimal malignant potential and are not the target of anticancer drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cross-linking DNA independent of the cell cycle describes alkylating and platinum agents, which have significant toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA polymerase inhibition is the mechanism of cytarabine, which affects normal dividing cells as well.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microtubule stabilization is the mechanism of taxanes, cytotoxic agents that affect all rapidly dividing cells.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is asked to sort chemotherapeutic agents by cell cycle specificity. Which of the following agents cross-links DNA and exerts its effect independently of the phase of the cell cycle?

explanation.summary: Alkylating agents like cyclophosphamide are cell cycle-independent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytotoxic drugs are classified by the phase of the cell cycle they inhibit. The alkylating agents (busulfan, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, nitrosoureas) and the platinum agents operate independently of the cell cycle, cross-linking DNA chains and causing them to break.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleomycin is a G2-phase-specific agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irinotecan is a topoisomerase I inhibitor with S-phase cell cycle specificity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate is an S-phase-specific antimetabolite.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine is an M-phase-specific microtubule inhibitor.

questions.stem: Leukemia cells exposed to vincristine in culture are examined under the microscope. Because the drug binds tubulin and disrupts formation of the mitotic spindle, the cells accumulate at a specific point in the cycle. At which of the following points are the cells arrested?

explanation.summary: Vinca alkaloids arrest cells at metaphase by preventing spindle formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vinca alkaloids bind to tubulin and inhibit microtubule formation, therefore arresting the cell at metaphase by disrupting formation of the mitotic spindle. They are specific for the M phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytokinesis follows anaphase; cells cannot reach it because the metaphase/anaphase checkpoint is never satisfied without a spindle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Arrest at the G1-to-S transition is produced by the S-phase antimetabolites such as methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G2 is the phase in which microtubules are synthesized and where bleomycin acts; vincristine acts on spindle assembly during M phase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S-phase DNA synthesis is the target of cytarabine and irinotecan, not the microtubule inhibitors.
